about: Every revision proposed by the 2026-10-13 difficulty audit and what happened to it. Proposals were finalized by one AI pass and checked by a separate AI pass that had not seen the finalization brief. Applied revisions are AI checked, not human verified.
reviewer: Claude (AI), two independent passes: finalize, then a separate check

entries.subject: Biochemistry/Genetics

original.title: Vitamin K-dependent clotting factors
original.explanation: All four coagulation factors require vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation for calcium binding and effective coagulation.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Biochemistry Jan 2025(1).pdf; Vitamins > Vitamin K, PDF p. 130

proposal.title: Vitamin K-dependent proteins
proposal.why: Breaks the four-numeral factor series; proteins C and S are definitely gamma-carboxylated vitamin K-dependent proteins, and the reviewer note already flags them.
proposal.changes: Title broadened from clotting factors to vitamin K-dependent proteins; Factor II written as Prothrombin; Factor VII and Factor X replaced by Protein C and Protein S.

entries.auditNote: 'Factor II/VII/IX/X' is a numbered series and one of the most memorized lists in medicine.
entries.reason: Title now covers six classic proteins (II, VII, IX, X, C, S); keeping IX but dropping VII and X makes the set arbitrary, and any VII or X tile elsewhere on a 16-tile board would fit equally well.

attempted.title: Vitamin K-dependent proteins
attempted.explanation: Each protein requires vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation of glutamate residues to bind calcium and function.
attempted.detail: Vitamin K is the cofactor for gamma-glutamyl carboxylase, which modifies procoagulant factors II, VII, IX and X and the anticoagulant proteins C and S. Warfarin blocks vitamin K epoxide reductase and lowers all of them. The group is broader than clotting factors: proteins C and S are anticoagulants, which is why early warfarin therapy can cause a transient hypercoagulable state and skin necrosis.
tileNotes: Prothrombin is factor II, the precursor of thrombin. It needs gamma-carboxylation to bind phospholipid surfaces through calcium.
Factor IX is the intrinsic pathway serine protease deficient in hemophilia B. It is one of the vitamin K-dependent procoagulant factors.

Protein C is an anticoagulant that, once activated, inactivates factors Va and VIIIa. Its synthesis requires vitamin K-dependent carboxylation, and its short half-life explains warfarin skin necrosis.
Protein S is the cofactor for activated protein C. It is also gamma-carboxylated in a vitamin K-dependent reaction.

problems: Title now covers six classic proteins (II, VII, IX, X, C, S); keeping IX but dropping VII and X makes the set arbitrary, and any VII or X tile elsewhere on a 16-tile board would fit equally well.
check.note: Accurate but the broadened title makes the four-member choice arbitrary.

entries.subject: Biochemistry/Genetics

original.title: Fat-soluble vitamins
original.explanation: These four vitamins depend on intact intestinal lipid absorption for dietary uptake and can be deficient in fat malabsorption.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Biochemistry Jan 2025(1).pdf; Vitamins > Introduction to Vitamins, PDF p. 127; Lipid Metabolism > Lipid Digestion and Absorption, PDF p. 83

proposal.why: Removes the shared 'Vitamin' stem and letter series using standard chemical names of each vitamin, so players must recall the identity of each compound.
proposal.changes: Vitamin A -> Retinol, Vitamin D -> Cholecalciferol (D3), Vitamin E -> Tocopherol, Vitamin K -> Phylloquinone (K1).

entries.auditNote: ADEK is the most familiar vitamin list, and the 'Vitamin _' format reveals the set.

revised.title: Fat-soluble vitamins
revised.explanation: These are the standard chemical forms of vitamins A, D, E and K, which depend on intact intestinal fat absorption.
revised.detail: Vitamins A, D, E and K are absorbed with dietary lipid in micelles and carried in chylomicrons, so they become deficient in fat malabsorption (cystic fibrosis, pancreatic insufficiency, celiac disease, cholestasis). They are stored in tissue and can accumulate to toxic levels, unlike most water-soluble vitamins. Vitamin D can also be made in skin and vitamin K by gut bacteria, but dietary uptake of both still requires fat absorption.
tileNotes: Retinol is vitamin A, needed for rhodopsin in rod photoreceptors and for epithelial differentiation.
Cholecalciferol is vitamin D3, made in skin with UV light or absorbed from the diet, then hydroxylated in liver and kidney.
Tocopherol is vitamin E, a lipid-soluble antioxidant that protects membranes from peroxidation.
Phylloquinone is vitamin K1, the plant form of vitamin K required for gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors.

entries.changeSummary: Vitamin letter names replaced with their standard chemical names (retinol, cholecalciferol, tocopherol, phylloquinone).
entries.checkNote: Chemical names remove the letter giveaway; cholecalciferol and phylloquinone are the standard D3 and K1 forms and all four remain fat-soluble vitamins.

check.note: Chemical names remove the letter giveaway; cholecalciferol and phylloquinone are the standard D3 and K1 forms and all four remain fat-soluble vitamins.

entries.subject: Biochemistry/Genetics

original.title: Enzymes requiring copper
original.explanation: Copper is a required cofactor for each, linking it to oxidative phosphorylation, pigment formation, connective-tissue cross-linking, and cytosolic antioxidant defense.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Biochemistry Jan 2025(1).pdf; Vitamins > Trace Elements, PDF p. 140; Connective Tissue > Menkes Disease, PDF p. 28

proposal.why: Removes the 'Cu' chemical symbol that leaks the title while keeping the same specific enzyme (SOD1 is the cytosolic Cu/Zn isoform).

entries.auditNote: The 'Cu/Zn' label in tile 4 announces copper; otherwise the set needs genuine recall.

revised.title: Enzymes requiring copper
revised.explanation: Copper is a required cofactor for each enzyme, linking it to oxidative phosphorylation, pigment formation, collagen cross-linking and cytosolic antioxidant defense.
revised.detail: Copper deficiency, as in Menkes disease, impairs all of these enzymes, which explains its combination of neurologic decline, hypopigmentation, connective tissue fragility and oxidative injury. Superoxide dismutase 1 is the cytosolic copper-zinc isoform; mitochondrial superoxide dismutase 2 uses manganese instead and would not fit. Zinc-dependent enzymes such as carbonic anhydrase are a common look-alike group.
tileNotes: Cytochrome c oxidase is complex IV of the electron transport chain. Its copper centers transfer electrons to oxygen.
Tyrosinase converts tyrosine toward melanin. Copper is its catalytic metal, so copper deficiency causes hypopigmentation.
Lysyl oxidase cross-links collagen and elastin. It is copper-dependent, and its loss in Menkes disease weakens connective tissue and vessels.
Superoxide dismutase 1 is the cytosolic copper-zinc enzyme that converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide. Copper is its catalytic metal.

entries.changeSummary: Tile 4 renamed from 'Cu/Zn superoxide dismutase (SOD1)' to 'Superoxide dismutase 1', the same enzyme without the copper symbol.
entries.checkNote: Removing the copper symbol from tile 4 removes a real giveaway; SOD1 is correctly the cytosolic Cu/Zn isoform.

check.note: Removing the copper symbol from tile 4 removes a real giveaway; SOD1 is correctly the cytosolic Cu/Zn isoform.

original.title: Enzymes that use NADPH
original.explanation: These enzymes use NADPH as reducing power in glutathione regeneration, cholesterol synthesis, fatty acid synthesis, and the phagocyte oxidative burst, respectively.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Biochemistry Jan 2025(1).pdf; Oxidative Stress > Pentose Phosphate Pathway and Respiratory Burst, PDF pp. 59-60

proposal.why: Removes the title leak while naming the same enzyme by its standard alternate name (phagocyte oxidase, NOX2).

entries.auditNote: 'NADPH oxidase' contains the title word and gives the link away; the rest requires recalling NADPH-consuming reactions.
entries.reason: 'Phagocyte oxidase (NOX2)' is not the name students know for this enzyme, so the swap trades a title leak for an unfamiliar synonym.

entries.subject: Biochemistry/Genetics

original.title: Findings associated with primary ciliary dyskinesia
original.explanation: Dysfunctional motile cilia impair airway clearance and sperm motility; abnormal embryonic nodal cilia can disrupt organ laterality.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Biochemistry Jan 2025(1).pdf; Cell Biology > Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia, PDF p. 9

proposal.why: Situs inversus is the giveaway; chronic otitis media is a very common, certain PCD manifestation, so players must discriminate PCD from cystic fibrosis rather than spot a buzzword.

entries.auditNote: Situs inversus with bronchiectasis and sinusitis is the instant Kartagener picture.

revised.title: Findings associated with primary ciliary dyskinesia
revised.explanation: Defective motile cilia impair mucociliary clearance in the airways, sinuses and middle ear and impair sperm motility.
revised.detail: Primary ciliary dyskinesia is usually autosomal recessive and often involves dynein arm defects. Poor clearance causes chronic wet cough, bronchiectasis, chronic rhinosinusitis and recurrent or chronic otitis media from childhood, and immotile sperm cause male infertility. Cystic fibrosis shares bronchiectasis, sinusitis and male infertility, but CF infertility comes from absent vas deferens rather than immotile sperm, and chronic otitis media is far more typical of PCD. Situs inversus occurs in about half of patients (Kartagener syndrome).
tileNotes: Bronchiectasis is permanent airway dilation from repeated infection when cilia cannot clear mucus.
Recurrent sinusitis reflects failed ciliary clearance of the paranasal sinuses and is nearly universal in PCD.
Chronic otitis media results from poor ciliary clearance of the middle ear and eustachian tube and is a typical childhood feature of PCD.
Male infertility occurs because sperm flagella share the defective axoneme and are immotile.

entries.changeSummary: Tile 3 'Situs inversus' replaced with 'Chronic otitis media'.
entries.checkNote: Chronic otitis media is a standard PCD feature and the CF contrast in the detail is correct.

check.note: Chronic otitis media is a standard PCD feature and the CF contrast in the detail is correct.

original.title: Characteristic clues for Tay-Sachs disease
original.explanation: Deficient hexosaminidase A allows GM2 storage, producing characteristic retinal and lysosomal findings.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Biochemistry Jan 2025(1).pdf; Lysosomal Storage Diseases > Tay-Sachs Disease, PDF p. 14

proposal.why: Replaces the most defining tile with a classic, certain Tay-Sachs clinical sign (hyperacusis/exaggerated startle), so players must recall the presentation and separate it from Niemann-Pick.

entries.auditNote: 'Hexosaminidase A deficiency' names the disease's defining enzyme and makes the group instant.

revised.title: Characteristic clues for Tay-Sachs disease
revised.explanation: Hexosaminidase A deficiency causes neuronal GM2 storage, producing hyperacusis, a cherry-red macula and lamellated lysosomes.
revised.detail: Tay-Sachs disease is an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disease, more common in Ashkenazi Jewish populations, with progressive neurodegeneration beginning in infancy. An exaggerated startle to sound is an early sign. Niemann-Pick disease also has a cherry-red macula but has hepatosplenomegaly and foamy macrophages, while Tay-Sachs has no hepatosplenomegaly.
tileNotes: An exaggerated startle response (hyperacusis) to noise is a classic early neurologic sign in infants with Tay-Sachs disease.
GM2 ganglioside accumulates because hexosaminidase A cannot degrade it, mainly in neurons.
A cherry-red macula appears because lipid-laden retinal ganglion cells surround the fovea, which lacks them.
Onion-skin lysosomes are concentric lamellated lysosomal inclusions of stored ganglioside seen on electron microscopy.

entries.changeSummary: Tile 1 'Hexosaminidase A deficiency' replaced with 'Exaggerated startle response'.
entries.checkNote: Hyperacusis/exaggerated startle is a classic Tay-Sachs sign and removing the enzyme name requires more reasoning.

check.note: Hyperacusis/exaggerated startle is a classic Tay-Sachs sign and removing the enzyme name requires more reasoning.

original.title: Characteristic Gaucher disease findings
original.explanation: Glucocerebroside storage in macrophages and involvement of bone, liver, and spleen explain these associations.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Biochemistry Jan 2025(1).pdf; Lysosomal Storage Diseases > Gaucher Disease, PDF p. 18

proposal.why: Swaps the pathognomonic histology tile for a common, certain Gaucher finding (cytopenias from hypersplenism and marrow infiltration), forcing discrimination from sickle cell disease.

entries.auditNote: Crumpled-paper macrophages are the Gaucher buzzword and give the group away instantly.

revised.title: Characteristic Gaucher disease findings
revised.explanation: Glucocerebroside-laden macrophages infiltrate the marrow, bone, liver and spleen, producing cytopenias, bone disease and organomegaly.
revised.detail: Gaucher disease is an autosomal recessive deficiency of glucocerebrosidase and the most common lysosomal storage disease. Storage macrophages (Gaucher cells) cause hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia from hypersplenism and marrow infiltration, bone pain crises, avascular necrosis of the femoral head and osteopenia. Sickle cell disease can also cause bone crises and avascular necrosis, but it causes hemolytic anemia and autosplenectomy rather than splenomegaly with pancytopenia in adults.
tileNotes: Pancytopenia results from hypersplenism and replacement of the marrow by Gaucher cells.
Bone crises are episodes of severe bone pain caused by marrow infiltration and bone infarction.
Avascular necrosis of the femoral head is a classic skeletal complication of Gaucher disease.
Hepatosplenomegaly reflects accumulation of glucocerebroside-laden macrophages in the liver and spleen.

entries.changeSummary: Tile 1 'Crumpled-paper macrophages' replaced with 'Pancytopenia'.
entries.checkNote: Pancytopenia is a standard Gaucher finding; removing the pathognomonic histology tile adds difficulty.

check.note: Pancytopenia is a standard Gaucher finding; removing the pathognomonic histology tile adds difficulty.

original.title: Diagnostic associations of metachromatic leukodystrophy
original.explanation: Deficient arylsulfatase A prevents sulfatide breakdown; storage causes demyelination and metachromatic staining of macrophage vacuoles.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Biochemistry Jan 2025(1).pdf; Lysosomal Storage Diseases > Metachromatic Leukodystrophy, PDF p. 16

proposal.why: Removes the title word; progressive gait disturbance/ataxia is a certain, characteristic presentation of late-infantile and juvenile MLD.

entries.auditNote: 'Metachromatic' in tile 4 repeats the title; arylsulfatase A also cues the disease directly.

revised.title: Diagnostic associations of metachromatic leukodystrophy
revised.explanation: Arylsulfatase A deficiency prevents sulfatide breakdown, and sulfatide storage demyelinates the central and peripheral nervous systems, causing ataxia.
revised.detail: Metachromatic leukodystrophy is an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disease. Sulfatide accumulates in myelin-forming cells, causing demyelination in both the brain and peripheral nerves, which presents with ataxia, gait disturbance and later dementia. Krabbe disease also demyelinates both systems but is caused by galactocerebrosidase deficiency with globoid cells, and adrenoleukodystrophy is a peroxisomal disorder with very long chain fatty acid accumulation.
tileNotes: Arylsulfatase A is the lysosomal enzyme deficient in metachromatic leukodystrophy.
Sulfatide (cerebroside sulfate) accumulates because arylsulfatase A cannot remove its sulfate group.
Sulfatide storage damages oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells, so demyelination involves both central and peripheral nerves.
Ataxia and gait disturbance are typical presenting features in late-infantile and juvenile metachromatic leukodystrophy.

entries.changeSummary: Tile 4 'Metachromatic macrophage vacuoles' replaced with 'Ataxia'.
entries.checkNote: Ataxia is a standard MLD presentation and removes the 'metachromatic' giveaway.

check.note: Ataxia is a standard MLD presentation and removes the 'metachromatic' giveaway.

entries.subject: Biochemistry/Genetics

original.title: Classical Ehlers-Danlos findings
original.explanation: Classical EDS combines joint and skin extensibility with tissue fragility, abnormal scarring, and poor healing.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Biochemistry Jan 2025(1).pdf; Connective Tissue > Ehlers Danlos Syndrome, PDF p. 27

proposal.why: Replaces the most obvious tile with a certain classical EDS feature that overlaps scurvy and bleeding disorders, requiring discrimination.

entries.auditNote: Hypermobile joints plus stretchy skin is the instant EDS picture.

revised.title: Classical Ehlers-Danlos findings
revised.explanation: Defective collagen in classical Ehlers-Danlos syndrome makes skin and vessels fragile and stretchy and impairs healing.
revised.detail: Classical Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is usually caused by type V collagen mutations (COL5A1, COL5A2). It combines skin hyperextensibility, widened atrophic scars, easy bruising and poor wound healing with joint hypermobility. Scurvy and bleeding disorders also cause easy bruising and poor healing, but they do not cause hyperextensible skin or atrophic scars.
tileNotes: Easy bruising reflects fragile capillaries and perivascular connective tissue in classical Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
Hyperextensible skin stretches beyond normal and recoils, a major feature of classical Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
Atrophic scars are wide, thin scars that form because collagen in healing skin is defective.
Poor wound healing results from abnormal collagen fibril formation, so wounds split and heal slowly.

entries.changeSummary: Tile 1 'Joint hypermobility' replaced with 'Easy bruising'.
entries.checkNote: Easy bruising is a standard classical EDS feature; COL5A1/COL5A2 attribution is correct.

check.note: Easy bruising is a standard classical EDS feature; COL5A1/COL5A2 attribution is correct.

entries.subject: Biochemistry/Genetics

original.title: Characteristic Menkes disease clues
original.explanation: Impaired copper export from enterocytes (ATP7A) causes systemic copper deficiency, with characteristic hair and pigmentation changes and low circulating copper and ceruloplasmin.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Biochemistry Jan 2025(1).pdf; Connective Tissue > Menkes Disease, PDF p. 28

proposal.why: Removes the 'kinky hair' giveaway; hypotonia is a certain, characteristic infantile Menkes finding, leaving players to distinguish Menkes from Wilson disease.

entries.auditNote: Kinky hair names the disease; the copper labs add a Wilson look-alike only once that tile is removed.

revised.title: Characteristic Menkes disease clues
revised.explanation: Defective ATP7A copper export causes systemic copper deficiency, producing infantile hypotonia, hypopigmentation and low serum copper and ceruloplasmin.
revised.detail: Menkes disease is an X-linked recessive disorder of ATP7A, so copper absorbed by enterocytes cannot reach the circulation. Copper-dependent enzymes fail, causing hypotonia, seizures, developmental regression, hypopigmentation, kinky hair and vascular fragility in male infants. Wilson disease (ATP7B) also has low ceruloplasmin, but it presents later with copper overload in the liver and brain.
tileNotes: Hypotonia is a characteristic neurologic finding in infants with Menkes disease, from copper-deficient neurodegeneration.
Hypopigmentation of skin and hair results from reduced activity of tyrosinase, a copper-dependent enzyme.
Serum copper is low because ATP7A defects block copper export from enterocytes into the blood.
Ceruloplasmin is low because little copper reaches the liver to be incorporated into it.

entries.changeSummary: Tile 1 'Kinky brittle hair' replaced with 'Hypotonia'.
entries.checkNote: Hypotonia is a characteristic Menkes finding and removing kinky hair removes the giveaway.

check.note: Hypotonia is a characteristic Menkes finding and removing kinky hair removes the giveaway.

original.title: B vitamins supplying PDH and alpha-KGDH cofactors
original.explanation: These vitamins supply TPP, FAD, NAD+, and CoA for both the pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complexes; lipoic acid is the additional nonvitamin cofactor.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Biochemistry Jan 2025(1).pdf; Energy Production > Pyruvate Dehydrogenase Complex and TCA Cycle, PDF pp. 36-37

proposal.why: Removes the 'Vitamin B_' series by using the standard names, so players must recall each vitamin's cofactor role rather than read a number sequence.
proposal.changes: Vitamin B1 -> Thiamine, B2 -> Riboflavin, B3 -> Niacin, B5 -> Pantothenic acid.

entries.auditNote: 'Vitamin B1/B2/B3/B5' is a numbered series that groups instantly regardless of the PDH link.

revised.title: B vitamins supplying PDH and alpha-KGDH cofactors
revised.explanation: These vitamins supply TPP, FAD, NAD+ and CoA for both the pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complexes.
revised.detail: Pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase share the same five cofactors: thiamine pyrophosphate, lipoic acid, CoA, FAD and NAD+. Four come from B vitamins (B1, B5, B2 and B3); lipoic acid is the fifth, nonvitamin cofactor. Pyridoxine (B6) and biotin (B7) are not used by these complexes; biotin is the cofactor for carboxylases such as pyruvate carboxylase.
tileNotes: Thiamine (B1) becomes thiamine pyrophosphate, which decarboxylates the alpha-keto acid substrate.
Riboflavin (B2) becomes FAD, which reoxidizes the lipoamide arm in the dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase step.
Niacin (B3) becomes NAD+, the final electron acceptor that leaves the complex as NADH.
Pantothenic acid (B5) is part of coenzyme A, which accepts the acyl group to form acetyl-CoA or succinyl-CoA.

entries.changeSummary: Vitamin B number names replaced with thiamine, riboflavin, niacin and pantothenic acid.
entries.checkNote: Vitamin names remove the B1-B5 numbering giveaway; cofactor roles are correct.

check.note: Vitamin names remove the B1-B5 numbering giveaway; cofactor roles are correct.

entries.subject: Biochemistry/Genetics

original.title: Hormones that increase PEPCK in the source
original.explanation: These four hormones increase PEP carboxykinase per the source, supporting increased glucose production.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Biochemistry Jan 2025(1).pdf; Carbohydrates > Gluconeogenesis, PDF p. 43

proposal.title: Hormones that induce PEPCK expression
proposal.why: 'In the source' makes the category depend on a citation rather than physiology; glucagon and epinephrine (via cAMP), glucocorticoids and thyroid hormone are all established inducers of PEPCK transcription.

entries.auditNote: Players will group these as counterregulatory hormones, where growth hormone is the expected fourth; the title 'in the source' is not a defensible category statement.

revised.title: Hormones that induce PEPCK expression
revised.explanation: Each hormone increases transcription of the gene for PEP carboxykinase, a key regulated step of gluconeogenesis.
revised.detail: PEP carboxykinase converts oxaloacetate to phosphoenolpyruvate and is regulated mainly by changes in gene expression. Glucagon and epinephrine raise cAMP and activate CREB, cortisol acts through the glucocorticoid receptor, and thyroid hormone acts through its nuclear receptor; all increase PEPCK transcription. Insulin represses PEPCK transcription. Growth hormone is a counterregulatory hormone but is not a classic PEPCK inducer, so this group is narrower than counterregulatory hormones.
tileNotes: Glucagon raises hepatic cAMP, which activates CREB and increases PEPCK transcription during fasting.
Cortisol binds the glucocorticoid receptor, which acts on glucocorticoid response elements of the PEPCK gene.
Epinephrine also raises hepatic cAMP, inducing PEPCK by the same CREB pathway as glucagon.
Thyroid hormone (T3) acts through its nuclear receptor to increase PEPCK gene transcription.

entries.changeSummary: Title changed from 'Hormones that increase PEPCK in the source' to 'Hormones that induce PEPCK expression'; tiles unchanged.
entries.checkNote: Title now states a general mechanism instead of citing the source; tiles are accepted PEPCK inducers, but 'rate-limiting' was corrected.

problems: Explanation called PEPCK a rate-limiting step of gluconeogenesis; standard teaching names fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase as rate-limiting, so this was softened.
check.note: Title now states a general mechanism instead of citing the source; tiles are accepted PEPCK inducers, but 'rate-limiting' was corrected.

fixes.explanation: Each hormone increases transcription of the gene for PEP carboxykinase, a key regulated step of gluconeogenesis.

original.title: Glycogen storage diseases with muscle involvement
original.explanation: GSD types II, III, IV, and V involve muscle, although the affected muscle types and presentations differ.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Biochemistry Jan 2025(1).pdf; Glycogen > Overview of Glycogen Storage Diseases, PDF p. 69

proposal.why: Tarui disease (GSD VII, muscle PFK deficiency) is unambiguously a muscle GSD; replacing Andersen removes a tile usually taught as hepatic and reduces interchangeability with BCH-015.

entries.auditNote: Andersen disease is taught mainly as a hepatic GSD (and sits in BCH-015), while Tarui disease, a classic muscle GSD, is missing.
entries.reason: Tarui disease (GSD VII) is beyond the standard board-review glycogen storage disease list, so it would be obscure for most players, and the swap adds no reasoning.

entries.subject: Biochemistry/Genetics

original.title: Pancreatic zymogens activated by trypsin
original.explanation: Trypsin proteolytically activates each pancreatic precursor into an active digestive protease.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Biochemistry Jan 2025(1).pdf; Protein Metabolism > Protein Digestion and Absorption, PDF p. 103

proposal.why: Breaks the carboxypeptidase A/B pair; prophospholipase A2 is a pancreatic zymogen certainly activated by trypsin and links to pancreatitis pathophysiology.

entries.auditNote: Three 'Pro-' zymogens plus an A/B pair make the set mechanical to sort.
entries.reason: Detail says trypsinogen does not belong, but trypsin also activates trypsinogen (autocatalytic positive feedback), so the title technically includes it. Procarboxypeptidase B fits equally well and is now missing alongside procarboxypeptidase A, making the set feel arbitrary.

attempted.title: Pancreatic zymogens activated by trypsin
attempted.explanation: Trypsin cleaves each inactive pancreatic precursor in the duodenum to release the active digestive enzyme.
attempted.detail: The pancreas secretes digestive enzymes as inactive zymogens to protect itself. Enteropeptidase (enterokinase) on the duodenal brush border activates trypsinogen to trypsin, and trypsin then activates the other protease zymogens and prophospholipase A2. Premature trypsin activation inside the pancreas drives acute pancreatitis. Trypsinogen itself and pepsinogen (activated by gastric acid) do not belong to this group.
tileNotes: Chymotrypsinogen is cleaved by trypsin to chymotrypsin, an endopeptidase that cuts after aromatic residues.
Proelastase is cleaved by trypsin to elastase, which digests elastin and other proteins.
Procarboxypeptidase A is cleaved by trypsin to carboxypeptidase A, which removes C-terminal amino acids.
Prophospholipase A2 is cleaved by trypsin to phospholipase A2, which hydrolyzes dietary phospholipids and contributes to tissue injury in pancreatitis.

problems: Detail says trypsinogen does not belong, but trypsin also activates trypsinogen (autocatalytic positive feedback), so the title technically includes it.
Procarboxypeptidase B fits equally well and is now missing alongside procarboxypeptidase A, making the set feel arbitrary.
check.note: Detail contains a factual error about trypsinogen and the set leaves out an equally valid sibling.

entries.subject: Biochemistry/Genetics

original.title: Products derived from tyrosine
original.explanation: These signaling molecules and the pigment melanin are downstream of tyrosine metabolism.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Biochemistry Jan 2025(1).pdf; Protein Metabolism > Phenylalanine, Tyrosine, and Catecholamines, PDF p. 105

proposal.why: Removes the consecutive catecholamine trio; thyroxine is certainly derived from tyrosine residues of thyroglobulin, so players must recognize tyrosine as the shared precursor.

entries.auditNote: The catecholamine pathway plus melanin is a drilled diagram, and thyroid hormone is a common tyrosine product players may expect.
entries.reason: Dopamine and epinephrine are kept but norepinephrine, the intermediate between them, is dropped; norepinephrine (or T3, DOPA) fits equally well, so the set feels arbitrary and invites ambiguity on a board.

attempted.title: Products derived from tyrosine
attempted.explanation: Tyrosine is the precursor for catecholamines, thyroid hormones and melanin.
attempted.detail: Tyrosine comes from the diet or from phenylalanine hydroxylation. Tyrosine hydroxylase makes DOPA, leading to dopamine, norepinephrine and epinephrine; tyrosinase makes DOPA and dopaquinone for melanin; and iodinated tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin form T3 and T4. Tryptophan-derived products (serotonin, melatonin, niacin) are the main look-alike group.
tileNotes: Dopamine is formed from tyrosine via DOPA by tyrosine hydroxylase and DOPA decarboxylase.
Thyroxine (T4) is made by iodinating and coupling tyrosine residues within thyroglobulin.
Epinephrine is made from tyrosine through dopamine and norepinephrine, with the final methylation in the adrenal medulla.
Melanin is made from tyrosine by tyrosinase in melanocytes.

problems: Dopamine and epinephrine are kept but norepinephrine, the intermediate between them, is dropped; norepinephrine (or T3, DOPA) fits equally well, so the set feels arbitrary and invites ambiguity on a board.
check.note: Breaking the catecholamine chain leaves an equally valid missing member.

entries.subject: Biochemistry/Genetics

original.title: Diagnostic clues for maple syrup urine disease
original.explanation: Deficient branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase causes accumulation of BCAAs and their ketoacids, with characteristic urine odor and neurologic dysfunction.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Biochemistry Jan 2025(1).pdf; Protein Metabolism > Branched Chain Amino Acids, PDF p. 110

proposal.why: Removes the repeated 'Elevated branched-chain' stem; cerebral edema is a certain, clinically important complication of acute MSUD decompensation.

entries.auditNote: Two 'Elevated branched-chain …' tiles plus sweet urine make MSUD instant.

revised.title: Features of maple syrup urine disease
revised.explanation: Branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency causes accumulation of leucine, isoleucine and valine, with a sweet urine odor and neurotoxicity.
revised.detail: Maple syrup urine disease is an autosomal recessive defect of the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex. Newborns present with poor feeding, vomiting, encephalopathy and abnormal tone or dystonia, and the urine and cerumen smell like maple syrup. Leucine is the most neurotoxic metabolite, and acute decompensation can cause life-threatening cerebral edema. Treatment restricts branched-chain amino acids, and some patients respond to thiamine.
tileNotes: Sweet-smelling urine comes from accumulated branched-chain ketoacids and their derivatives, giving the maple syrup odor.
Plasma leucine, isoleucine and valine are elevated because their ketoacids cannot be oxidatively decarboxylated.
Cerebral edema is a dangerous complication of acute metabolic decompensation, driven mainly by high leucine.
Dystonia and other abnormal tone are neurologic manifestations of branched-chain amino acid toxicity in affected infants.

original.title: Diagnostic clues for cystinuria
original.explanation: Failure of cystine reabsorption causes urinary cystine accumulation and crystallization; the stone pattern and qualitative test are diagnostic clues.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Biochemistry Jan 2025(1).pdf; Protein Metabolism > Cystinuria and Organic Acidemias, PDF p. 109

proposal.why: Removes the tile that restates the diagnosis. Cystine stones are a classic cause of staghorn calculi, which also makes players think of struvite.

entries.auditNote: Hexagonal crystals are instantly diagnostic, and 'Increased urinary cystine' just restates the title.
entries.reason: Staghorn calculi belong much more classically to struvite (urease-producing infection) stones than to cystinuria and are not a diagnostic clue for cystinuria, as the detail itself concedes.

attempted.title: Diagnostic clues for cystinuria
attempted.explanation: Defective renal reabsorption of cystine leads to cystine crystals and recurrent stones, which can be staghorn, and a positive nitroprusside screen.
attempted.detail: Cystinuria is an autosomal recessive defect of the proximal tubule transporter for cystine, ornithine, lysine and arginine. Cystine is poorly soluble, so it forms hexagonal crystals and recurrent stones beginning in childhood, and the stones can grow into staghorn calculi. Struvite stones from urease-producing bacteria are the more common cause of staghorn calculi, so the hexagonal crystals and nitroprusside test point to cystine.
tileNotes: Hexagonal crystals in urine are characteristic of cystine.
Recurrent kidney stones, often starting in childhood, result from persistent cystine supersaturation.
Cystine stones can grow to fill the renal pelvis and calyces as staghorn calculi, like struvite stones.
The cyanide-nitroprusside test turns red-purple when urinary cystine is elevated and is used as a screening test.

problems: Staghorn calculi belong much more classically to struvite (urease-producing infection) stones than to cystinuria and are not a diagnostic clue for cystinuria, as the detail itself concedes.
check.note: Staghorn calculi is a struvite clue, not a cystinuria diagnostic clue.

original.title: Source-described sideroblastic anemia findings
original.explanation: Defective heme production traps iron in erythroid mitochondria, producing this marrow, blood-film, red-cell-size, and iron pattern.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Biochemistry Jan 2025(1).pdf; Porphyrias > Heme Synthesis Regulation and Sideroblastic Anemia, PDF p. 121; Vitamins > Vitamin B6, PDF p. 136

proposal.title: Classic sideroblastic anemia findings
proposal.why: 'Source-described' is internal wording that does not belong in a player-facing title.

entries.auditNote: Ringed sideroblasts anchor it quickly, but stippling and microcytosis still need separating from lead poisoning and iron deficiency.

revised.title: Classic sideroblastic anemia findings
revised.explanation: Defective heme synthesis traps iron in erythroblast mitochondria, producing ringed sideroblasts, stippled microcytic red cells and iron overload labs.
revised.detail: Sideroblastic anemia results from impaired protoporphyrin synthesis, as with X-linked ALA synthase defects, alcohol, lead, isoniazid or vitamin B6 deficiency. Iron enters the mitochondria but cannot be incorporated into heme, so it accumulates around the nucleus as ringed sideroblasts, while red cells are microcytic and serum iron and ferritin rise. Iron deficiency is also microcytic but has low serum iron, and lead poisoning shares basophilic stippling.
tileNotes: Ringed sideroblasts are erythroid precursors with iron-laden mitochondria surrounding the nucleus, seen with Prussian blue stain of marrow.
Basophilic stippling is coarse blue granules of residual ribosomal RNA in red cells, seen in sideroblastic anemia and lead poisoning.
Microcytosis occurs because hemoglobin production is reduced when heme cannot be made.
Serum iron is elevated because iron is absorbed and delivered but not used for heme synthesis.

revised.title: Precipitants of acute intermittent porphyria attacks
revised.explanation: Each exposure induces hepatic ALA synthase, increasing porphyrin precursor production when porphobilinogen deaminase is deficient.
revised.detail: Acute intermittent porphyria is an autosomal dominant deficiency of porphobilinogen deaminase. Anything that raises hepatic heme demand, especially CYP450-inducing drugs, derepresses ALA synthase, so ALA and porphobilinogen accumulate and cause abdominal pain, neuropathy and psychiatric symptoms. Other classic triggers include sulfonamides, fasting and progesterone. Treatment is glucose and hemin, which suppress ALA synthase.
tileNotes: Barbiturates induce CYP450 enzymes, raising heme demand and ALA synthase activity.
Phenytoin is an enzyme-inducing antiseizure drug that can precipitate attacks.
Alcohol induces hepatic ALA synthase and CYP450 enzymes and is a recognized trigger.
Smoking induces hepatic CYP enzymes and is a recognized trigger of acute attacks.

original.title: Ocular findings of vitamin A deficiency
original.explanation: Vitamin A deficiency impairs rod vision and causes ocular surface injury, producing these classic findings.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Biochemistry Jan 2025(1).pdf; Vitamins > Vitamin A, PDF p. 128

proposal.title: Findings of vitamin A deficiency
proposal.why: Removes the umbrella term that overlaps the other tiles and adds the classic skin finding, so the set is not purely ocular.
proposal.changes: Replaced 'Xerophthalmia' with 'Follicular hyperkeratosis' and broadened the title from ocular to all findings.

entries.auditNote: Night blindness and Bitot spots are instant, and xerophthalmia is an umbrella term that includes the other ocular signs.

revised.title: Findings of vitamin A deficiency
revised.explanation: Vitamin A deficiency impairs rod function and epithelial differentiation, affecting the eye and the skin.
revised.detail: Retinal is required for rhodopsin, so the earliest symptom is night blindness. Retinoic acid maintains specialized epithelium, and its loss causes keratinizing metaplasia: conjunctival Bitot spots, corneal softening and ulceration (keratomalacia) and follicular hyperkeratosis of the skin. Deficiency also increases infection risk, especially measles severity. Vitamin A toxicity, by contrast, causes headache, intracranial hypertension and teratogenicity.
tileNotes: Night blindness occurs because rods need retinal to regenerate rhodopsin.
Bitot spots are foamy, keratinized plaques on the bulbar conjunctiva from squamous metaplasia.
Follicular hyperkeratosis is keratin plugging of hair follicles on the skin, a classic cutaneous sign of vitamin A deficiency.
Keratomalacia is softening and ulceration of the cornea in severe deficiency, which can lead to blindness.

entries.changeSummary: Replaced 'Xerophthalmia' with 'Follicular hyperkeratosis' and broadened the title from ocular findings to findings of vitamin A deficiency.
entries.checkNote: Follicular hyperkeratosis is a classic vitamin A deficiency skin sign and removes the xerophthalmia umbrella-term overlap.

check.note: Follicular hyperkeratosis is a classic vitamin A deficiency skin sign and removes the xerophthalmia umbrella-term overlap.

original.title: Classic skeletal findings of rickets
original.explanation: Deficient mineralization of growing bone produces these limb, costochondral, and skull findings.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Biochemistry Jan 2025(1).pdf; Vitamins > Vitamin D, PDF p. 129

proposal.why: 'Rachitic' shares its root with the title.
proposal.changes: 'Rachitic rosary' became 'Costochondral beading', which means the same thing.

entries.auditNote: 'Rachitic' is the adjective form of rickets, so it gives away the group.

revised.title: Classic skeletal findings of rickets
revised.explanation: Deficient mineralization of growing bone and growth plates produces these limb, rib and skull findings.
revised.detail: Rickets is defective mineralization of the growth plate and osteoid in children, most often from vitamin D deficiency but also from phosphate wasting and other causes. Soft bone bends under weight (genu varum), unmineralized cartilage expands at the costochondral junctions, and the skull is soft with slow fontanelle closure. Adults with the same mineralization defect have osteomalacia, without growth plate or skull findings.
tileNotes: Bowed legs (genu varum) develop when undermineralized long bones bend under body weight.
Costochondral beading (the rachitic rosary) is palpable enlargement of the rib costochondral junctions from excess unmineralized cartilage.
Craniotabes is softening of the skull bones that yields to pressure, an early sign in infants.
Delayed closure of the anterior fontanelle reflects slow mineralization of the skull.

entries.changeSummary: Tile 2 'Rachitic rosary' renamed 'Costochondral beading', the same finding without the rickets root.
entries.checkNote: Costochondral beading is the same finding as rachitic rosary without the rickets root, a real giveaway removal.

original.title: Syndromes associated with thiamine deficiency
original.explanation: Thiamine deficiency causes acute and chronic neurocognitive syndromes and neurologic or cardiovascular beriberi.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Biochemistry Jan 2025(1).pdf; Vitamins > Vitamin B1, PDF p. 133

proposal.title: Manifestations of thiamine deficiency
proposal.why: Names what dry and wet beriberi actually cause (neuropathy and high-output failure) instead of repeating the word 'beriberi'. The medical content is the same.
proposal.changes: Dry beriberi became symmetric peripheral neuropathy, wet beriberi became high-output heart failure, and the title now says manifestations instead of syndromes.

entries.auditNote: Two 'beriberi' tiles plus the Wernicke-Korsakoff pair make this instant.

revised.title: Manifestations of thiamine deficiency
revised.explanation: Thiamine deficiency impairs glucose oxidation in neurons and myocardium, causing encephalopathy, amnesia, neuropathy and high-output cardiac failure.
revised.detail: Thiamine pyrophosphate is the cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, transketolase and branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase. Deficiency, classically in alcohol use disorder or malnutrition, causes Wernicke encephalopathy (confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia) and Korsakoff amnestic syndrome. Dry beriberi is a symmetric peripheral neuropathy, and wet beriberi is high-output heart failure from peripheral vasodilation. Giving glucose before thiamine can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy.
tileNotes: Wernicke encephalopathy is acute confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia with damage to the mammillary bodies and periaqueductal gray.
Korsakoff syndrome is chronic anterograde and retrograde amnesia with confabulation following Wernicke encephalopathy.
Symmetric peripheral neuropathy with distal sensory and motor loss is dry beriberi.
High-output heart failure from peripheral vasodilation, with edema, is wet beriberi.

entries.changeSummary: Dry and wet beriberi replaced by the findings they denote (symmetric peripheral neuropathy and high-output heart failure), and the title changed from syndromes to manifestations.
entries.checkNote: Replacing dry and wet beriberi with the findings they denote requires more reasoning and is accurate.

original.title: Contributors to niacin deficiency
original.explanation: Inadequate intake, impaired tryptophan-to-niacin conversion (B6), reduced tryptophan absorption (Hartnup), and diversion of tryptophan to serotonin (carcinoid) each reduce niacin availability.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Biochemistry Jan 2025(1).pdf; Vitamins > Vitamin B3, PDF p. 135; Protein Metabolism > Tryptophan, Niacin, and Serotonin, PDF p. 107

proposal.why: A corn-based diet is the classic dietary cause of pellagra (its niacin is poorly available) and is more specific than 'malnutrition'.

entries.auditNote: 'Malnutrition' is vague and fits almost any deficiency, and isoniazid is a classic pellagra cause many players will look for.

revised.title: Contributors to niacin deficiency
revised.explanation: Each reduces niacin supply, through poor dietary niacin, impaired tryptophan-to-niacin conversion, reduced tryptophan absorption or diversion of tryptophan to serotonin.
revised.detail: Niacin comes from the diet and from tryptophan, a pathway that requires vitamin B6. Pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia) results when either source fails. Corn contains niacin in a poorly available bound form and is low in tryptophan; Hartnup disease impairs neutral amino acid absorption; carcinoid tumors consume tryptophan to make serotonin. Isoniazid causes deficiency by depleting B6.
tileNotes: A corn-based diet is the classic dietary cause of pellagra because corn niacin is bound and corn is low in tryptophan.
Vitamin B6 is needed to convert tryptophan to niacin, so B6 deficiency reduces endogenous niacin synthesis.
Hartnup disease is a defect in neutral amino acid transport that reduces intestinal and renal tryptophan uptake.
Carcinoid syndrome diverts tryptophan to serotonin synthesis, leaving less for niacin.

entries.changeSummary: Tile 1 'Malnutrition' replaced with 'Corn-based diet'.
entries.checkNote: Corn-based diet is the classic dietary cause of pellagra and the explanation is correct.

check.note: Corn-based diet is the classic dietary cause of pellagra and the explanation is correct.

original.title: Vitamin B12 deficiency diagnostic associations
original.explanation: B12 deficiency impairs DNA synthesis and both homocysteine and methylmalonyl-CoA metabolism, and causes characteristic spinal cord injury.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Biochemistry Jan 2025(1).pdf; Vitamins > Vitamins B9 and B12, PDF p. 138

proposal.why: Three tiles now also fit folate deficiency, so players must use subacute combined degeneration to tell B12 apart. Hypersegmented neutrophils are a certain B12 deficiency finding.

entries.auditNote: Methylmalonic acid with subacute combined degeneration is the textbook B12 pair.

revised.title: Vitamin B12 deficiency diagnostic associations
revised.explanation: B12 deficiency impairs DNA synthesis and homocysteine remethylation and damages myelin in the spinal cord.
revised.detail: B12 is needed by methionine synthase (homocysteine to methionine, regenerating tetrahydrofolate) and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase. Impaired DNA synthesis causes megaloblastic anemia with hypersegmented neutrophils, and homocysteine rises. Folate deficiency shares the anemia, hypersegmented neutrophils and high homocysteine, but it does not raise methylmalonic acid or cause subacute combined degeneration.
tileNotes: Megaloblastic anemia results from impaired DNA synthesis with nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony in marrow precursors.
Homocysteine rises because methionine synthase needs B12 to remethylate it.
Hypersegmented neutrophils, with six or more lobes, are a peripheral smear sign of megaloblastic anemia.
Subacute combined degeneration is demyelination of the dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts, specific to B12 rather than folate deficiency.

entries.changeSummary: Tile 3 'Elevated methylmalonic acid' replaced with 'Hypersegmented neutrophils'.
entries.checkNote: Hypersegmented neutrophils are a standard B12 deficiency finding; subacute combined degeneration still anchors B12 over folate.

original.title: Zinc-dependent enzymes
original.explanation: Zinc is a cofactor for each enzyme or family, linking it to peptide processing, acid-base chemistry, phosphate hydrolysis, and DNA synthesis.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Biochemistry Jan 2025(1).pdf; Vitamins > Trace Elements, PDF p. 140

proposal.why: Alcohol dehydrogenase is an unambiguous zinc metalloenzyme, which removes the arguable DNA polymerase tile.

entries.auditNote: Zinc is only loosely tied to 'DNA polymerase' as a family, and Mg2+ is its standard catalytic metal, so that tile is arguable.

revised.title: Zinc-dependent enzymes
revised.explanation: Each is a zinc metalloenzyme that requires zinc at its active site for catalysis.
revised.detail: Zinc is a catalytic or structural cofactor for many enzymes and forms zinc finger motifs in transcription factors. These four are standard examples spanning peptide cleavage, carbon dioxide hydration, phosphate ester hydrolysis and ethanol oxidation. Zinc deficiency causes delayed wound healing, hypogonadism, dysgeusia, alopecia and acrodermatitis. Copper-dependent enzymes such as lysyl oxidase and tyrosinase are the main look-alike group.
tileNotes: Angiotensin-converting enzyme is a zinc metallopeptidase that converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II and degrades bradykinin.
Carbonic anhydrase uses a zinc-bound hydroxide to interconvert carbon dioxide and bicarbonate.
Alkaline phosphatase is a zinc metalloenzyme that hydrolyzes phosphate esters, important in bone mineralization.
Alcohol dehydrogenase is a zinc enzyme that oxidizes ethanol to acetaldehyde using NAD+.

entries.changeSummary: Tile 4 'DNA polymerase' replaced with 'Alcohol dehydrogenase'.
entries.checkNote: Alcohol dehydrogenase is a classic zinc metalloenzyme and is cleaner than the family-level DNA polymerase tile.

check.note: Alcohol dehydrogenase is a classic zinc metalloenzyme and is cleaner than the family-level DNA polymerase tile.

original.title: Storage diseases with enzyme replacement described in the source
original.explanation: Enzyme replacement therapy is a described management approach for each of these lysosomal storage disorders.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Biochemistry Jan 2025(1).pdf; Lysosomal Storage Diseases > Fabry, Gaucher, Mucopolysaccharidoses, PDF pp. 15, 18, 20; Glycogen > Pompe Disease, PDF p. 71

proposal.title: Lysosomal storage diseases treated with enzyme replacement
proposal.why: 'Described in the source' is internal wording; the new title states the shared feature directly.
proposal.changes: Removed the source wording and specified lysosomal disease.

entries.auditNote: These read instantly as lysosomal storage diseases, and Hunter syndrome and ASMD (Niemann-Pick type B) also have approved ERT.

revised.title: Lysosomal storage diseases treated with enzyme replacement
revised.explanation: Each is a lysosomal enzyme deficiency for which intravenous recombinant enzyme replacement therapy is an established treatment.
revised.detail: Recombinant enzymes are taken up by cells through mannose or mannose-6-phosphate receptors and delivered to lysosomes. Approved therapies include agalsidase for Fabry disease, imiglucerase for Gaucher disease, laronidase for Hurler syndrome and alglucosidase alfa for Pompe disease. Enzyme replacement does not cross the blood-brain barrier well, so it treats visceral and muscle disease better than neurologic disease. Hunter syndrome and acid sphingomyelinase deficiency also have approved enzyme replacement.
tileNotes: Fabry disease is X-linked alpha-galactosidase A deficiency, treated with recombinant alpha-galactosidase A.
Gaucher disease is glucocerebrosidase deficiency, treated with recombinant glucocerebrosidase such as imiglucerase.
Hurler syndrome (MPS I) is alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency, treated with laronidase, often with stem cell transplant.
Pompe disease (GSD II) is lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency, treated with recombinant acid alpha-glucosidase.

entries.changeSummary: Title changed from 'Storage diseases with enzyme replacement described in the source' to 'Lysosomal storage diseases treated with enzyme replacement'; tiles unchanged.

original.title: Recognized amiodarone toxicities
original.explanation: The source associates amiodarone with pulmonary, thyroid, hepatic and pigment-related adverse effects.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Cardiology.pdf; Antiarrhythmics / Other Drug Properties and Adverse Effects, PDF p.97

proposal.why: Without the thyroid tile, pulmonary fibrosis, liver injury and photosensitivity also suggest methotrexate, so players must reason toward amiodarone. Photosensitivity is a well-established amiodarone effect.

entries.auditNote: Pulmonary, thyroid, liver and blue-gray skin toxicities form the classic amiodarone list and are recognized instantly.

revised.title: Recognized amiodarone toxicities
revised.explanation: Amiodarone accumulates in tissues and causes pulmonary, cutaneous and hepatic toxicity.
revised.detail: Amiodarone is a lipophilic, iodine-rich class III antiarrhythmic with a very long half-life, so it deposits in lung, liver, skin, cornea and thyroid. Monitoring includes pulmonary, liver and thyroid function tests. Thyroid dysfunction and corneal microdeposits are other classic toxicities. Methotrexate also causes pulmonary fibrosis, liver injury and photosensitivity, but not blue-gray skin.
tileNotes: Pulmonary fibrosis (interstitial pneumonitis progressing to fibrosis) is the most serious amiodarone toxicity.
Photosensitivity, with sunburn after limited sun exposure, is a common amiodarone skin reaction.
Liver injury ranges from asymptomatic transaminase elevation to hepatitis, so liver tests are monitored.
Blue-gray skin discoloration occurs in sun-exposed areas from long-term amiodarone deposition in the skin.

entries.changeSummary: Tile 2 'Thyroid dysfunction' replaced with 'Photosensitivity'.
entries.checkNote: Photosensitivity is a classic amiodarone toxicity and removing thyroid dysfunction removes the iodine giveaway.

original.title: Classic clues to Takotsubo cardiomyopathy
original.explanation: The source describes a stress-associated syndrome with transient ventricular dysfunction and a classic ballooning pattern.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Cardiology.pdf; Cardiomyopathy / Takotsubo Cardiomyopathy, PDF p.133

proposal.why: Normal coronaries in a stressed postmenopausal woman with an apparent infarct is a core Takotsubo diagnostic clue, and it takes reasoning rather than naming the imaging pattern.
proposal.changes: Replaced 'LV apical ballooning' with 'Nonobstructive coronary arteries'.

entries.auditNote: LV apical ballooning names Takotsubo outright.

revised.title: Classic clues to Takotsubo cardiomyopathy
revised.explanation: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy is a catecholamine-mediated, transient left ventricular dysfunction, typically after stress in older women, with no culprit coronary obstruction.
revised.detail: Patients present like an acute coronary syndrome, with chest pain, ECG changes and troponin rise, but angiography shows no obstructive coronary disease to explain the wall motion abnormality. The classic pattern is apical ballooning with basal hyperkinesis, and function usually recovers within weeks. A myocardial infarction with obstructive coronary disease is the main look-alike.
tileNotes: Acute emotional stress, such as bereavement, is a classic trigger; physical stressors also occur.
A catecholamine surge is the proposed mechanism, causing myocardial stunning.
Most patients are postmenopausal women.
Coronary angiography shows no obstructive disease that explains the wall motion abnormality, a core diagnostic feature.

entries.changeSummary: Tile 4 'LV apical ballooning' replaced with 'Nonobstructive coronary arteries'.
entries.checkNote: Nonobstructive coronary arteries is a core Takotsubo feature and removing apical ballooning removes the name giveaway.

original.title: Classic associations of Chagas disease
original.explanation: The source links this parasite and its insect vector to chronic cardiac and gastrointestinal disease, including esophageal and colonic dilation.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Cardiology.pdf; Cardiomyopathy / Chagas Disease, PDF p.132

proposal.why: Swapping the organism for Chagas's main cardiac complication means players must link the vector and GI findings to it, without the disease being named.

entries.auditNote: Naming T. cruzi gives away the group, and two 'mega-' tiles reinforce it.

revised.title: Classic associations of Chagas disease
revised.explanation: Trypanosoma cruzi, spread by reduviid bugs, causes chronic myocardial damage and destruction of enteric neurons with esophageal and colonic dilation.
revised.detail: Chagas disease is endemic in Latin America and transmitted when the feces of a reduviid (triatomine, kissing) bug contaminate a bite or mucosa. Years later, chronic disease causes dilated cardiomyopathy with arrhythmias and apical aneurysm, and myenteric plexus loss causes megaesophagus and megacolon. Achalasia shares megaesophagus and Hirschsprung disease shares megacolon, but neither involves the heart. Treatment uses benznidazole or nifurtimox.
tileNotes: Dilated cardiomyopathy is the main chronic cardiac complication of Chagas disease and a leading cause of heart failure in endemic areas.
The reduviid (triatomine) bug transmits Trypanosoma cruzi in its feces.
Megaesophagus results from destruction of myenteric neurons, causing an achalasia-like picture.
Megacolon results from the same loss of enteric neurons in the colon, causing chronic constipation.

entries.changeSummary: Tile 1 'Trypanosoma cruzi' replaced with 'Dilated cardiomyopathy'.
entries.checkNote: Dilated cardiomyopathy is the main chronic Chagas complication and removing the organism name adds reasoning.

original.title: Classic clues to aortic coarctation
original.explanation: These are source-listed anatomic and clinical clues to aortic coarctation, with collateral-related rib changes in established disease.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Cardiology.pdf; Aortic Disease / Aortic Coarctation, PDF p.144

proposal.why: Replaces the defining tile, which also repeats 'aortic' from the title, with a classic clinical clue to coarctation.

entries.auditNote: 'Juxtaductal aortic narrowing' is the definition of coarctation, and rib notching is a classic giveaway.

revised.title: Classic clues to aortic coarctation
revised.explanation: Narrowing near the ductus arteriosus raises pressure proximally and reduces flow distally, with collateral vessels eroding the ribs.
revised.detail: Adult-type coarctation causes hypertension in the arms with lower blood pressure and weak, delayed femoral pulses (radiofemoral delay). Enlarged intercostal collateral arteries notch the inferior rib margins, and reduced leg perfusion causes claudication. It is associated with Turner syndrome and bicuspid aortic valve. Other causes of secondary hypertension lack the arm-leg pressure gradient.
tileNotes: Hypertension in the arms reflects high pressure proximal to the narrowing.
Femoral pulses are weak and delayed compared with radial pulses because flow beyond the narrowing is reduced.
Rib notching is erosion of the inferior rib margins by dilated intercostal collateral arteries in established disease.
Leg claudication results from reduced blood flow to the lower extremities.

entries.changeSummary: Tile 1 'Juxtaductal aortic narrowing' replaced with 'Upper-extremity hypertension'.
entries.checkNote: Upper-extremity hypertension is a classic coarctation clue and removes the anatomic giveaway.

check.note: Upper-extremity hypertension is a classic coarctation clue and removes the anatomic giveaway.

original.title: Classic symptomatic aortic stenosis findings
original.explanation: The three exertional symptoms form the classic symptomatic AS triad, and a small delayed pulse reflects impaired ventricular ejection.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Cardiology.pdf; Valvular Disease / Aortic Stenosis, PDF p.148

proposal.why: Removes the repeated 'Exertional' stem while keeping the same standard symptoms.
proposal.changes: Exertional breathlessness became dyspnea on exertion, exertional chest pain became angina pectoris, and exertional syncope became effort syncope.

entries.auditNote: Three 'Exertional' tiles spell out the classic syncope, angina, dyspnea (SAD) triad.

revised.title: Classic symptomatic aortic stenosis findings
revised.explanation: Exertional dyspnea, angina and syncope form the classic symptom triad of aortic stenosis, and a small delayed pulse reflects obstructed ejection.
revised.detail: Fixed outflow obstruction limits the rise in cardiac output with exercise and raises left ventricular pressure and oxygen demand. This causes angina, effort syncope and heart failure symptoms; their onset markedly worsens prognosis and is an indication for valve replacement. The carotid pulse is weak and late (pulsus parvus et tardus). Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy shares the exertional symptoms but has a brisk, often bifid pulse.
tileNotes: Dyspnea on exertion reflects raised left ventricular filling pressure and heart failure.
Angina pectoris (exertional chest pain) results from increased oxygen demand of hypertrophied myocardium with reduced coronary reserve.
Effort syncope occurs when cardiac output cannot rise across the fixed obstruction during exertion.
A small, delayed carotid pulse (pulsus parvus et tardus) reflects slow, reduced ejection through the narrowed valve.

entries.changeSummary: Exertional breathlessness, chest pain and syncope reworded to dyspnea on exertion, angina pectoris and effort syncope, removing the repeated 'Exertional' stem.
entries.checkNote: Standard terms for the AS triad remove the repeated 'Exertional' stem giveaway with the same meaning.

check.note: Standard terms for the AS triad remove the repeated 'Exertional' stem giveaway with the same meaning.

entries.subject: Cardiology

original.title: Classic chronic aortic regurgitation findings
original.explanation: Chronic AR can produce a large systolic-diastolic pressure difference and peripheral pulsations alongside its characteristic diastolic murmur.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Cardiology.pdf; Valvular Disease / Aortic Regurgitation, PDF p.149

proposal.why: Uses the standard eponyms in place of descriptions that repeat 'pulse'.
proposal.changes: Rapidly collapsing pulse became Corrigan pulse, and head movement with each pulse became de Musset sign.

entries.auditNote: Three tiles contain 'pulse', and an early diastolic decrescendo murmur instantly signals AR.

revised.title: Classic chronic aortic regurgitation findings
revised.explanation: Chronic aortic regurgitation produces a large stroke volume with diastolic runoff, causing bounding peripheral signs and a characteristic diastolic murmur.
revised.detail: In chronic AR the left ventricle dilates and ejects a large stroke volume that partly leaks back in diastole, so systolic pressure rises and diastolic pressure falls. This produces a wide pulse pressure and hyperdynamic peripheral signs such as a water-hammer pulse and head bobbing. The murmur is a high-pitched early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal border. Acute AR lacks these peripheral signs because the ventricle has not dilated.
tileNotes: Wide pulse pressure results from high systolic pressure with low diastolic pressure from regurgitant runoff.
Corrigan pulse is the water-hammer pulse: a forceful upstroke followed by rapid collapse.

revised.title: Transposition of the great arteries clues
revised.explanation: Ventriculoarterial discordance creates two parallel circuits, so survival depends on mixing, which balloon atrial septostomy improves, and the narrow mediastinum gives an egg-on-string radiograph.
revised.detail: In D-transposition the aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery from the left, so systemic and pulmonary circulations run in parallel. Newborns are profoundly cyanotic and depend on mixing through a patent foramen ovale, atrial septal defect or ductus arteriosus. Prostaglandin E1 keeps the ductus open and balloon atrial septostomy (Rashkind procedure) enlarges the atrial communication until the arterial switch operation. Tetralogy of Fallot is the other classic cyanotic lesion, with a boot-shaped heart instead.
tileNotes: Parallel circulations mean deoxygenated blood recirculates to the body and oxygenated blood to the lungs.
The right ventricle supplies the aorta because the great arteries are switched.
Balloon atrial septostomy enlarges the atrial communication to improve mixing in cyanotic newborns with transposition.
The egg-on-string radiograph shows an egg-shaped heart with a narrow superior mediastinum from the anteroposterior great arteries.

revised.title: Classic cardiac tamponade findings
revised.explanation: Pericardial fluid under pressure compresses the heart, causing venous congestion, muffled sounds, an exaggerated inspiratory fall in systolic pressure and beat-to-beat swinging of the heart.
revised.detail: Tamponade limits diastolic filling of all chambers, so venous pressure rises and stroke volume falls. With inspiration the right ventricle fills at the expense of the left, producing pulsus paradoxus (a systolic drop over 10 mm Hg). A large effusion lets the heart swing within the pericardium, giving electrical alternans on ECG. Beck triad is hypotension, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds; constrictive pericarditis shares venous congestion but has a pericardial knock and Kussmaul sign rather than alternans.
tileNotes: Electrical alternans is beat-to-beat variation in QRS amplitude from the heart swinging in a large effusion.
Distended neck veins reflect raised right atrial pressure from impaired filling.
Heart sounds are muffled because pericardial fluid dampens their transmission.
Pulsus paradoxus is an inspiratory fall in systolic pressure of more than 10 mm Hg from ventricular interdependence.

revised.title: Causes of tamponade from acute hemopericardium
revised.explanation: Each causes rapid bleeding into the pericardial sac, so even a small volume of blood raises pericardial pressure enough to cause tamponade.
revised.detail: The pericardium stretches slowly, so rapid accumulation of blood causes tamponade at volumes that a slow effusion would tolerate. Proximal (type A) aortic dissection can rupture into the pericardium, LV free wall rupture occurs days after transmural infarction, penetrating trauma lacerates the heart, and bleeding after cardiac surgery collects around the heart. Malignant, uremic and infectious effusions also cause tamponade, but they usually accumulate more slowly and do not share this acute bleeding mechanism.

Postoperative bleeding after cardiac surgery can collect in the pericardial space and cause tamponade.

revised.title: Complications of myocardial infarction
revised.explanation: Each is a recognized complication of acute myocardial infarction, occurring on different timelines.
revised.detail: Ventricular arrhythmias are the main cause of early death after MI. Papillary muscle and interventricular septal rupture are mechanical complications that classically occur about 3 to 5 days after a transmural infarct, when the necrotic tissue is weakest. LV mural thrombus forms over akinetic or aneurysmal myocardium (especially large anterior infarcts) and can embolize to cause stroke. The group spans electrical, mechanical and thrombotic complications rather than a single mechanism.
tileNotes: Ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation arise from ischemic myocardium and are the leading cause of sudden death in the first hours after MI.
Rupture of a necrotic papillary muscle (most often posteromedial) causes acute severe mitral regurgitation, typically 3 to 5 days after MI.
Rupture of the infarcted septum creates an acquired VSD with a new holosystolic murmur and left-to-right shunt, typically 3 to 5 days after MI.
Thrombus forms on akinetic infarcted LV wall, especially after large anterior MI, and can embolize systemically.

revised.title: Drug exposures associated with coronary vasospasm
revised.explanation: Each can precipitate coronary artery vasospasm and vasospastic angina.
revised.detail: Coronary vasospasm can be triggered by drugs that act on vascular smooth muscle. Cocaine causes alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction, triptans and ergot alkaloids act on serotonin receptors to constrict vessels, and 5-fluorouracil (and its prodrug capecitabine) causes cardiotoxicity that most often presents as vasospastic chest pain. Triptans and ergots are contraindicated in coronary artery disease and vasospastic angina for this reason.
tileNotes: Cocaine blocks catecholamine reuptake, producing alpha-mediated coronary vasoconstriction, and is a classic cause of chest pain from vasospasm in young patients.
5-Fluorouracil, a pyrimidine analog chemotherapy drug, is a well-known cause of coronary vasospasm and anginal chest pain during infusion.
Triptans are 5-HT1B/1D agonists that can constrict coronary arteries and are contraindicated in CAD and Prinzmetal angina.
Ergot alkaloids such as ergotamine are potent vasoconstrictors that can cause coronary vasospasm; ergonovine was historically used to provoke spasm diagnostically.

revised.title: Chronic venous insufficiency findings
revised.explanation: Incompetent venous valves cause chronic venous hypertension in the legs, producing each of these findings.
revised.detail: In chronic venous insufficiency, valve failure lets blood reflux and pool, raising venous pressure in the lower legs. This dilates superficial veins, drives fluid and red cells into tissue (edema and hemosiderin deposition, classically at the medial ankle) and is confirmed by demonstrating reflux on duplex ultrasound. Edema that improves with leg elevation helps distinguish venous edema from established lymphedema, and the brown pigmentation distinguishes it from arterial disease, which causes pallor and hair loss.

Extravasated red cells break down into hemosiderin, giving brown pigmentation, classically over the medial ankle (gaiter area).
Duplex ultrasound demonstrating retrograde flow through incompetent valves is the standard diagnostic test.
Venous edema is dependent and decreases with leg elevation, unlike the firmer, less positional swelling of lymphedema.

revised.explanation: VZV causes primary varicella and later reactivates from sensory ganglia as shingles, including ophthalmic and otic forms.
revised.detail: Primary varicella-zoster virus infection is chickenpox. The virus becomes latent in dorsal root and cranial nerve ganglia and can reactivate as shingles in a dermatomal distribution. Reactivation in the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve is herpes zoster ophthalmicus (Hutchinson sign predicts eye involvement), and reactivation in the geniculate ganglion is Ramsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster oticus).

Ramsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster oticus) is reactivation in the geniculate ganglion, causing ear vesicles and ipsilateral facial palsy.
