attempted.title: Dermatophyte infections
attempted.explanation: Each is a superficial infection of keratinized tissue by dermatophyte fungi (Trichophyton, Microsporum, Epidermophyton).
attempted.detail: Dermatophytes infect skin, hair and nails and are named by site: tinea corporis (body, commonly called ringworm), tinea capitis (scalp), tinea pedis (feet, athlete's foot) and tinea manuum (hands). Diagnosis is by KOH preparation showing branching septate hyphae. Tinea versicolor is caused by Malassezia, a yeast rather than a dermatophyte, and does not belong in this group.
tileNotes: Ringworm is the common name for tinea corporis, an annular scaly plaque with central clearing on the body.
Tinea capitis is dermatophyte infection of the scalp and hair shafts, mostly in children, and needs oral antifungal therapy.
Athlete's foot is tinea pedis, dermatophyte infection of the feet, often between the toes.
Tinea manuum is dermatophyte infection of the hand, often one hand together with both feet.

problems: 'Ringworm' is a generic lay term for dermatophytosis of any site (scalp ringworm, etc.), not a precise synonym of tinea corporis, so the tile meaning loosens and nearly restates the new title.
Mixes lay names (Ringworm, Athlete's foot) with Latin names in one set, which is inconsistent terminology.
check.note: Wording swap changes tile meaning; keep the original site-named set.

entries.subject: Dermatology

original.title: DRESS syndrome presentation
original.explanation: DRESS refers to a delayed drug reaction with an exanthem, eosinophilia, and systemic manifestations. The group describes a characteristic syndrome rather than mandatory findings at every time point.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Dermatology.pdf; Reactive Disease > DRESS Syndrome, PDF p. 80

proposal.title: DRESS syndrome associations
proposal.why: Stops the tiles spelling out the acronym. Carbamazepine (an aromatic anticonvulsant) is a classic DRESS culprit and also tempts toward SJS/TEN; HHV-6 reactivation is a well-established DRESS association.
proposal.changes: Tile 1: 'Delayed drug reaction' becomes 'Carbamazepine'; tile 4: 'Systemic involvement' becomes 'HHV-6 reactivation'; title changed from 'presentation' to 'associations'.

entries.auditNote: Tiles 1, 3 and 4 spell out the DRESS acronym (Drug Reaction, Eosinophilia, Systemic).

revised.title: DRESS syndrome associations
revised.explanation: Each is a classic association of drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS): a typical culprit drug, the rash, the blood finding and the linked viral reactivation.
revised.detail: DRESS is a delayed (2 to 8 weeks) drug hypersensitivity syndrome with fever, a widespread morbilliform rash, facial edema, eosinophilia or atypical lymphocytes, and internal organ involvement (most often liver). Aromatic anticonvulsants such as carbamazepine are common culprits, along with allopurinol and sulfonamides. Reactivation of HHV-6 is characteristic and is linked to disease severity. Unlike SJS/TEN, DRESS does not cause widespread epidermal necrosis or mucosal sloughing.
tileNotes: Carbamazepine, an aromatic anticonvulsant, is one of the most common causes of DRESS (associated with HLA-A*31:01); it can also cause SJS/TEN.
A widespread morbilliform (maculopapular) eruption is present in nearly all cases and may progress to exfoliation.
Peripheral eosinophilia is a defining laboratory feature, although it may appear later in the course.
Reactivation of human herpesvirus 6 is a well-established feature of DRESS, typically detected a few weeks after onset.

entries.changeSummary: Replaced 'Delayed drug reaction' with 'Carbamazepine' and 'Systemic involvement' with 'HHV-6 reactivation', and retitled to 'DRESS syndrome associations', so the tiles no longer spell out the acronym.
entries.checkNote: Removes the acronym spell-out; all four are standard DRESS associations.

problems: Carbamazepine also belongs to SJS/TEN and CYP-inducer lists; avoid co-placing those groups.
check.note: Removes the acronym spell-out; all four are standard DRESS associations.

entries.subject: Dermatology

original.title: Psoriasis clinical associations
original.explanation: Psoriasis is associated with scaly plaques, pinpoint bleeding after scale removal, nail changes, and inflammatory joint disease. These features are not universal.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Dermatology.pdf; Red Plaque Disease > Psoriasis, PDF p. 93

proposal.why: Psoriatic arthritis leaks the title word; Koebner phenomenon is a certain, classic psoriasis association that also tempts toward lichen planus and vitiligo.

entries.auditNote: Psoriatic arthritis repeats the title root and, with Auspitz sign and silvery plaques, makes the group instant.

revised.title: Psoriasis clinical associations
revised.explanation: Each is a classic clinical feature of psoriasis.
revised.detail: Psoriasis presents with well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale, most often on extensor surfaces. Removing the scale causes pinpoint bleeding (Auspitz sign) from dilated dermal papillary vessels. Nail pitting is the most common nail change, and new lesions can appear at sites of skin trauma (Koebner phenomenon). Koebner phenomenon also occurs in lichen planus and vitiligo, so it alone does not identify psoriasis.
tileNotes: Well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale, typically on extensor surfaces and the scalp, are the classic psoriasis lesion.
Pinpoint bleeding when scale is removed reflects thinned suprapapillary epidermis over dilated capillaries.
Small depressions in the nail plate are the most common psoriatic nail finding and are linked to psoriatic arthritis.
New psoriatic lesions develop at sites of skin trauma such as scratches; this isomorphic response is also seen in lichen planus and vitiligo.

entries.changeSummary: Replaced 'Psoriatic arthritis', which repeated the title root, with 'Koebner phenomenon'.
entries.checkNote: Koebner phenomenon is a classic psoriasis feature and removes the title-root repeat.

check.note: Koebner phenomenon is a classic psoriasis feature and removes the title-root repeat.

entries.subject: Endocrine

original.title: Components of the source thyroid-storm regimen
original.explanation: The source four-part regimen combines adrenergic control, a thionamide, a glucocorticoid and iodine. This is a regimen association, not a shared mechanism.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Endocrinology.pdf; Graves Disease: Complications, p. 26

proposal.title: Thyroid storm management
proposal.why: Hydrocortisone is the glucocorticoid guidelines recommend in thyroid storm, so it is certainly correct and breaks the all-'P' giveaway; the title drops internal 'source' wording.
proposal.changes: Replace 'Prednisolone' with 'Hydrocortisone'; retitle to 'Thyroid storm management'.

entries.auditNote: All four begin with 'P' (the '4 Ps' mnemonic), and 'source regimen' in the title is internal wording.

revised.title: Thyroid storm management
revised.explanation: These four drugs make up standard treatment of thyroid storm: beta-blockade, a thionamide, a glucocorticoid and iodine.
revised.detail: Thyroid storm is treated by attacking several steps at once. A beta-blocker controls adrenergic symptoms, propylthiouracil blocks new hormone synthesis and peripheral T4 to T3 conversion, a glucocorticoid such as hydrocortisone also reduces T4 to T3 conversion and treats possible relative adrenal insufficiency, and iodide blocks hormone release. Iodide is given at least an hour after the thionamide so it is not used as substrate for new hormone synthesis.
tileNotes: Propranolol controls tachycardia and other adrenergic symptoms and at high doses also decreases peripheral T4 to T3 conversion.
PTU inhibits thyroid peroxidase and peripheral 5'-deiodinase, so it blocks both synthesis and T4 to T3 conversion; it is often favored in thyroid storm.
Hydrocortisone is the glucocorticoid commonly recommended in thyroid storm; it reduces T4 to T3 conversion and covers relative adrenal insufficiency.
Iodide (for example SSKI) blocks thyroid hormone release and, at high doses, organification (Wolff-Chaikoff effect); it is given at least 1 hour after the thionamide.

entries.changeSummary: Replaced 'Prednisolone' with 'Hydrocortisone' (breaking the all-P pattern) and retitled to 'Thyroid storm management'.
entries.checkNote: Hydrocortisone is the canonical glucocorticoid and breaks the all-P pattern; two tile notes tightened.

problems: Tile note 2 stated PTU is preferred; guidelines allow either thionamide, with PTU often favored.
Tile note 4 attributed blocked hormone release to the Wolff-Chaikoff effect, which is inhibition of organification.

tileNotes: Propranolol controls tachycardia and other adrenergic symptoms and at high doses also decreases peripheral T4 to T3 conversion.
PTU inhibits thyroid peroxidase and peripheral 5'-deiodinase, so it blocks both synthesis and T4 to T3 conversion; it is often favored in thyroid storm.
Hydrocortisone is the glucocorticoid commonly recommended in thyroid storm; it reduces T4 to T3 conversion and covers relative adrenal insufficiency.
Iodide (for example SSKI) blocks thyroid hormone release and, at high doses, organification (Wolff-Chaikoff effect); it is given at least 1 hour after the thionamide.

original.title: Classic findings in congenital hypothyroidism
original.explanation: Congenital thyroid hormone deficiency can produce an enlarged protruding tongue, a protruding umbilicus, a hoarse cry and reduced muscle tone.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Endocrinology.pdf; Hypothyroidism: Other Causes, p. 30

proposal.why: 'Umbilical hernia' is the standard term for the classic finding.

original.title: Classic clinical consequences of hypercalcemia
original.explanation: The source associates elevated calcium with stone disease, slowed intestinal transit, skeletal pain and psychiatric or cognitive symptoms.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Endocrinology.pdf; Parathyroid Location and Function, p. 35; Hyperparathyroidism, p. 38

proposal.why: Removes the word 'calcium', which repeats the title, with an exact standard synonym.

entries.auditNote: The 'stones, bones, groans, psychiatric overtones' mnemonic; 'Calcium' in the first tile echoes the title.

revised.title: Classic clinical consequences of hypercalcemia
revised.explanation: Elevated serum calcium causes kidney stones, slowed gut motility, skeletal pain and psychiatric or cognitive symptoms ('stones, bones, groans and psychiatric overtones').
revised.detail: Chronic hypercalcemia, most often from primary hyperparathyroidism or malignancy, increases urinary calcium and promotes calcium stone formation. High extracellular calcium raises the threshold for nerve and muscle depolarization, which slows intestinal motility (constipation) and causes fatigue, depression, confusion and in severe cases coma. Bone pain reflects the underlying increased bone resorption. These features depend on severity and chronicity and are not all present in every patient.
tileNotes: Hypercalciuria promotes calcium oxalate and calcium phosphate kidney stones.
Hypercalcemia reduces smooth muscle excitability in the gut, slowing transit and causing constipation (the 'groans').
Bone pain reflects increased bone resorption, as in hyperparathyroidism or osteolytic malignancy.
Depression, fatigue, confusion and, in severe cases, stupor or coma result from depressed neuronal excitability.

entries.changeSummary: Renamed 'Calcium kidney stones' to 'Nephrolithiasis', removing the title word 'calcium'.
entries.checkNote: Nephrolithiasis keeps the meaning and removes the title word; small but real gain.

check.note: Nephrolithiasis keeps the meaning and removes the title word; small but real gain.

entries.subject: Endocrine

original.title: Calcium-raising and phosphate-lowering actions of PTH
original.explanation: PTH conserves renal calcium, promotes phosphaturia, stimulates calcitriol formation and indirectly increases osteoclast-mediated resorption through osteoblast-lineage cells.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Endocrinology.pdf; Parathyroid Location and Function, p. 35

proposal.why: Removes the repeated 'Increased' and 'renal' stems; title already states the actions are increases, and meaning is unchanged (PTH acts on distal convoluted tubule calcium reabsorption).
proposal.changes: Drop 'Increased' from all tiles; 'Increased urinary phosphate excretion' becomes 'Phosphaturia'; 'renal calcium reabsorption' specified as distal tubule.

entries.auditNote: All four tiles begin 'Increased' and three say 'renal', so the group sorts on format before physiology.

revised.title: Actions of parathyroid hormone
revised.explanation: PTH increases distal tubular calcium reabsorption, causes phosphate wasting, stimulates calcitriol synthesis and indirectly increases osteoclastic bone resorption.
revised.detail: PTH raises serum calcium and lowers serum phosphate through kidney and bone. In the kidney it increases calcium reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule, inhibits proximal tubule phosphate reabsorption (phosphaturia) and induces 1-alpha-hydroxylase, which makes calcitriol and increases intestinal calcium absorption. In bone, sustained PTH acts on osteoblasts to increase RANKL, which activates osteoclasts; osteoclasts have no PTH receptors. Calcitriol, by contrast, raises both calcium and phosphate.
tileNotes: PTH increases calcium reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule, reducing urinary calcium loss.
PTH inhibits the Na-phosphate cotransporter in the proximal tubule, increasing urinary phosphate excretion.
PTH stimulates proximal tubule 1-alpha-hydroxylase, converting 25-hydroxyvitamin D to active calcitriol.
Sustained PTH increases RANKL expression on osteoblasts, which indirectly activates osteoclasts and releases calcium and phosphate from bone.

entries.changeSummary: Removed the repeated 'Increased' and 'renal' stems from the tiles ('Increased urinary phosphate excretion' became 'Phosphaturia') and simplified the title to 'Actions of parathyroid hormone' so each tile's direction is implied as a PTH action.
entries.checkNote: Tiles keep their meaning under the PTH-actions title and lose the repeated 'Increased' stems.

check.note: Tiles keep their meaning under the PTH-actions title and lose the repeated 'Increased' stems.

original.explanation: Autonomous PTH secretion can raise calcium, promote phosphate loss and increase bone turnover with alkaline phosphatase elevation.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Endocrinology.pdf; Hyperparathyroidism: Primary, p. 38

proposal.changes: 'Elevated serum calcium' to 'Hypercalcemia'; 'Low serum phosphate' to 'Hypophosphatemia'.

entries.subject: Endocrine

original.title: Steroid and electrolyte pattern of 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency
original.explanation: Impaired 11-beta-hydroxylation accumulates a mineralocorticoid-active precursor and increases androgen production, causing hypertension with possible potassium loss and virilization.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Endocrinology.pdf; 11-beta-hydroxylase Deficiency, p. 54

proposal.why: Elevated 11-deoxycortisol is the standard diagnostic marker of 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency (it is low in 17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency), removing a verbatim duplicate tile shared with ENDO-033.

entries.auditNote: Three tiles are identical to ENDO-033, so the pair only differ by the androgen tile; 11-deoxycortisol is the diagnostic marker unique to this deficiency.

revised.title: Steroid and electrolyte pattern of 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency
revised.explanation: Blocked 11-beta-hydroxylation causes buildup of 11-deoxycortisol and 11-deoxycorticosterone, shunting to androgens, with mineralocorticoid-driven hypertension and potassium loss.
revised.detail: 11-beta-hydroxylase (CYP11B1) converts 11-deoxycortisol to cortisol and 11-deoxycorticosterone (DOC) to corticosterone. When it is deficient, both substrates accumulate: elevated 11-deoxycortisol is the diagnostic marker, and DOC acts as a mineralocorticoid causing hypertension and hypokalemia with low renin. Low cortisol raises ACTH and drives excess adrenal androgens, causing virilization. 17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency also causes hypertension and hypokalemia but with low androgens and low 11-deoxycortisol, and 21-hydroxylase deficiency causes salt wasting rather than hypertension.
tileNotes: 11-deoxycortisol, the immediate substrate of 11-beta-hydroxylase, accumulates and is the diagnostic marker for this deficiency.
Low cortisol increases ACTH, and steroid precursors are shunted toward adrenal androgens, causing virilization.
Accumulated 11-deoxycorticosterone has mineralocorticoid activity, causing sodium retention and low-renin hypertension.
DOC-driven mineralocorticoid excess increases renal potassium excretion, causing hypokalemia (not present in every case).

entries.changeSummary: Replaced 'Elevated 11-deoxycorticosterone' with 'Elevated 11-deoxycortisol', the marker specific to this deficiency, removing a tile shared with ENDO-033.
entries.checkNote: 11-deoxycortisol is the specific diagnostic marker and removes overlap with ENDO-033.

check.note: 11-deoxycortisol is the specific diagnostic marker and removes overlap with ENDO-033.

original.explanation: Insulin promotes anabolic metabolism and brings GLUT4 to the surface of responsive skeletal muscle and adipose cells, increasing glucose uptake.

entries.subject: Endocrine

original.title: Classic clues to diabetic ketoacidosis
original.explanation: Insulin deficiency promotes ketone formation. Acid accumulation produces an anion gap acidosis with compensatory deep breathing; acetone contributes to fruity breath.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Endocrinology.pdf; Diabetic Ketoacidosis: Pathophysiology and Presentation, p. 65

proposal.why: Fruity breath is the most instantly recognizable DKA tile; abdominal pain is a classic, well-documented DKA presentation (correlates with acidosis severity) that forces players to connect it with the metabolic tiles.

entries.auditNote: Kussmaul breathing plus fruity breath is a textbook DKA giveaway.
entries.reason: 'Abdominal pain' is a generic symptom that fits other classic Endocrine lists equally or better (adrenal crisis, hypercalcemia 'groans', pancreatitis), creating unfair cross-group ambiguity on a 16-tile board.

attempted.title: Classic clues to diabetic ketoacidosis
attempted.explanation: Insulin deficiency drives ketone production, causing a high anion gap metabolic acidosis with compensatory deep breathing and frequent abdominal pain.
attempted.detail: In DKA, absent insulin and excess counterregulatory hormones increase lipolysis and hepatic ketogenesis. Accumulating beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate produce ketonemia and a high anion gap metabolic acidosis, and the respiratory center compensates with deep, rapid Kussmaul breathing. Abdominal pain, often with nausea and vomiting, is common and correlates with the severity of acidosis; it can mimic an acute abdomen. Alcoholic and starvation ketoacidosis share some of these findings, so diabetes context matters.
tileNotes: Deep, rapid breathing is respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis, blowing off CO2.
Abdominal pain with nausea and vomiting is common in DKA, especially with severe acidosis, and can mimic an acute abdomen.
Increased lipolysis and hepatic ketogenesis raise blood beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate.
Unmeasured ketoacid anions raise the anion gap and lower serum bicarbonate.

problems: 'Abdominal pain' is a generic symptom that fits other classic Endocrine lists equally or better (adrenal crisis, hypercalcemia 'groans', pancreatitis), creating unfair cross-group ambiguity on a 16-tile board.
check.note: Replacement tile is too nonspecific to belong cleanly to DKA.

entries.subject: Endocrine

original.title: Sulfonylureas that stimulate insulin release via KATP-channel closure
original.explanation: These sulfonylureas close beta-cell ATP-sensitive potassium channels, causing depolarization and calcium-dependent insulin secretion.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Endocrinology.pdf; Diabetes Type 2: Management - Sulfonylureas, p. 68

proposal.why: Reduces the revealing 'gli-' stem from three tiles to two; chlorpropamide is a standard first-generation sulfonylurea (known for disulfiram-like reaction and SIADH) and certainly closes beta-cell K-ATP channels.

entries.auditNote: Three 'gli-' names plus tolbutamide are sorted by suffix alone; meglitinides also close K-ATP channels.

revised.title: Sulfonylureas that stimulate insulin release via KATP-channel closure
revised.explanation: Each is a sulfonylurea that closes beta-cell ATP-sensitive potassium channels, depolarizing the cell and triggering calcium-dependent insulin release.
revised.detail: Sulfonylureas bind the SUR1 subunit of the beta-cell KATP channel, closing it, which depolarizes the membrane, opens voltage-gated calcium channels and releases insulin. Tolbutamide and chlorpropamide are first generation; glipizide and glyburide are second generation and more potent. All require functioning beta cells and can cause hypoglycemia and weight gain. Meglitinides (repaglinide, nateglinide) act on the same channel but are not sulfonylureas.
tileNotes: Tolbutamide is a short-acting first-generation sulfonylurea that closes beta-cell KATP channels.
Chlorpropamide is a long-acting first-generation sulfonylurea, known for disulfiram-like reactions and SIADH, that closes beta-cell KATP channels.
Glipizide is a second-generation sulfonylurea that closes beta-cell KATP channels and has a shorter duration with hepatic clearance.
Glyburide (glibenclamide) is a second-generation sulfonylurea with a higher hypoglycemia risk, especially in kidney impairment.

entries.changeSummary: Replaced 'Glimepiride' with 'Chlorpropamide', reducing the 'gli-' names from three to two.
entries.checkNote: Chlorpropamide is a standard first-generation sulfonylurea; notes are accurate.

original.title: Source-listed glucose-lowering agents associated with weight loss
original.explanation: The source associates metformin, SGLT2 inhibition and the two named GLP1 agonists with weight loss. These effects differ in magnitude and are not guaranteed.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Endocrinology.pdf; Diabetes Type 2: Management, p. 68

proposal.title: Glucose-lowering agents associated with weight loss
proposal.why: 'Source-listed' is meta wording that does not belong in a player-facing title.

entries.auditNote: Well-known weight-loss trio; metformin is closer to weight-neutral, and semaglutide, empagliflozin or pramlintide fit equally well.

revised.title: Glucose-lowering agents associated with weight loss
revised.explanation: Each glucose-lowering drug is associated with weight loss rather than weight gain, unlike insulin, sulfonylureas and thiazolidinediones.
revised.detail: GLP-1 receptor agonists (exenatide, liraglutide) cause the largest weight loss by slowing gastric emptying and increasing satiety. SGLT2 inhibitors such as dapagliflozin cause caloric loss through glucosuria, and metformin produces modest weight loss or is weight neutral. This contrasts with insulin, sulfonylureas and pioglitazone, which cause weight gain. The magnitude of loss differs between classes and is not guaranteed.
tileNotes: Metformin decreases hepatic gluconeogenesis and is weight neutral or causes modest weight loss.
Dapagliflozin, an SGLT2 inhibitor, causes urinary glucose and calorie loss with modest weight loss.
Exenatide, a GLP-1 receptor agonist, slows gastric emptying and increases satiety, causing weight loss.
Liraglutide, a longer-acting GLP-1 receptor agonist, causes weight loss and is also approved for obesity treatment.

revised.title: Systemic diseases associated with recurrent oral ulcers

Oral aphthous ulcers are a recognized extraintestinal manifestation of IBD, particularly Crohn disease.

entries.subject: GI

original.title: Gastrointestinal causes of vitamin B12 deficiency
original.explanation: Each can cause B12 deficiency by a distinct GI mechanism: loss of intrinsic factor (pernicious anemia), failure to cleave R-protein-B12 (pancreatic insufficiency), mucosal malabsorption +/- concomitant autoimmune gastritis (celiac disease), and luminal competition (D. latum).

entries.source: Bootcamp.com; Gasteroenterology V2 Master PDF.pdf; Stomach / Pernicious Anemia; PDF pp. 40

proposal.why: Terminal ileal resection definitely causes B12 deficiency (loss of the IF-B12 absorption site) and is the classic GI cause players expect; celiac is weaker for B12 and already appears in other groups in this set.

entries.auditNote: Celiac B12 deficiency is a weak association (terminal ileum spared) while the most expected GI cause, ileal disease/resection, is missing.

revised.title: Gastrointestinal causes of vitamin B12 deficiency
revised.explanation: Each causes B12 deficiency by disrupting a different step of absorption: intrinsic factor, R-protein cleavage, ileal uptake or luminal competition.
revised.detail: Dietary B12 binds R-protein in the stomach, is released by pancreatic proteases in the duodenum, binds intrinsic factor from parietal cells, and is absorbed in the terminal ileum. Pernicious anemia removes intrinsic factor, pancreatic insufficiency prevents release from R-protein, terminal ileal resection removes the absorption site, and the fish tapeworm consumes B12 in the lumen. Folate, by contrast, is absorbed in the jejunum, and folate deficiency does not raise methylmalonic acid.
tileNotes: Autoimmune destruction of parietal cells (anti-intrinsic factor and anti-parietal cell antibodies) causes loss of intrinsic factor.
Without pancreatic proteases, B12 is not released from R-protein to bind intrinsic factor.
The terminal ileum is the site of intrinsic factor-B12 absorption, so its resection (or Crohn ileitis) causes deficiency.
The fish tapeworm, acquired from undercooked freshwater fish, competes for B12 in the intestinal lumen.

Pernicious anemia removes intrinsic factor, pancreatic insufficiency prevents release from R-protein, terminal ileal resection removes the absorption site, and the fish tapeworm consumes B12 in the lumen. Folate, by contrast, is absorbed in the jejunum, and folate deficiency does not raise methylmalonic acid.

original.title: Extrahepatic organ effects of hemochromatosis
original.explanation: Iron deposition causes skin hyperpigmentation (bronze), pancreatic islet damage (diabetes - 'bronze diabetes'), myocardial iron loading (restrictive/dilated cardiomyopathy), and pituitary/gonadal deposition (hypogonadotropic hypogonadism).

entries.source: Bootcamp.com; Gasteroenterology V2 Master PDF.pdf; Liver / Hereditary Hemochromatosis; PDF pp. 66

proposal.why: Second/third MCP joint arthropathy is a common, definitely correct extrahepatic manifestation of hemochromatosis and requires more recall than the bronze-skin giveaway.

entries.auditNote: 'Bronze skin' plus diabetes is the textbook 'bronze diabetes' giveaway.

revised.title: Extrahepatic manifestations of hemochromatosis
revised.explanation: Iron deposition outside the liver damages the joints, pancreatic islets, myocardium and pituitary or gonads.
revised.detail: In hereditary hemochromatosis, excess iron deposits in parenchymal tissues. Arthropathy classically involves the second and third MCP joints with hook-like osteophytes and chondrocalcinosis. Islet damage causes diabetes, myocardial iron causes cardiomyopathy (dilated or restrictive) and arrhythmias, and pituitary iron causes hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. Skin bronzing is another classic feature but is not used here.
tileNotes: Arthropathy of the second and third MCP joints, often with chondrocalcinosis, is a common and characteristic hemochromatosis finding.
Iron deposition in pancreatic islets impairs insulin secretion, the basis of 'bronze diabetes'.
Myocardial iron loading causes dilated or restrictive cardiomyopathy and arrhythmias, an important cause of death.
Iron in the anterior pituitary reduces gonadotropins, causing hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (low libido, impotence, amenorrhea).

original.title: Manifestations of portal hypertension
original.explanation: Elevated portal pressure dilates portosystemic collaterals (esophageal and anorectal varices, caput medusae) and causes congestive splenomegaly.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com; Gasteroenterology V2 Master PDF.pdf; Liver / Portal Hypertension; PDF pp. 71

proposal.why: Ascites is a definite, classic manifestation of (sinusoidal) portal hypertension whose absence made the group feel arbitrary; removing esophageal varices also removes the repeated 'varices' stem and the most obvious tile.

entries.auditNote: Varices and caput medusae make this instant, and ascites, the most expected manifestation, is absent.

revised.title: Manifestations of portal hypertension
revised.explanation: Raised portal venous pressure causes fluid transudation (ascites), portosystemic collaterals (anorectal varices, caput medusae) and congestive splenomegaly.
revised.detail: Portal hypertension, most often from cirrhosis, increases sinusoidal pressure and causes ascites, especially with hypoalbuminemia and renal sodium retention. Blood diverts through portosystemic anastomoses, dilating veins at the rectum (superior with middle/inferior rectal veins) and around the umbilicus (paraumbilical with superficial epigastric veins). Back-pressure through the splenic vein causes congestive splenomegaly and hypersplenism. Anorectal varices are distinct from ordinary internal hemorrhoids.
tileNotes: Increased sinusoidal pressure, low albumin and renal sodium retention cause peritoneal fluid accumulation, with a SAAG of 1.1 g/dL or more.
Portosystemic collaterals between the superior and middle/inferior rectal veins dilate into anorectal varices.
Recanalized paraumbilical veins draining into superficial abdominal wall veins produce dilated periumbilical veins.
Back-pressure through the splenic vein causes congestive splenomegaly, often with thrombocytopenia from hypersplenism.

original.title: Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia from reduced UGT1A1 conjugation
original.explanation: Each features reduced bilirubin UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT1A1) activity - mild in Gilbert, near-absent in Crigler-Najjar type I, partial in type II, and developmentally immature in physiologic neonatal jaundice - producing indirect hyperbilirubinemia.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com; Gasteroenterology V2 Master PDF.pdf; Biliary System / Hereditary Hyperbilirubinemia; Neonatal Hyperbilirubinemia; PDF pp. 88, 90

proposal.why: Atazanavir competitively inhibits UGT1A1 and characteristically causes benign unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia; it breaks the type I/II series and reduces overlap with GI-033.

entries.auditNote: Crigler-Najjar type I and II form an obvious pair, and Gilbert plus Crigler-Najjar also repeat GI-033.

revised.title: Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia from reduced UGT1A1 conjugation
revised.explanation: Each lowers bilirubin UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT1A1) activity, causing indirect hyperbilirubinemia: mildly reduced, absent, drug-inhibited or developmentally immature.
revised.detail: UGT1A1 conjugates bilirubin with glucuronic acid in hepatocytes. Gilbert syndrome has mildly reduced enzyme activity with benign jaundice during stress or fasting, Crigler-Najjar type I has absent activity with severe neonatal jaundice and kernicterus risk, and the newborn liver has immature UGT1A1 activity. The protease inhibitor atazanavir competitively inhibits UGT1A1, causing a benign unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia similar to Gilbert syndrome. Dubin-Johnson and Rotor syndromes, in contrast, cause conjugated hyperbilirubinemia.
tileNotes: Gilbert syndrome is a common inherited mild decrease in UGT1A1 activity causing benign unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia with fasting or stress.
Crigler-Najjar type I is complete absence of UGT1A1 activity, causing severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia and kernicterus in infancy.
The HIV protease inhibitor atazanavir competitively inhibits UGT1A1 and commonly causes benign unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia.
Immature neonatal UGT1A1 activity (with increased red cell turnover) causes transient unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia in the first week of life.

entries.changeSummary: Replaced 'Crigler-Najjar type II' with 'Atazanavir', breaking the type I/II pair.

original.title: Neonatal causes of indirect (unconjugated) hyperbilirubinemia
original.explanation: Each raises unconjugated bilirubin in neonates through immature clearance (physiologic), beta-glucuronidase-enhanced enterohepatic recycling (breast milk jaundice), dehydration/reduced stooling (suboptimal intake), or increased production (hemolytic disease).

entries.source: Bootcamp.com; Gasteroenterology V2 Master PDF.pdf; Biliary System / Neonatal Hyperbilirubinemia; PDF pp. 90

proposal.why: Removes the title word 'neonatal' and the long parenthetical while keeping standard terms with identical meaning.

entries.auditNote: Three 'jaundice' tiles and 'neonatal' in a tile give the group away; distinguishing breast milk from suboptimal-intake jaundice is the real content.

revised.title: Neonatal causes of indirect (unconjugated) hyperbilirubinemia
revised.explanation: Each raises unconjugated bilirubin in newborns through immature conjugation, increased enterohepatic recycling, poor intake or increased red cell breakdown.
revised.detail: Physiologic jaundice reflects immature hepatic conjugation and high red cell turnover and peaks around days 3 to 5. Suboptimal intake (breastfeeding failure) jaundice occurs in the first week when poor feeding reduces stooling and increases enterohepatic reabsorption. Breast milk jaundice starts later (after the first week) and is attributed to milk factors such as beta-glucuronidase that increase enterohepatic recycling. Hemolytic disease of the newborn increases bilirubin production and typically causes jaundice in the first 24 hours.
tileNotes: Immature UGT1A1 activity and high neonatal red cell turnover cause mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia peaking around days 3 to 5.
Factors in breast milk such as beta-glucuronidase increase enterohepatic bilirubin recycling, causing prolonged jaundice starting after the first week.
Inadequate breastfeeding in the first week causes dehydration and reduced stooling, increasing enterohepatic reabsorption of bilirubin.
Maternal antibodies (Rh or ABO) cause fetal red cell hemolysis, increasing bilirubin production, often with jaundice in the first 24 hours.

original.title: Clinical findings of obstructive cholestasis
original.explanation: Impaired bile flow raises conjugated bilirubin (jaundice, bilirubinuria/dark urine), reduces stercobilin delivery to stool (pale/acholic stools), and causes pruritus (bile acid/other retained pruritogens).

entries.source: Bootcamp.com; Gasteroenterology V2 Master PDF.pdf; Biliary System / Choledocholithiasis; Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis; Primary Biliary Cholangitis; PDF pp. 99, 104, 108

proposal.why: Steatorrhea definitely results from bile acid deficiency in obstructive cholestasis and invites confusion with pancreatic causes, removing the most obvious tile.

entries.auditNote: Jaundice, dark urine and pale stools is the textbook obstructive triad.
entries.reason: 'Steatorrhea' belongs more classically to pancreatic insufficiency and malabsorption lists, creating cross-group ambiguity on GI boards. Dropping jaundice, the cardinal finding of obstructive cholestasis, makes the set feel arbitrary.

attempted.title: Clinical findings of obstructive cholestasis
attempted.explanation: Impaired bile flow reduces bile acids and bilirubin reaching the gut (steatorrhea, pale stools) and returns conjugated bilirubin and retained pruritogens to the blood (dark urine, pruritus).
attempted.detail: In biliary obstruction, conjugated bilirubin regurgitates into blood and, being water soluble, is excreted in urine, darkening it. Less bilirubin reaches the gut, so less stercobilin is formed and stools become pale. Lack of intestinal bile acids impairs micelle formation and fat absorption, causing steatorrhea and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency, and retained pruritogens cause itching. Steatorrhea also occurs in pancreatic insufficiency, but pancreatic disease alone does not cause dark urine or pale stools.
tileNotes: Without intestinal bile acids, micelles do not form and dietary fat is malabsorbed, causing fatty stools.
Water-soluble conjugated bilirubin spills into urine (bilirubinuria), giving dark, tea-colored urine.
Reduced bilirubin delivery to the gut means less stercobilin, giving pale or clay-colored (acholic) stools.
Retained bile acids and other pruritogens cause generalized itching.

problems: 'Steatorrhea' belongs more classically to pancreatic insufficiency and malabsorption lists, creating cross-group ambiguity on GI boards.
Dropping jaundice, the cardinal finding of obstructive cholestasis, makes the set feel arbitrary.
check.note: Replacement tile fits other GI groups better than this one.

original.title: Drugs associated with acute pancreatitis
original.explanation: Each is reported to cause drug-induced pancreatitis; evidence strength differs - didanosine and azathioprine have strong/definite associations, whereas thiazide and loop diuretics have weaker, more circumstantial evidence.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com; Gasteroenterology V2 Master PDF.pdf; Pancreas / Acute Pancreatitis; PDF pp. 123

proposal.why: Valproic acid has a well-established association with acute pancreatitis (boxed warning), unlike furosemide; it also removes the paired-diuretic hint.

entries.auditNote: Furosemide is a weak, circumstantial association while valproate, a classic strong culprit, is missing.

revised.title: Drugs associated with acute pancreatitis
revised.explanation: Each is a classic cause of drug-induced acute pancreatitis.
revised.detail: Drugs are an uncommon but important cause of acute pancreatitis and are considered after gallstones, alcohol and hypertriglyceridemia are excluded. Didanosine, azathioprine and valproic acid have strong associations, and valproate carries a boxed warning for pancreatitis. Thiazide diuretics are on the classic list, though their evidence is weaker. Causation in an individual patient is shown by resolution after stopping the drug.
tileNotes: Didanosine, a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor, is one of the drugs most strongly linked to pancreatitis.
Azathioprine causes pancreatitis as an idiosyncratic reaction, usually within the first weeks of therapy.
Thiazide diuretics such as hydrochlorothiazide are a classically listed cause, although the evidence is weaker than for the other drugs here.
Valproic acid carries a boxed warning for potentially fatal pancreatitis, alongside hepatotoxicity and teratogenicity.

entries.changeSummary: Replaced 'Furosemide' (a weak association) with 'Valproic acid'.
entries.checkNote: Valproic acid is a strong, boxed-warning association replacing weak furosemide.

problems: Tile note 3 presented hypercalcemia and hyperlipidemia as established thiazide pancreatitis mechanisms; these are speculative.

tileNotes: Didanosine, a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor, is one of the drugs most strongly linked to pancreatitis.

original.title: Complications of acute pancreatitis
original.explanation: Local complications include pseudocyst and hemorrhagic (necrotizing) pancreatitis; systemic inflammatory response can cause ARDS and DIC.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com; Gasteroenterology V2 Master PDF.pdf; Pancreas / Complications of Pancreatitis; PDF pp. 124

proposal.why: Hypocalcemia (fat saponification) is a definite, classic complication of acute pancreatitis and removes the title leak.

entries.auditNote: 'Hemorrhagic pancreatitis' repeats a title word and is a severe form rather than a complication.

revised.title: Complications of acute pancreatitis
revised.explanation: Each is a recognized local, metabolic or systemic complication of acute pancreatitis.
revised.detail: Acute pancreatitis releases activated enzymes that cause local tissue injury and systemic inflammation. A pseudocyst is an encapsulated fluid collection without an epithelial lining that matures over about 4 weeks. Fat necrosis binds calcium (saponification), causing hypocalcemia, which is a marker of severity. Systemic inflammation and circulating enzymes damage the alveolar-capillary membrane (ARDS) and activate coagulation (DIC), usually early in severe disease.
tileNotes: A collection of fluid and debris walled off by granulation or fibrous tissue without an epithelial lining, developing weeks after the attack.
Calcium deposits in areas of peripancreatic fat necrosis (saponification), lowering serum calcium; low calcium indicates severe disease.
Circulating enzymes and cytokines injure the alveolar-capillary membrane, causing noncardiogenic pulmonary edema.
Release of activated enzymes and tissue factor triggers widespread coagulation and consumption of clotting factors and platelets.

entries.changeSummary: Replaced 'Hemorrhagic pancreatitis', which repeated the title word, with 'Hypocalcemia'.
entries.checkNote: Hypocalcemia from fat saponification is a classic complication and removes the title-word repeat.

check.note: Hypocalcemia from fat saponification is a classic complication and removes the title-word repeat.

original.title: Clues to abetalipoproteinemia
original.explanation: Loss-of-function MTP (MTTP) prevents assembly/secretion of ApoB-containing lipoproteins (chylomicrons, VLDL), causing fat malabsorption with lipid-laden enterocytes, very low plasma lipids, acanthocytosis, and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com; Gasteroenterology V2 Master PDF.pdf; Small Intestine / Additional Malabsorption Syndromes; PDF pp. 157

proposal.why: The MTP defect tile names the disease mechanism directly; pigmented retinopathy from fat-soluble vitamin (E/A) deficiency is a classic, certain clinical clue that requires linking the findings.
proposal.changes: Replaced 'Microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTP) defect' with 'Retinitis pigmentosa'.

entries.auditNote: The MTP tile names the defect outright; acanthocytes plus low ApoB lipoproteins make the link quick.

revised.title: Clues to abetalipoproteinemia
revised.explanation: Loss of microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTP) prevents assembly of ApoB-containing lipoproteins, causing fat malabsorption, lipid-laden enterocytes, acanthocytes and vitamin E deficiency with retinopathy.
revised.detail: Abetalipoproteinemia is an autosomal recessive defect in MTP, which loads lipid onto ApoB-48 and ApoB-100. Without it, chylomicrons and VLDL cannot be assembled or secreted, so enterocytes fill with lipid and plasma ApoB lipoproteins are nearly absent. Abnormal red cell membrane lipids produce acanthocytes, and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency (especially vitamin E) causes retinitis pigmentosa and spinocerebellar degeneration. Infants present with steatorrhea and failure to thrive.
tileNotes: Pigmentary retinopathy from fat-soluble vitamin deficiency, especially vitamin E, develops later in childhood.
Without MTP, chylomicrons, VLDL and LDL are nearly absent from plasma, with very low cholesterol and triglycerides.
Abnormal red cell membrane lipid composition produces spiculated red cells (acanthocytes).
Absorbed fat cannot be exported as chylomicrons, so it accumulates in small intestinal enterocytes, seen on biopsy.

entries.changeSummary: Replaced 'Microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTP) defect', which named the mechanism, with 'Retinitis pigmentosa'.
entries.checkNote: Retinitis pigmentosa is a classic abetalipoproteinemia clue and removes the mechanism giveaway.

original.title: Potential lead points for intussusception
original.explanation: Each can act as a lead point around which proximal bowel telescopes into distal bowel - a structural lesion (Meckel diverticulum, tumor, polyp) or lymphoid hypertrophy (enlarged Peyer patches, often post-viral in children).

entries.source: Bootcamp.com; Gasteroenterology V2 Master PDF.pdf; Small Intestine / Intussusception; PDF pp. 161

proposal.why: 'Intestinal tumor' overlaps with 'Intestinal polyp' and shares a stem; bowel-wall hematoma in IgA vasculitis is a well-established lead point and needs more reasoning.

entries.auditNote: Standard lead-point list, but 'Intestinal tumor' is vague and IgA vasculitis (HSP), a classic lead point, is a likely expected member.

revised.title: Potential lead points for intussusception
revised.explanation: Each can create a focus that is pulled forward by peristalsis, so proximal bowel telescopes into distal bowel.
revised.detail: Most childhood intussusception is ileocolic and idiopathic, often after a viral illness that enlarges Peyer patches. Pathologic lead points include a Meckel diverticulum, polyps and tumors, and submucosal hemorrhage in IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein purpura), which classically causes ileoileal intussusception. In adults, a pathologic lead point such as a tumor is usually present.
tileNotes: An inverted Meckel diverticulum is a classic pathologic lead point in children.
Submucosal bowel wall hemorrhage and edema in IgA vasculitis can act as a lead point, typically causing ileoileal intussusception.
A polyp (for example a juvenile or Peutz-Jeghers polyp) can be pulled forward by peristalsis to start intussusception.
Lymphoid hyperplasia after viral infection or rotavirus vaccination is thought to act as a lead point in typical pediatric ileocolic cases.

entries.changeSummary: Replaced 'Intestinal tumor', which overlapped with 'Intestinal polyp', with 'IgA vasculitis (HSP)'.
entries.checkNote: IgA vasculitis is a recognized lead point (ileoileal) and removes the tumor/polyp overlap.

original.title: Extraintestinal manifestations of inflammatory bowel disease
original.explanation: These musculoskeletal (enteropathic arthritis), ocular (uveitis), and cutaneous (erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum) manifestations occur in both Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com; Gasteroenterology V2 Master PDF.pdf; Large Intestine / Crohn Disease; Ulcerative Colitis; PDF pp. 173, 176

proposal.why: 'Enteropathic (IBD-associated) arthritis' states the category; sacroiliitis is a standard, certain axial IBD manifestation that also tempts toward spondyloarthropathy groups.

entries.auditNote: The first tile spells out 'IBD-associated', and primary sclerosing cholangitis is a very common expected member.

revised.title: Extraintestinal manifestations of inflammatory bowel disease
revised.explanation: These axial joint, ocular and skin manifestations occur in both Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis.
revised.detail: IBD has extraintestinal manifestations in several organs. Sacroiliitis and ankylosing spondylitis (often HLA-B27 associated) run a course independent of bowel activity, as does anterior uveitis. Erythema nodosum often parallels bowel disease activity, and pyoderma gangrenosum is a neutrophilic ulcerating skin disease strongly linked to IBD. Sacroiliitis and uveitis also occur in the other seronegative spondyloarthropathies, and primary sclerosing cholangitis is another classic manifestation not used here.
tileNotes: Inflammation of the sacroiliac joints, an axial spondyloarthritis, occurs in IBD independent of bowel activity.
Anterior uveitis causes a painful red eye with photophobia and is associated with IBD and spondyloarthropathies.
Tender red nodules on the shins (septal panniculitis), which tend to parallel IBD activity.
A neutrophilic dermatosis that forms painful ulcers with undermined violaceous borders, strongly associated with IBD.

original.title: Causes of appendiceal luminal obstruction
original.explanation: Each can obstruct the appendiceal lumen, causing secretion retention, rising intraluminal pressure, venous/arterial compromise, and acute appendicitis.

revised.title: Causes of appendiceal luminal obstruction
revised.explanation: Each can obstruct the appendiceal lumen, raising intraluminal pressure and leading to acute appendicitis.
revised.detail: Obstruction of the appendiceal lumen lets mucus and bacteria accumulate, raising pressure until venous outflow and then arterial supply are compromised, causing inflammation, ischemia and perforation. Lymphoid hyperplasia is the usual cause in children and fecaliths in adults. Less often a tumor (the carcinoid, or neuroendocrine, tumor is the most common appendiceal neoplasm) or a foreign body such as a seed or parasite blocks the lumen.
tileNotes: Hyperplasia of submucosal lymphoid follicles, often after infection, is the most common cause of obstruction in children.
A hardened mass of stool (appendicolith) is the most common cause of obstruction in adults.
The carcinoid (neuroendocrine) tumor is the most common appendiceal neoplasm and can obstruct the lumen, especially near the base.
Ingested material such as seeds or other small objects can lodge in and block the appendiceal lumen.

original.title: Hirschsprung disease clues
original.explanation: Failed craniocaudal migration of enteric neural crest cells leaves the distal rectum/colon aganglionic and tonically contracted, causing functional obstruction, delayed meconium passage (>48 h), and dilation of the proximal ganglionic bowel (megacolon).

entries.source: Bootcamp.com; Gasteroenterology V2 Master PDF.pdf; Large Intestine / Hirschsprung Disease; PDF pp. 186

proposal.why: The aganglionosis tile names the disease; the explosive expulsion of stool on rectal exam (squirt sign) is a classic, certain bedside clue that requires recall.
proposal.changes: Replaced 'Distal colonic aganglionosis' with 'Explosive stool after rectal exam'.

entries.auditNote: 'Distal colonic aganglionosis' is essentially the definition of Hirschsprung disease.

revised.title: Hirschsprung disease clues
revised.explanation: Failed migration of neural crest cells leaves distal bowel aganglionic and tonically contracted, causing functional obstruction with delayed meconium, proximal dilation and explosive stool release on rectal exam.
revised.detail: In Hirschsprung disease, enteric neural crest cells fail to migrate down to the rectum and variable lengths of distal colon, which lack Meissner and Auerbach plexuses. The aganglionic segment cannot relax, so newborns fail to pass meconium within 48 hours and the proximal normal bowel dilates (megacolon). Digital rectal exam briefly relieves the obstruction and produces an explosive release of stool and gas (squirt sign). Diagnosis is by rectal suction biopsy showing absent ganglion cells.
tileNotes: Enteric neural crest cells fail to migrate caudally to the distal colon; RET mutations are the most common genetic cause.
Digital rectal exam transiently relieves the functional obstruction, producing an explosive gush of stool and gas (squirt sign).
Failure to pass meconium within 48 hours of birth is a classic presentation.
Normally innervated bowel proximal to the aganglionic segment dilates (megacolon) from chronic functional obstruction.

entries.changeSummary: Replaced 'Distal colonic aganglionosis', which is the definition of the disease, with 'Explosive stool after rectal exam'.

original.title: Osmotic laxatives
original.explanation: Each draws water into the bowel lumen by an osmotic effect (poorly absorbed magnesium salts, PEG, and nonabsorbable lactulose), softening stool and promoting evacuation.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com; Gasteroenterology V2 Master PDF.pdf; Large Intestine / Anticonstipation Medications; PDF pp. 200

proposal.why: Two magnesium tiles reveal the group; sorbitol is a certain osmotic laxative and is also tempting toward sugar-alcohol or diarrhea-cause groups.

entries.auditNote: Two magnesium salts side by side plus PEG and lactulose make the osmotic-laxative link instant.

revised.title: Osmotic laxatives
revised.explanation: Each is poorly absorbed and draws water into the bowel lumen by osmosis, softening stool and promoting evacuation.
revised.detail: Osmotic laxatives contain solutes the gut cannot absorb, so water is retained in the lumen. Magnesium salts, the sugar alcohol sorbitol, polyethylene glycol and the synthetic disaccharide lactulose all work this way. Lactulose is also used in hepatic encephalopathy because colonic bacteria convert it to acids that trap ammonia as ammonium. Stimulant laxatives such as senna and bisacodyl instead increase motility, and bulk-forming agents such as psyllium add fiber.
tileNotes: Poorly absorbed magnesium ions retain water in the bowel; magnesium hydroxide is also used as an antacid.
Sorbitol, a poorly absorbed sugar alcohol, draws water into the lumen and is a cause of osmotic diarrhea from sugar-free products.
Polyethylene glycol is a nonabsorbable polymer that retains water in the bowel and is used for constipation and bowel preparation.
Lactulose is a nonabsorbable disaccharide fermented by colonic bacteria; it acts osmotically and also lowers ammonia in hepatic encephalopathy.

entries.changeSummary: Replaced 'Magnesium citrate' with 'Sorbitol', removing the second magnesium tile.
entries.checkNote: Sorbitol is a standard osmotic laxative and removes the double magnesium giveaway.

entries.subject: Genetics

original.title: Anticancer drugs targeting topoisomerases
original.explanation: Irinotecan and topotecan (camptothecin derivatives) inhibit topoisomerase I; etoposide and teniposide (epipodophyllotoxins) inhibit topoisomerase II. The unifying category is the topoisomerase enzyme family, spanning both isoforms.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Genetics.pdf; PDF p. 10 | DNA Replication > Enzymes

proposal.why: Teniposide pairs visibly with etoposide; doxorubicin is a certain topoisomerase II poison and the most common member players would expect.

entries.auditNote: Paired -tecan and -poside suffixes reveal the set, and anthracyclines (doxorubicin) also inhibit topoisomerase II and fit the title equally.

revised.title: Anticancer drugs targeting topoisomerases
revised.explanation: Irinotecan and topotecan inhibit topoisomerase I; etoposide and doxorubicin inhibit topoisomerase II.
revised.detail: Topoisomerase inhibitors trap the enzyme on DNA after it has cut the strand, so breaks accumulate and the cell dies. The camptothecins (irinotecan, topotecan) act on topoisomerase I, which makes single-strand breaks. Etoposide (an epipodophyllotoxin) and the anthracyclines such as doxorubicin act on topoisomerase II, which makes double-strand breaks. Doxorubicin is often remembered only as a DNA intercalator and free-radical generator, but topoisomerase II inhibition is a core part of its mechanism. Do not confuse this group with microtubule inhibitors (vincristine, paclitaxel) or alkylating agents.
tileNotes: A camptothecin derivative that inhibits topoisomerase I; used in colorectal cancer and known for causing severe diarrhea.
A camptothecin derivative that inhibits topoisomerase I; used in small cell lung and ovarian cancer.
An epipodophyllotoxin that inhibits topoisomerase II, acting in late S and G2 phase; used in testicular and small cell lung cancer.
An anthracycline that intercalates into DNA, generates free radicals, and inhibits topoisomerase II; its signature toxicity is dilated cardiomyopathy.

revised.title: Hereditary UMP synthase deficiency findings
revised.explanation: Loss of UMP synthase blocks pyrimidine synthesis, causing orotic acid buildup, megaloblastic anemia, and failure to thrive with normal ammonia.
revised.detail: UMP synthase converts orotic acid to UMP in de novo pyrimidine synthesis. When it is deficient (hereditary orotic aciduria, autosomal recessive), orotic acid accumulates and is excreted in urine, and impaired DNA synthesis causes megaloblastic anemia that does not respond to vitamin B12 or folate. Children also show failure to thrive. Ammonia is normal because the urea cycle is intact; this separates it from ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, which also raises urinary orotic acid but with hyperammonemia. Treatment is uridine supplementation.

revised.title: ATM deficiency clinical and laboratory clues
revised.explanation: Ataxia-telangiectasia (ATM gene defect) causes cerebellar ataxia, sensitivity to ionizing radiation, recurrent sinopulmonary infections, and elevated alpha-fetoprotein.
revised.detail: ATM is a kinase that senses double-strand DNA breaks and halts the cell cycle for repair. Loss of ATM (autosomal recessive ataxia-telangiectasia) leaves cells unable to respond to DNA damage, so ionizing radiation is especially harmful and cancer risk (notably lymphoma and leukemia) is high. Patients develop progressive cerebellar ataxia in early childhood, oculocutaneous telangiectasias, and immunodeficiency (often IgA deficiency) with recurrent sinopulmonary infections. Serum AFP is elevated and is a useful diagnostic marker after age 2. Distinguish it from Friedreich ataxia, which has no immunodeficiency or radiosensitivity.

Without ATM, cells cannot arrest the cell cycle to repair radiation-induced double-strand breaks, so x-ray exposure should be limited.
Immunodeficiency, often with low IgA and IgG subclasses, leads to repeated sinus and lung infections.
Alpha-fetoprotein is elevated in most patients and is a characteristic laboratory marker (unreliable under age 2).

revised.title: Neurofibromatosis type 1 manifestations
revised.explanation: Each is a recognized manifestation of NF1, an autosomal dominant disorder caused by loss of the tumor suppressor neurofibromin.
revised.detail: NF1 results from mutations in the NF1 gene on chromosome 17, which encodes neurofibromin, a negative regulator of Ras. Diagnostic criteria include cafe-au-lait macules, axillary or inguinal freckling, Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas), neurofibromas, optic pathway glioma, and characteristic bone lesions. Pheochromocytoma is an associated tumor seen in a minority of patients rather than a universal finding. NF2 differs: it is caused by merlin loss on chromosome 22 and presents with bilateral vestibular schwannomas and meningiomas rather than Lisch nodules.

A catecholamine-secreting adrenal medullary tumor that occurs with increased frequency in NF1, though not in all patients.

revised.title: Prader-Willi syndrome associations
revised.explanation: Each is a classic feature of Prader-Willi syndrome, caused by loss of paternally expressed genes at 15q11-q13.
revised.detail: Prader-Willi syndrome results from paternal deletion or maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 15q11-q13, so the paternally expressed genes are silent. Features are age dependent: neonatal hypotonia and poor feeding come first, followed in early childhood by hyperphagia leading to obesity. Other classic features include hypogonadism, short stature, small hands and feet, and intellectual disability. Angelman syndrome involves the same region but loss of the maternal UBE3A gene and presents with seizures, ataxia, and inappropriate laughter instead.

Marked neonatal hypotonia with weak suck and poor feeding is often the first sign, preceding the hyperphagia.

revised.title: Intrinsic-pathway components in the classic cascade
revised.explanation: Each is a component of the intrinsic (contact activation) arm of the classic coagulation cascade, measured by the aPTT.
revised.detail: In the classic laboratory model, the intrinsic pathway begins with contact activation: factor XII, prekallikrein, and high-molecular-weight kininogen interact on a negatively charged surface, which then activates factor XI. Factor XIa activates factor IX, and factor IXa with its cofactor VIIIa activates factor X. Deficiency of any of these prolongs the aPTT, although prekallikrein, HMWK, and factor XII deficiencies do not cause bleeding. The extrinsic pathway (tissue factor and factor VII) is assessed by the PT instead.

A vitamin K-dependent serine protease activated by factor XIa; deficiency causes hemophilia B.
The cofactor for factor IXa in the tenase complex that activates factor X; deficiency causes hemophilia A.

revised.title: Oxidative triggers in G6PD deficiency
revised.explanation: Each can raise oxidative stress and precipitate hemolysis in people with G6PD deficiency.
revised.detail: G6PD generates NADPH, which keeps glutathione reduced so red cells can neutralize oxidants. When G6PD is deficient, oxidant drugs or infection overwhelm this defense, hemoglobin denatures into Heinz bodies, and splenic macrophages remove pieces of the membrane, producing bite cells. Classic drug triggers include primaquine, dapsone, sulfonamides, and nitrofurantoin; fava beans and infection are non-drug triggers. Risk varies by drug, dose, and enzyme variant.

Sulfa antibiotics such as sulfamethoxazole are oxidant drugs that can trigger hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
A urinary tract antibiotic with oxidant properties that can precipitate hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
Infection is the most common trigger, as activated phagocytes release oxidants during the inflammatory response.

original.title: Typical laboratory pattern of hemolysis
original.explanation: Red-cell destruction releases LDH and hemoglobin and increases bilirubin generation; functioning marrow usually compensates with increased reticulocytes.

revised.title: Typical laboratory pattern of hemolysis
revised.explanation: Red cell destruction releases LDH and hemoglobin and increases bilirubin production, while a functioning marrow usually responds with more reticulocytes.
revised.detail: When red cells break down, intracellular LDH is released, heme is converted to unconjugated bilirubin faster than the liver can conjugate it, and free hemoglobin binds haptoglobin, which is then cleared. A healthy marrow responds with a reticulocytosis. Haptoglobin falls most reliably in intravascular hemolysis, and the reticulocyte response can be absent if the marrow is suppressed or nutrient deficient. This pattern distinguishes hemolysis from anemia of underproduction, where reticulocytes are low and LDH and bilirubin are usually normal.
tileNotes: LDH is abundant in red cells and is released into plasma when they are destroyed.
Increased heme breakdown produces indirect (unconjugated) bilirubin faster than the liver can conjugate it.
Haptoglobin binds free hemoglobin and the complex is cleared, so levels fall, especially in intravascular hemolysis.
The marrow compensates for red cell loss by releasing more young red cells, unless marrow function is impaired.

revised.title: Schistocyte-producing red-cell destruction
revised.explanation: Each mechanically fragments red cells and produces schistocytes on the peripheral smear.
revised.detail: Schistocytes form when red cells are sheared, either by microthrombi or fibrin strands in small vessels (microangiopathic hemolytic anemia) or by turbulent flow across an abnormal surface such as a mechanical heart valve (macroangiopathic hemolysis). TTP, DIC, and HELLP syndrome are microangiopathic; prosthetic-valve hemolysis is macroangiopathic. HUS and malignant hypertension are other classic causes. Autoimmune and other extravascular hemolysis typically produce spherocytes rather than schistocytes.
tileNotes: ADAMTS13 deficiency leaves large vWF multimers that form platelet microthrombi, which shear passing red cells.
A severe preeclampsia variant with Hemolysis (microangiopathic, with schistocytes), Elevated Liver enzymes, and Low Platelets.
Widespread fibrin deposition in small vessels fragments red cells, alongside consumption of platelets and clotting factors.
Turbulent, high-shear flow across a mechanical valve damages red cells directly (macroangiopathic hemolysis).

revised.title: Sickle-cell disease smear findings
revised.explanation: Each can be seen on the peripheral smear in sickle cell disease, reflecting sickling, chronic hemolysis, and functional asplenia.
revised.detail: HbS polymerizes when deoxygenated, deforming red cells into sickle shapes. Target cells reflect the altered membrane-to-hemoglobin ratio. Repeated splenic infarction causes functional asplenia (autosplenectomy), so nuclear remnants called Howell-Jolly bodies are no longer cleared. Chronic hemolysis drives a reticulocyte response, seen on the smear as polychromasia (larger, bluish-gray young red cells). Polychromasia falls during parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis, when reticulocyte production stops.
tileNotes: Crescent-shaped red cells formed when deoxygenated HbS polymerizes and distorts the cell.
Red cells with a central dark spot, common in hemoglobinopathies including sickle cell disease.
Basophilic nuclear remnants that persist in red cells when the spleen is absent or nonfunctional, as after autosplenectomy.
Bluish-gray, slightly larger red cells on Wright stain that are reticulocytes, reflecting the marrow response to chronic hemolysis.

revised.title: Lead-toxicity clinical clues
revised.explanation: Lead exposure can damage peripheral nerves, the gastrointestinal tract, the gingiva, and the brain.
revised.detail: Lead poisoning has multisystem effects that vary with age. Adults more often develop a motor neuropathy with wrist or foot drop and abdominal colic, while children are more prone to encephalopathy and lasting cognitive deficits. Lead deposits in the gums form a blue-gray line along the gingival margin. Hematologic findings (basophilic stippling, microcytic anemia) are separate laboratory clues. Treatment is chelation, for example succimer in children or dimercaprol with EDTA in severe cases.

original.explanation: Lead disrupts heme synthesis at two enzyme steps and can impair red-cell RNA degradation, producing these biochemical and smear findings.

revised.title: Lead-toxicity hematologic clues
revised.explanation: Lead blocks heme synthesis at ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase and impairs red cell RNA degradation, producing these biochemical and smear findings.
revised.detail: Lead inhibits two heme synthesis enzymes. Blocking ALA dehydratase raises aminolevulinic acid, and blocking ferrochelatase prevents iron insertion into protoporphyrin, so zinc is inserted instead and iron accumulates in mitochondria, forming ringed sideroblasts (an acquired sideroblastic anemia). Lead also inhibits pyrimidine 5'-nucleotidase, so ribosomal RNA aggregates appear as basophilic stippling. The result is a microcytic anemia. Blood lead level is the diagnostic test.
tileNotes: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase (porphobilinogen synthase), so aminolevulinic acid accumulates in blood and urine.
Ferrochelatase inhibition leaves iron trapped in mitochondria around the nucleus of erythroblasts, seen on Prussian blue stain of marrow.
Inhibition of pyrimidine 5'-nucleotidase leaves undegraded ribosomal RNA, seen as blue dots in red cells.
With ferrochelatase blocked, zinc is incorporated into protoporphyrin in place of iron, raising zinc protoporphyrin levels.

revised.title: Beta-thalassemia major associations
revised.explanation: Severely reduced beta-globin synthesis causes ineffective erythropoiesis, compensatory HbF, characteristic red cell morphology, marrow expansion, and dependence on transfusion.
revised.detail: In beta-thalassemia major, little or no beta-globin is made, so excess alpha chains precipitate and destroy erythroid precursors. Patients become severely anemic after HbF declines in infancy and need lifelong transfusions, which cause iron overload (hemosiderosis) affecting the heart, liver, and endocrine organs unless chelation is given. HbF is markedly increased, the smear shows microcytic hypochromic cells with target cells, and marrow expansion produces crew-cut skull x-ray and chipmunk facies. Elevated HbA2 is the hallmark of beta-thalassemia trait (minor), not a reliable feature of major.
tileNotes: With little beta-globin available, gamma chains pair with alpha chains, so fetal hemoglobin (alpha2 gamma2) rises markedly.
Chronic transfusion therapy adds iron the body cannot excrete, causing cardiac, hepatic, and endocrine damage unless chelation is used.
Hypochromic red cells with a central dark spot, typical of thalassemias.
Massive erythroid hyperplasia expands the marrow, causing crew-cut skull on x-ray and chipmunk facies.

revised.title: Von Willebrand-disease laboratory clues
revised.explanation: Impaired vWF function prolongs bleeding time and lowers ristocetin cofactor activity, can lower factor VIII and prolong the aPTT, and leaves the PT normal.
revised.detail: vWF mediates platelet adhesion to subendothelial collagen through GpIb and carries factor VIII, protecting it from degradation. In von Willebrand disease, primary hemostasis is impaired (prolonged bleeding time), and the ristocetin cofactor assay, which measures the ability of the patient's vWF to agglutinate platelets, is reduced. The aPTT is prolonged only when factor VIII falls enough. The PT is normal because the extrinsic pathway is unaffected. Bernard-Soulier syndrome also impairs ristocetin-induced agglutination of the patient's own platelets, but the defect is in platelet GpIb, so the platelet count is low with giant platelets, the plasma vWF assays are normal, and adding normal plasma does not correct it.
tileNotes: The extrinsic pathway (tissue factor and factor VII) is intact, so the PT is normal.
Defective vWF-mediated platelet adhesion impairs primary hemostasis and lengthens bleeding time.
The ristocetin cofactor assay measures vWF function in agglutinating platelets via GpIb; it is reduced in most types of vWD.
vWF stabilizes factor VIII, so when vWF is low enough, factor VIII falls and the aPTT lengthens; it can be normal in mild disease.

original.title: Anatomic sites of developmental erythropoiesis
original.explanation: These locations contribute to red-cell production at different stages of prenatal development, with marrow later becoming dominant.

revised.title: Anatomic sites of developmental erythropoiesis
revised.explanation: Each site produces red cells at a stage of prenatal development, with the bone marrow eventually becoming dominant.
revised.detail: Fetal erythropoiesis moves through a sequence of sites, remembered as 'Young Liver Synthesizes Blood'. The yolk sac starts it in the first weeks, the liver becomes the main site from about week 6, the spleen contributes from about week 10 to 28, and the bone marrow takes over in the third trimester and remains the site after birth. The periods overlap and the cutoffs are approximate. The liver and spleen can resume red cell production after birth as extramedullary hematopoiesis when the marrow fails or is overwhelmed.
tileNotes: The first site of erythropoiesis, active from about week 3 of development.
The main site of fetal erythropoiesis from about week 6 until late in gestation.
Contributes to fetal erythropoiesis from about week 10 to 28, overlapping with the liver.
Becomes the dominant site in the third trimester and remains the site of erythropoiesis after birth.

original.title: Pyrimidine-analogue cancer agents
original.explanation: These pyrimidine-related antimetabolites interfere with nucleic-acid synthesis; capecitabine is converted to 5-fluorouracil.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Hematology & Oncology.pdf; Principles of Oncology and Therapeutics - Drug Targets; PDF p. 73

proposal.why: Capecitabine is simply the 5-FU prodrug and adds a third -abine suffix; azacitidine is a definite pyrimidine (cytidine) analogue used for MDS/AML.

entries.auditNote: Three tiles end in -abine, and 5-FU with its prodrug capecitabine is an easy pair.

revised.title: Pyrimidine-analogue cancer agents
revised.explanation: Each is a pyrimidine analogue antimetabolite used in cancer therapy, though their exact mechanisms differ.
revised.detail: These drugs mimic pyrimidine bases or nucleosides and disrupt nucleic acid synthesis or regulation. 5-Fluorouracil is converted to 5-FdUMP, which inhibits thymidylate synthase. Cytarabine and gemcitabine are cytidine analogues incorporated into DNA; cytarabine inhibits DNA polymerase, and gemcitabine also inhibits ribonucleotide reductase. Azacitidine is a cytidine analogue that inhibits DNA methyltransferase (hypomethylating agent) and is used in myelodysplastic syndromes. Purine analogues such as 6-mercaptopurine, cladribine, and fludarabine belong to a different group.
tileNotes: A cytidine analogue (cytosine arabinoside) that inhibits DNA polymerase; used for AML and causes pancytopenia.
A cytidine analogue that inhibits ribonucleotide reductase and DNA synthesis; used in pancreatic cancer.
A uracil analogue whose metabolite 5-FdUMP inhibits thymidylate synthase; its effect is enhanced by leucovorin.
A cytidine analogue that inhibits DNA methyltransferase, causing DNA hypomethylation; used for myelodysplastic syndromes.

entries.changeSummary: Replaced Capecitabine, the oral prodrug of 5-FU, with Azacitidine.
entries.checkNote: Azacitidine is a cytidine-analogue antimetabolite, so it is a valid pyrimidine analogue and replaces the capecitabine/5-FU prodrug duplicate.

original.title: Chronic myeloid-leukemia clues
original.explanation: BCR-ABL1-driven granulocytic proliferation produces the classic CML laboratory and smear pattern.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Hematology & Oncology.pdf; Leukemias and Lymphomas - CML; PDF p. 78

proposal.why: Removes the BCR-ABL1 giveaway and the cross-group duplicate tile; splenomegaly is a certain, common CML finding, and the remaining set still points to CML through reasoning.

entries.auditNote: BCR-ABL1 gives CML away and duplicates the BCR-ABL1 tile in PLX-HEM-050.

revised.title: Chronic myeloid-leukemia clues
revised.explanation: BCR-ABL1-driven granulocytic proliferation produces splenomegaly and the classic CML blood picture.
revised.detail: CML is a myeloproliferative neoplasm caused by the Philadelphia chromosome, t(9;22), which creates the constitutively active BCR-ABL1 tyrosine kinase. It produces marked leukocytosis with granulocytes at all stages of maturation (left shift), basophilia, and often splenomegaly, which can be massive. A low leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score helps separate CML from a leukemoid reaction, in which LAP is high and basophilia is absent. Confirmation is by detecting BCR-ABL1, and treatment is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor such as imatinib.
tileNotes: Extramedullary hematopoiesis and leukemic infiltration enlarge the spleen, often markedly, causing left upper quadrant fullness or early satiety.
An increased absolute basophil count is characteristic of CML and helps distinguish it from a reactive leukocytosis.
Neoplastic neutrophils have low LAP activity, unlike the high LAP of a leukemoid reaction.
Granulocytes at every stage of maturation (myelocytes, metamyelocytes, bands) appear in the blood.

entries.changeSummary: Replaced BCR-ABL1 fusion with Splenomegaly to remove the giveaway and the duplicate tile; separate it on a board from the myelofibrosis group, which has Massive splenomegaly.
entries.checkNote: Splenomegaly is a classic CML finding; keep it apart on a board from the myelofibrosis and hairy cell groups.

problems: Board overlap: splenomegaly also fits PLX-HEM-064 (Massive splenomegaly) and hairy cell leukemia; do not place them together.
check.note: Splenomegaly is a classic CML finding; keep it apart on a board from the myelofibrosis and hairy cell groups.

entries.subject: Heme/Onc

original.title: Acute promyelocytic-leukemia clues
original.explanation: PML-RARA disrupts myeloid differentiation; the classic subtype has abnormal promyelocytes that may contain Auer rods and responds to differentiation therapy.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Hematology & Oncology.pdf; Leukemias and Lymphomas - AML and APL; PDF p. 77

proposal.why: PML-RARA duplicates t(15;17); DIC at presentation is a certain, clinically important APL association that requires recall.

entries.auditNote: t(15;17) and PML-RARA are the same lesion stated twice, both instant giveaways.

revised.title: Acute promyelocytic-leukemia clues
revised.explanation: The t(15;17) PML-RARA fusion arrests myeloid differentiation at the promyelocyte stage, producing Auer rod-rich promyelocytes, a high risk of DIC, and responsiveness to differentiation therapy.
revised.detail: APL (AML M3) is defined by t(15;17), which fuses PML with the retinoic acid receptor alpha gene and blocks maturation beyond the promyelocyte. The abnormal promyelocytes contain numerous Auer rods (faggot cells), and their granules release procoagulant and fibrinolytic material, so DIC is common at presentation and is a major cause of early death. All-trans retinoic acid (often with arsenic trioxide) induces the cells to mature. Other AML subtypes have Auer rods too but lack the specific translocation and ATRA response.
tileNotes: The defining translocation of APL, fusing PML on chromosome 15 with RARA on chromosome 17.
Granule contents of the abnormal promyelocytes trigger coagulation and fibrinolysis, so DIC is common at presentation and can worsen as cells die.
Needle-shaped cytoplasmic inclusions of fused primary granules (myeloperoxidase positive); bundles of them form faggot cells in APL.
ATRA, a vitamin A derivative, binds the fusion receptor and lets the promyelocytes differentiate into mature neutrophils.

entries.changeSummary: Replaced PML-RARA fusion, which restated t(15;17), with Disseminated intravascular coagulation.
entries.checkNote: DIC is a classic APL association and removes the PML-RARA restatement; separate it on a board from PLX-HEM-011, which has the identical DIC tile.

problems: Exact tile text "Disseminated intravascular coagulation" also appears in PLX-HEM-011; never place both on one board.
check.note: DIC is a classic APL association and removes the PML-RARA restatement; separate it on a board from PLX-HEM-011, which has the identical DIC tile.
