entries.subject: Renal

original.title: Classic nephrotic syndrome findings
original.explanation: Marked glomerular protein loss lowers serum albumin and promotes edema; altered lipid metabolism produces hyperlipidemia. Adult nephrotic-range proteinuria is typically above 3.5 g/day.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Nephrology.pdf; Nephrotic Syndromes > Glomerular Disease Overview (PDF pp. 57)

proposal.why: Heavy proteinuria is the defining giveaway; the hypercoagulable state (urinary antithrombin III loss, renal vein thrombosis risk) is a certain classic nephrotic feature that requires recall.

entries.auditNote: The textbook nephrotic tetrad; heavy proteinuria plus hypoalbuminemia names the syndrome.

revised.title: Classic nephrotic syndrome findings
revised.explanation: Each is a classic consequence of the heavy glomerular protein loss that defines nephrotic syndrome.
revised.detail: Nephrotic syndrome is defined by proteinuria above 3.5 g/day in adults, which causes hypoalbuminemia and edema. The liver increases lipoprotein synthesis, causing hyperlipidemia and lipiduria. Urinary loss of anticoagulant proteins such as antithrombin III, together with increased hepatic clotting factor synthesis, causes a hypercoagulable state with risk of renal vein thrombosis and other venous thromboembolism. Nephritic syndrome instead features hematuria, hypertension, and RBC casts with less proteinuria.
tileNotes: Urinary loss of antithrombin III and increased hepatic clotting factor production make nephrotic syndrome hypercoagulable, with risk of renal vein thrombosis.
Urinary albumin loss exceeds hepatic synthesis, causing hypoalbuminemia.
Reduced plasma oncotic pressure and renal sodium retention cause edema, often periorbital at first.
The liver increases lipoprotein synthesis in response to low oncotic pressure, causing hyperlipidemia.

entries.changeSummary: Replaced 'Heavy proteinuria' with 'Hypercoagulability' so the defining feature no longer names the syndrome.
entries.checkNote: Hypercoagulability is a classic nephrotic consequence and removes the defining-feature giveaway.

check.note: Hypercoagulability is a classic nephrotic consequence and removes the defining-feature giveaway.

entries.subject: Renal

original.title: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis clues
original.explanation: PSGN follows a nephritogenic streptococcal infection and classically produces complement consumption with subepithelial deposits and granular staining.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Nephrology.pdf; Nephritic Syndromes > Poststreptococcal Glomerulonephritis (PDF pp. 52, 64, 65)

proposal.why: Removes the title leak; cola-colored urine is a certain classic PSGN presenting clue that also tempts toward IgA nephropathy, so players must discriminate.

entries.auditNote: 'Recent streptococcal infection' restates the title; with subepithelial humps the group is immediate.

revised.title: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis clues
revised.explanation: Each is a classic laboratory, biopsy, or clinical clue to poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.
revised.detail: PSGN follows pharyngeal or skin infection with a nephritogenic group A streptococcus, after a latent period of about 1 to 3 weeks after pharyngitis or 3 to 6 weeks after impetigo. Immune complex deposition activates complement, lowering C3, and biopsy shows subepithelial humps on electron microscopy and granular IgG and C3 on immunofluorescence. Patients present with nephritic syndrome, including cola-colored urine from hematuria. IgA nephropathy also causes cola-colored urine, but it occurs during or within days of infection and has normal C3 with mesangial IgA deposits.
tileNotes: Complement activation by immune complexes lowers serum C3 in PSGN, which usually normalizes within about 8 weeks.
Electron microscopy shows subepithelial immune complex deposits called humps.
Immunofluorescence shows granular (lumpy-bumpy) IgG and C3 deposits along the capillary walls.
Glomerular hematuria gives a cola-colored or tea-colored urine, a classic presenting sign of PSGN.

entries.changeSummary: Replaced 'Recent streptococcal infection' (which restated the title) with 'Cola-colored urine'.
entries.checkNote: Cola-colored urine is a classic PSGN presenting sign; content accurate.

check.note: Cola-colored urine is a classic PSGN presenting sign; content accurate.

entries.subject: Renal

original.title: Calcium oxalate stone risk exposures
original.explanation: Oxalate production or absorption can rise with ethylene glycol, high vitamin C intake, and fat malabsorption (enteric hyperoxaluria); low urinary citrate removes an inhibitor of calcium crystallization.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Nephrology.pdf; Nephrolithiasis > Calcium Stones (PDF pp. 72, 75)

proposal.title: Calcium oxalate stone risk factors
proposal.why: Hypocitraturia is not an exposure, so 'risk factors' accurately covers all four members.
proposal.changes: Title 'Calcium oxalate stone risk exposures' to 'Calcium oxalate stone risk factors'.

entries.auditNote: Players must reason through oxalate load and citrate inhibition; hypocitraturia is a urinary abnormality rather than an exposure, and hypercalciuria is a likely expected member.
entries.reason: Broadening the title to 'risk factors' makes hypercalciuria, the most common calcium oxalate stone risk factor, an equally fitting missing member.

entries.subject: Renal

original.title: Renal papillary necrosis associations
original.explanation: Each can compromise the vulnerable renal papilla through ischemic, infectious, or analgesic-related injury and predispose to papillary necrosis.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Nephrology.pdf; Kidney Injury > Renal Papillary Necrosis (PDF pp. 86, 95, 100)

proposal.why: Breaks the SAAD mnemonic; urinary tract obstruction is an established papillary necrosis cause (the O in POSTCARDS).

entries.auditNote: Exactly the SAAD mnemonic (Sickle cell, Analgesics, Acute pyelonephritis, Diabetes), so it is sorted instantly.

revised.title: Renal papillary necrosis associations
revised.explanation: Each condition predisposes to necrosis of the renal papilla, which has a tenuous blood supply.
revised.detail: The renal papillae are supplied by the vasa recta and sit in a hypoxic, hypertonic environment, which makes them vulnerable to ischemia. Sickling in the medulla, chronic high-dose analgesic use, diabetic microvascular disease, and urinary tract obstruction (often with infection) can all cause papillary necrosis. Sloughed papillae can cause hematuria, flank pain, and ureteral obstruction. The POSTCARDS mnemonic covers pyelonephritis, obstruction, sickle cell disease, tuberculosis, cirrhosis, analgesics, renal transplant rejection, diabetes, and systemic vasculitis.
tileNotes: Sickling in the hypoxic, hypertonic renal medulla causes ischemia of the papillae; papillary necrosis occurs in both sickle cell disease and trait.
Urinary tract obstruction raises pressure in the collecting system and compromises papillary blood flow, especially when infection is also present.
Chronic high-dose NSAID or analgesic use inhibits vasodilatory prostaglandins in the medulla, causing papillary ischemia.
Diabetic microvascular disease, often combined with pyelonephritis, is one of the most common causes of papillary necrosis.

entries.changeSummary: Replaced 'Acute pyelonephritis' with 'Urinary tract obstruction' to break the SAAD mnemonic.
entries.checkNote: Obstruction is a POSTCARDS member and breaks the SAAD mnemonic; content accurate.

check.note: Obstruction is a POSTCARDS member and breaks the SAAD mnemonic; content accurate.

entries.subject: Renal

original.title: Typical prerenal azotemia laboratory pattern
original.explanation: Preserved tubular sodium and water retention during reduced renal perfusion often yields concentrated urine, low sodium excretion, and a disproportionate BUN elevation.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Nephrology.pdf; Kidney Injury > Prerenal AKI (PDF pp. 87)

proposal.why: Urine sodium below 20 duplicates FENa below 1%; a bland sediment with hyaline casts is the standard prerenal urinalysis and breaks the numeric format.
proposal.changes: Urine sodium below 20 mEq/L -> Hyaline casts

entries.auditNote: Four numeric above/below thresholds share a format and form the memorized prerenal table.

revised.title: Typical prerenal azotemia laboratory pattern
revised.explanation: Each is part of the typical laboratory picture of prerenal azotemia, in which tubules are intact and avidly retain sodium and water during reduced renal perfusion.
revised.detail: In prerenal azotemia, reduced perfusion activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and ADH, so intact tubules reabsorb sodium, water, and urea. This produces a BUN-to-creatinine ratio above 20, FENa below 1%, concentrated urine, and a bland sediment with at most hyaline casts. Acute tubular necrosis instead shows muddy brown granular casts, FENa above 2%, and isosthenuric urine. Diuretics, CKD, and some intrinsic injuries (contrast, pigment) can blur these patterns.
tileNotes: Increased proximal urea reabsorption raises BUN out of proportion to creatinine, giving a ratio above 20.
The urine sediment in prerenal azotemia is bland, showing at most hyaline casts, in contrast to the muddy brown granular casts of ATN.
Intact tubules avidly reabsorb sodium, so the fractional excretion of sodium falls below 1%.
ADH-driven water reabsorption by intact tubules produces concentrated urine, typically above 500 mOsm/kg.

entries.changeSummary: Replaced 'Urine sodium below 20 mEq/L' (redundant with FENa) with 'Hyaline casts', breaking the four-number format.
entries.checkNote: Bland sediment with hyaline casts is the standard prerenal finding; content accurate.

check.note: Bland sediment with hyaline casts is the standard prerenal finding; content accurate.

entries.subject: Renal

original.title: Normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis associations
original.explanation: GI bicarbonate loss and renal bicarbonate loss or impaired acid excretion can produce hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis without an increased anion gap.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Nephrology.pdf; Acid-Base Physiology > Metabolic Acidosis; RTA Type 1; RTA Type 2 (PDF pp. 22, 40, 41, 42, 46, 47, 48, 49, 93, 118)

proposal.why: Removes the revealing RTA pair and the acetazolamide/proximal RTA overlap; pancreatic fistula causes bicarbonate loss and a normal anion gap acidosis (HARDASS member).
proposal.changes: Proximal renal tubular acidosis -> Pancreatic fistula

entries.auditNote: The paired distal/proximal RTA tiles give it away, and acetazolamide duplicates the proximal RTA mechanism.

revised.title: Normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis associations
revised.explanation: Each causes a hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis with a normal anion gap, through bicarbonate loss or impaired renal acid excretion.
revised.detail: When bicarbonate is lost from the gut or kidney, or the kidney cannot excrete acid, chloride rises to replace it and the anion gap stays normal. Diarrhea and pancreatic fistulas lose bicarbonate-rich fluid, acetazolamide blocks proximal bicarbonate reabsorption, and distal RTA impairs distal hydrogen ion secretion. This contrasts with high-anion-gap acidoses (lactic acidosis, ketoacidosis, uremia, toxic alcohols, salicylates), in which an unmeasured anion accumulates.
tileNotes: Diarrhea causes loss of bicarbonate-rich intestinal fluid and is the most common cause of normal-anion-gap acidosis.
Acetazolamide inhibits proximal tubule carbonic anhydrase, causing bicarbonate wasting and normal-anion-gap acidosis.
In distal (type 1) RTA, the collecting duct cannot secrete hydrogen ions, so urine pH stays above 5.5 despite acidemia.
Pancreatic secretions are rich in bicarbonate, so external pancreatic fistula drainage causes normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis.

entries.changeSummary: Replaced 'Proximal renal tubular acidosis' with 'Pancreatic fistula', removing the paired RTA tiles and the overlap with acetazolamide.
entries.checkNote: Pancreatic fistula is a standard NAGMA cause and removes the paired RTA tiles.

check.note: Pancreatic fistula is a standard NAGMA cause and removes the paired RTA tiles.

entries.subject: Renal

original.title: Diabetic glomerulopathy structural findings
original.explanation: Diabetic kidney injury can produce nodular mesangial sclerosis, expanded mesangial matrix, thickened basement membrane, and podocyte injury; findings evolve with disease stage.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Nephrology.pdf; Nephrotic Syndromes > Diabetic Glomerulonephropathy (PDF pp. 56, 62)

proposal.title: Diabetic nephropathy histologic findings
proposal.why: Efferent (as well as afferent) arteriolar hyalinosis is a characteristic, relatively specific diabetic lesion scored in the RPS classification, replacing the nonspecific effacement tile; the title is widened to histology to include the vascular pole.
proposal.changes: Podocyte foot-process effacement -> Efferent arteriolar hyalinosis; title broadened

entries.auditNote: KW nodules are a form of mesangial expansion and foot-process effacement is nonspecific, while classic arteriolar hyalinosis is missing.

revised.title: Diabetic nephropathy histologic findings
revised.explanation: Each is a characteristic histologic lesion of diabetic kidney disease.
revised.detail: Diabetic nephropathy begins with glomerular basement membrane thickening, progresses to diffuse mesangial matrix expansion, and can develop nodular mesangial sclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules). Nonenzymatic glycation of vessel wall proteins causes hyaline arteriolosclerosis of both afferent and efferent arterioles, and efferent involvement is relatively specific for diabetes. Hypertensive nephrosclerosis typically causes hyaline change of afferent arterioles only. Light-chain deposition disease and amyloidosis can mimic nodular lesions and need immunofluorescence or Congo red staining to separate.
tileNotes: Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules are round, acellular nodules of mesangial matrix that are characteristic of advanced diabetic nephropathy.
Diffuse expansion of mesangial matrix is a core diabetic glomerular lesion that progresses with disease duration.
Glomerular basement membrane thickening is the earliest structural change of diabetic nephropathy, seen on electron microscopy.
Hyaline arteriolosclerosis of the efferent arteriole, as well as the afferent arteriole, is characteristic of diabetes; hypertension usually affects only the afferent arteriole.

entries.changeSummary: Replaced 'Podocyte foot-process effacement' (nonspecific) with 'Efferent arteriolar hyalinosis' and changed the title from glomerulopathy structural findings to nephropathy histologic findings.
entries.checkNote: Efferent arteriolar hyalinosis is a characteristic diabetic lesion; content accurate.

entries.subject: Neurology

original.title: Upper motor neuron examination signs
original.explanation: A corticospinal (upper motor neuron) lesion can produce increased deep tendon reflexes, velocity-dependent spasticity, increased tone, and a Babinski (extensor plantar) response.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Neurology.pdf; Descending Spinal Cord Tracts; Ischemic Cerebrovascular Accidents; PDF pp. 25, 157

proposal.why: Replaces the hypertonia tile, which duplicates spasticity, with pronator drift, a standard sensitive UMN exam sign.

entries.auditNote: Textbook UMN list, and spasticity is a subtype of hypertonia, so two tiles are redundant.

revised.title: Upper motor neuron examination signs
revised.explanation: Each is a classic examination sign of an upper motor neuron (corticospinal tract) lesion.
revised.detail: Damage to the corticospinal pathway removes descending inhibition and causes hyperreflexia, velocity-dependent spasticity, and an extensor plantar (Babinski) response. Subtle weakness of arm supinators in UMN lesions shows up as pronator drift when the arms are held outstretched with palms up. Lower motor neuron lesions instead cause atrophy, fasciculations, hyporeflexia, and flaccid tone. Right after an acute UMN injury (spinal shock), tone and reflexes can be reduced before UMN signs develop.
tileNotes: Loss of descending inhibition increases deep tendon reflexes in upper motor neuron lesions.
Spasticity is velocity-dependent increased tone, a hallmark of upper motor neuron lesions.
With arms outstretched and palms up, the weak arm pronates and drifts downward, a sensitive sign of a corticospinal tract lesion.
The Babinski sign, dorsiflexion of the big toe on plantar stimulation, indicates a corticospinal tract lesion in anyone past infancy.

entries.changeSummary: Replaced 'Hypertonia' (overlapping spasticity) with 'Pronator drift'.
entries.checkNote: Pronator drift is a classic UMN sign and removes the spasticity-hypertonia overlap.

check.note: Pronator drift is a classic UMN sign and removes the spasticity-hypertonia overlap.

entries.subject: Neurology

original.title: Lower motor neuron examination signs
original.explanation: Loss of lower motor neuron input can produce muscle wasting, fasciculations, reduced or absent reflexes, and low tone.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Neurology.pdf; Descending Spinal Cord Tracts; Invasive Spinal Cord Disease; PDF pp. 25, 64

proposal.title: Lower motor neuron lesion findings
proposal.why: Fibrillation potentials are the standard electrodiagnostic sign of LMN denervation, which takes some reasoning; the title is widened from examination signs to findings to fit.
proposal.changes: Hypotonia -> Fibrillation potentials on EMG; title adjusted

entries.auditNote: Textbook LMN list, recognized instantly, especially next to the UMN set.

revised.title: Lower motor neuron lesion findings
revised.explanation: Each is a characteristic clinical or electrodiagnostic finding when a muscle loses its lower motor neuron supply.
revised.detail: Damage to anterior horn cells, roots, or peripheral nerves denervates muscle. Clinically this causes atrophy, fasciculations, weakness, hyporeflexia, and reduced tone. On needle EMG, denervated muscle fibers fire spontaneously as fibrillation potentials (and positive sharp waves) a few weeks after injury. Upper motor neuron lesions instead cause spasticity, hyperreflexia, and a Babinski sign with little atrophy.
tileNotes: Fasciculations are visible spontaneous twitches of motor units, typical of anterior horn cell or motor axon disease.
Loss of neural trophic input and disuse causes marked muscle atrophy in lower motor neuron lesions.
Interruption of the reflex arc at the motor neuron, root, or nerve reduces or abolishes deep tendon reflexes.
Spontaneous discharges of single denervated muscle fibers appear on needle EMG a few weeks after lower motor neuron injury.

entries.changeSummary: Replaced 'Hypotonia' with 'Fibrillation potentials on EMG' and changed the title from examination signs to lesion findings.
entries.checkNote: Fibrillation potentials are a standard LMN denervation finding; content accurate.

check.note: Fibrillation potentials are a standard LMN denervation finding; content accurate.

entries.subject: Neurology

original.title: Four medial brainstem localization structures
original.explanation: These motor and sensory structures form the classic 'medial brainstem' localization framework (the 4 M's).

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Neurology.pdf; Brainstem Anatomy; PDF pp. 37

proposal.why: A specific medial motor nucleus replaces the vague collective tile and reduces the mnemonic feel; the hypoglossal nucleus is certainly paramedian.
proposal.changes: Somatic motor cranial nerve nuclei -> Hypoglossal nucleus

entries.auditNote: These are the rule-of-4 '4 M's', two tiles contain 'medial' from the title, and tile 4 is a collective item that overlaps NEU-005.

revised.title: Medial brainstem structures
revised.explanation: Each structure lies near the midline of the brainstem, so a paramedian lesion can damage it.
revised.detail: By the rule of 4, medial brainstem structures are the motor (corticospinal) pathway, the medial lemniscus, the medial longitudinal fasciculus, and the motor nuclei of cranial nerves that divide evenly into 12 (III, IV, VI, XII). Medial medullary syndrome from anterior spinal artery occlusion damages the corticospinal tract, medial lemniscus, and hypoglossal nucleus or nerve. Lateral structures instead include the spinothalamic tract, sympathetic pathway, spinocerebellar tracts, and sensory nucleus of CN V.
tileNotes: The corticospinal tract runs in the ventromedial brainstem (cerebral peduncle, basis pontis, medullary pyramid), so medial lesions cause contralateral hemiparesis.
The medial lemniscus carries dorsal column touch, vibration, and proprioception near the midline; a lesion causes contralateral loss of these modalities.
The MLF runs near the midline throughout the brainstem; a lesion causes internuclear ophthalmoplegia.
The hypoglossal nucleus lies next to the midline in the medulla; a medial medullary lesion causes ipsilateral tongue deviation.

entries.changeSummary: Replaced the collective tile 'Somatic motor cranial nerve nuclei' with 'Hypoglossal nucleus' and removed 'Four' and 'localization' from the title.
entries.checkNote: Hypoglossal nucleus is a correct medial brainstem structure replacing a collective tile.

entries.subject: Neurology

original.title: Functional regions of the frontal lobe
original.explanation: These frontal regions govern voluntary movement, executive behavior, conjugate gaze, and speech production respectively.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Neurology.pdf; Cerebral Cortex; PDF pp. 40

proposal.why: Removes one title-leaking tile; the supplementary motor area is certainly frontal (medial area 6).

entries.auditNote: 'Prefrontal' and 'Frontal eye fields' echo the title, and premotor cortex and the supplementary motor area fit equally.

revised.title: Functional regions of the frontal lobe
revised.explanation: Each is a functional region within the frontal lobe.
revised.detail: The primary motor cortex in the precentral gyrus (area 4) controls contralateral voluntary movement. The supplementary motor area on the medial surface of area 6 plans and sequences movement. The frontal eye fields (area 8) drive voluntary saccades to the opposite side, and Broca area (areas 44 and 45) in the dominant inferior frontal gyrus controls speech production. Nearby regions in other lobes include the primary somatosensory cortex (parietal), Wernicke area (temporal), and primary visual cortex (occipital).
tileNotes: The primary motor cortex occupies the precentral gyrus (Brodmann area 4) of the frontal lobe and controls contralateral voluntary movement.
The supplementary motor area lies on the medial frontal lobe (medial area 6) and plans and sequences movement; lesions cause transient contralateral akinesia and reduced initiation of speech.
The frontal eye fields (area 8) generate voluntary saccades to the opposite side; a destructive lesion causes the eyes to deviate toward the lesion.
Broca area (areas 44 and 45) in the dominant inferior frontal gyrus controls speech production; damage causes nonfluent aphasia.

entries.checkNote: Connection sound; tightened the SMA lesion description.

tileNotes: The primary motor cortex occupies the precentral gyrus (Brodmann area 4) of the frontal lobe and controls contralateral voluntary movement.
The supplementary motor area lies on the medial frontal lobe (medial area 6) and plans and sequences movement; lesions cause transient contralateral akinesia and reduced initiation of speech.
The frontal eye fields (area 8) generate voluntary saccades to the opposite side; a destructive lesion causes the eyes to deviate toward the lesion.
Broca area (areas 44 and 45) in the dominant inferior frontal gyrus controls speech production; damage causes nonfluent aphasia.

entries.subject: Neurology

original.title: Clinical clues supporting multiple sclerosis
original.explanation: Inflammatory CNS demyelination can cause optic nerve dysfunction, MLF-related internuclear gaze dysfunction, heat-related worsening (Uhthoff), and an electric sensation on neck flexion (Lhermitte).

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Neurology.pdf; Demyelinating Disease; PDF pp. 71-74

proposal.why: Trigeminal neuralgia in a young adult is an established MS clue but is usually idiopathic, so it needs reasoning, unlike the MS-only Uhthoff tile.

entries.auditNote: Uhthoff and bilateral INO are taught almost only as MS clues.
entries.reason: Trigeminal neuralgia supports multiple sclerosis only in a young adult or when bilateral, so as a bare tile it carries an unstated exception and is usually idiopathic.

entries.subject: Neurology

original.title: Multiple sclerosis investigation clues
original.explanation: MRI can reveal periventricular demyelinating lesions (including the perivenular 'Dawson fingers' pattern), while CSF may show intrathecal oligoclonal bands and mild lymphocytic inflammation.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Neurology.pdf; Demyelinating Disease; PDF pp. 75

proposal.why: Removes the tile 1/2 overlap; delayed VEP latency is a standard MS investigation finding showing subclinical optic nerve demyelination.
proposal.changes: Periventricular white matter lesions -> Delayed visual evoked potentials

entries.auditNote: Dawson fingers are a subtype of periventricular lesions, so tiles 1 and 2 overlap, and Dawson fingers gives the group away.

revised.title: Multiple sclerosis investigation clues
revised.explanation: Each is a test result that supports multiple sclerosis: slowed conduction in a demyelinated optic pathway, a characteristic MRI lesion pattern, and CSF evidence of intrathecal immune activity.
revised.detail: Multiple sclerosis is supported by paraclinical evidence of CNS demyelination and intrathecal inflammation. Visual evoked potentials can reveal clinically silent optic nerve demyelination as a prolonged P100 latency. MRI shows ovoid periventricular lesions oriented perpendicular to the ventricles (Dawson fingers), and CSF typically shows oligoclonal bands absent from serum with at most a mild lymphocytic pleocytosis. A markedly raised CSF cell count or high protein points away from MS toward infection or another inflammatory process.
tileNotes: Visual evoked potentials measure conduction along the visual pathway. In MS, demyelination of the optic nerve prolongs the P100 latency, which can show a lesion even without a history of optic neuritis.
Dawson fingers are ovoid demyelinating plaques that radiate perpendicular to the lateral ventricles along medullary veins. They are a characteristic MRI pattern of MS.
Oligoclonal IgG bands present in CSF but not in serum indicate antibody synthesis within the CNS. They are found in the large majority of patients with MS.
MS commonly produces a mild lymphocytic CSF pleocytosis, typically under about 50 cells per microliter. Higher counts suggest an alternative diagnosis.

entries.changeSummary: Replaced 'Periventricular white matter lesions', which overlapped with Dawson fingers, with 'Delayed visual evoked potentials'.
entries.checkNote: Delayed VEPs are a standard MS paraclinical clue and remove the MRI tile overlap.

check.note: Delayed VEPs are a standard MS paraclinical clue and remove the MRI tile overlap.

entries.subject: Neurology

original.title: Complete (pupil-involving) CN III palsy findings
original.explanation: A complete oculomotor palsy impairs eyelid elevation and most extraocular muscles; parasympathetic involvement produces mydriasis and a 'down-and-out' eye.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Neurology.pdf; Cranial Nerves I-VI; PDF pp. 98-99

proposal.why: Loss of accommodation (parasympathetic supply to the ciliary muscle) is a certain feature of a complete pupil-involving CN III palsy and replaces both the catchphrase and the redundancy.
proposal.changes: Down-and-out resting eye -> Loss of accommodation

entries.auditNote: 'Down-and-out' is the iconic CN III phrase and tiles 3 and 4 overlap.

revised.title: Complete (pupil-involving) CN III palsy findings
revised.explanation: A complete oculomotor nerve lesion paralyzes levator palpebrae and the extraocular muscles CN III supplies, and interrupts its parasympathetic fibers to the pupillary sphincter and ciliary muscle.
revised.detail: CN III supplies levator palpebrae superioris, the medial, superior and inferior recti and inferior oblique, and carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibers to the ciliary ganglion. The parasympathetic fibers run superficially on the nerve, so compressive lesions such as a posterior communicating artery aneurysm affect them early, producing a dilated pupil and loss of accommodation. Ischemic (diabetic) palsies damage the core of the nerve and classically spare the pupil. The unopposed lateral rectus (CN VI) and superior oblique (CN IV) leave the eye resting down and out.
tileNotes: Levator palpebrae superioris is innervated by CN III, so a complete palsy causes ptosis, often marked.
Loss of parasympathetic supply to the sphincter pupillae leaves the pupil dilated and poorly reactive to light. This is the hallmark of a compressive, pupil-involving lesion.
The medial, superior and inferior recti and inferior oblique are paralyzed, so adduction, elevation and depression are impaired. Abduction (CN VI) and intorsion (CN IV) are preserved.
Parasympathetic fibers from the ciliary ganglion also supply the ciliary muscle. Their loss prevents lens accommodation, so near vision blurs in the affected eye.

entries.changeSummary: Replaced 'Down-and-out resting eye', a catchphrase that overlapped the motility tile, with 'Loss of accommodation'.
entries.checkNote: Loss of accommodation is a correct parasympathetic CN III finding; content accurate.

check.note: Loss of accommodation is a correct parasympathetic CN III finding; content accurate.

entries.subject: Neurology

original.title: Retrochiasmal sites causing homonymous visual field loss
original.explanation: Unilateral lesions posterior to the optic chiasm disrupt corresponding portions of the contralateral visual field in both eyes (homonymous defects).

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Neurology.pdf; Vision; PDF pp. 119-121

proposal.why: A Meyer loop lesion causes a contralateral homonymous superior quadrantanopia, so it is certainly a retrochiasmal homonymous site and it breaks the obvious pathway series.

entries.auditNote: These are the consecutive post-chiasmal visual pathway stations, so the only task is excluding the optic nerve and chiasm.

revised.title: Retrochiasmal sites causing homonymous visual field loss
revised.explanation: A unilateral lesion at any of these sites, all posterior to the optic chiasm, causes a homonymous defect in the contralateral visual field of both eyes.
revised.detail: Behind the chiasm, each side of the visual pathway carries fibers from the ipsilateral temporal retina and contralateral nasal retina, representing the contralateral visual hemifield. Lesions anywhere from the optic tract to the occipital cortex therefore produce homonymous defects. The pattern depends on the site: a complete tract lesion causes a contralateral homonymous hemianopia, a Meyer loop (temporal lobe) lesion causes a contralateral superior quadrantanopia, and an occipital lesion can produce hemianopia with macular sparing. Optic nerve lesions cause monocular loss and chiasmal lesions cause bitemporal hemianopia, so neither is homonymous.
tileNotes: The optic tract runs from the chiasm to the lateral geniculate nucleus. A lesion causes a contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often incongruous.
The lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus relays tract fibers to the optic radiations. A lesion produces a contralateral homonymous field defect.

Meyer loop is the inferior part of the optic radiation that sweeps through the temporal lobe, carrying fibers from the inferior retina. A lesion causes a contralateral homonymous superior quadrantanopia ('pie in the sky').

The primary visual cortex lies along the calcarine fissure of the occipital lobe. A lesion causes a contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often with macular sparing in posterior cerebral artery infarction.

entries.changeSummary: Replaced 'Optic radiations' with 'Meyer loop', its temporal-lobe portion, which breaks the obvious station-by-station pathway series.
entries.checkNote: Meyer loop lesions cause homonymous superior quadrantanopia; content accurate.

check.note: Meyer loop lesions cause homonymous superior quadrantanopia; content accurate.

entries.subject: Neurology

original.title: Causes of conductive hearing loss
original.explanation: These conditions impair external- or middle-ear sound transmission rather than primarily damaging cochlear sensory transduction.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Neurology.pdf; Auditory Sensation; PDF pp. 127

proposal.why: TM perforation is a standard, unambiguous conductive cause and replaces the near-duplicate canal-mass tile.
proposal.changes: Obstructing external canal mass (non-cerumen) -> Tympanic membrane perforation

entries.auditNote: Tile 4 is an awkward near-duplicate of cerumen impaction that needs a 'non-cerumen' qualifier.

revised.title: Causes of conductive hearing loss
revised.explanation: Each impairs transmission of sound through the external or middle ear rather than damaging the cochlea or auditory nerve.
revised.detail: Conductive hearing loss arises when sound cannot reach the inner ear efficiently. On tuning fork testing, bone conduction exceeds air conduction on the affected side (Rinne negative) and the Weber test lateralizes to the affected ear. Sensorineural loss, from cochlear or CN VIII damage (presbycusis, noise, acoustic neuroma), gives Rinne positive with Weber lateralizing to the normal ear.
tileNotes: Impacted cerumen occludes the external auditory canal and blocks sound from reaching the tympanic membrane.
Middle ear effusion or pus in otitis media damps movement of the tympanic membrane and ossicles.
Otosclerosis is abnormal bone remodeling that fixes the stapes footplate in the oval window, typically causing progressive conductive loss in young adults.
A perforated tympanic membrane loses surface area and vibratory efficiency, reducing sound transfer to the ossicles.

entries.changeSummary: Replaced the awkward near-duplicate 'Obstructing external canal mass (non-cerumen)' with 'Tympanic membrane perforation'.
entries.checkNote: TM perforation is a clean conductive cause and removes the awkward near-duplicate tile.

check.note: TM perforation is a clean conductive cause and removes the awkward near-duplicate tile.

entries.subject: Neurology

original.title: Peripheral causes of vertigo
original.explanation: These disorders affect the peripheral vestibular apparatus or CN VIII and can produce vertigo with differing timing and hearing features.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Neurology.pdf; Vertigo; PDF pp. 133-137

proposal.why: Labyrinthitis is an unequivocal peripheral vertigo cause; this removes the weak schwannoma member and one overlap with NEU-025.

entries.auditNote: Vestibular schwannoma rarely causes true vertigo, labyrinthitis is the expected missing member, and two tiles duplicate NEU-025.

revised.title: Peripheral causes of vertigo
revised.explanation: Each disorder affects the inner ear vestibular apparatus or the vestibular nerve, producing true rotational vertigo of peripheral origin.
revised.detail: Peripheral vertigo arises from the labyrinth or vestibular nerve and is usually accompanied by horizontal or torsional nystagmus that is suppressed by visual fixation, without other brainstem signs. The disorders differ by timing and hearing: BPPV causes brief positional episodes, vestibular neuritis causes days of continuous vertigo with normal hearing, labyrinthitis adds hearing loss, and Meniere disease causes recurrent attacks lasting hours with fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness. Central vertigo (cerebellar or brainstem stroke, MS) is the key contrast and may cause vertical or direction-changing nystagmus and other neurologic deficits.
tileNotes: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo is caused by displaced otoconia in a semicircular canal, producing brief vertigo triggered by head position changes.
Vestibular neuritis is inflammation of the vestibular nerve, usually presumed viral, causing acute continuous vertigo lasting days with preserved hearing.
Meniere disease is endolymphatic hydrops causing recurrent vertigo attacks with fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness.
Labyrinthitis is inflammation of the inner ear labyrinth, causing acute vertigo together with sensorineural hearing loss.

entries.changeSummary: Replaced 'Vestibular schwannoma', which more often causes imbalance and hearing loss than true vertigo, with 'Labyrinthitis'.
entries.checkNote: Labyrinthitis is a standard peripheral vertigo cause and replaces the contested schwannoma tile.

check.note: Labyrinthitis is a standard peripheral vertigo cause and replaces the contested schwannoma tile.

entries.subject: Neurology

original.title: Posterior-canal BPPV associations
original.explanation: Displaced otoconia (canaliths) cause brief positional vertigo; posterior-canal BPPV is diagnosed with the Dix-Hallpike maneuver and treated with the Epley canalith-repositioning maneuver.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Neurology.pdf; Vertigo; PDF pp. 133, 137

proposal.why: Torsional upbeating nystagmus is the defining Dix-Hallpike finding in posterior-canal BPPV and asks for more knowledge than 'positional vertigo'.
proposal.changes: Brief position-triggered vertigo -> Torsional upbeating nystagmus

entries.auditNote: Dix-Hallpike plus Epley plus positional vertigo is instantly BPPV.

revised.title: Posterior-canal BPPV associations
revised.explanation: Free-floating otoconia in the posterior semicircular canal cause BPPV, which produces torsional upbeating nystagmus on Dix-Hallpike testing and is treated with the Epley repositioning maneuver.
revised.detail: In posterior-canal BPPV, otoconia detached from the utricle move within the canal when the head changes position, deflecting the cupula. The Dix-Hallpike maneuver provokes, after a short latency, a fatigable burst of upbeating nystagmus with a torsional component toward the lower ear. The Epley maneuver moves the debris back into the utricle. Horizontal-canal BPPV instead produces horizontal nystagmus on the supine roll test and is treated with different maneuvers.
tileNotes: Otoconia (calcium carbonate crystals) displaced from the utricle float freely in the posterior canal endolymph, the mechanism called canalithiasis.

Posterior canal stimulation drives the eyes in that canal's plane, producing upbeating nystagmus with a torsional component toward the lower ear. It is brief, appears after a few seconds' latency, and fatigues with repetition.
The Dix-Hallpike maneuver moves the patient from sitting to supine with the head turned and extended, provoking vertigo and nystagmus from the dependent posterior canal.
The Epley maneuver is a sequence of head positions that moves the otoconia out of the posterior canal into the utricle, treating the vertigo.

entries.changeSummary: Replaced 'Brief position-triggered vertigo' with 'Torsional upbeating nystagmus', the characteristic Dix-Hallpike finding.
entries.checkNote: Torsional upbeating nystagmus is the correct Dix-Hallpike finding and requires more reasoning than the symptom tile.

check.note: Torsional upbeating nystagmus is the correct Dix-Hallpike finding and requires more reasoning than the symptom tile.

original.title: Pilocytic astrocytoma associations
original.explanation: Pilocytic astrocytoma is a low-grade (WHO grade 1) astrocytic tumor, often cystic and cerebellar in children, with GFAP expression and characteristic Rosenthal fibers.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Neurology.pdf; Pediatric Brain Tumors; PDF pp. 142

proposal.why: Removes the 'piloid' echo of the title while keeping the standard histologic description.

entries.auditNote: Rosenthal fibers is a strong clue, and 'piloid' echoes 'pilocytic' in the title.

revised.title: Pilocytic astrocytoma associations
revised.explanation: Pilocytic astrocytoma is a low-grade (WHO grade 1) astrocytic tumor, often a cystic cerebellar mass in children, composed of GFAP-positive bipolar astrocytes with hair-like processes and containing Rosenthal fibers.
revised.detail: Pilocytic astrocytoma is the most common primary brain tumor of childhood and has an excellent prognosis after resection. It classically appears as a cyst with an enhancing mural nodule in the cerebellum, though optic pathway and brainstem sites occur, especially with neurofibromatosis type 1. Histology shows elongated bipolar astrocytes with long, thin processes, eosinophilic Rosenthal fibers and eosinophilic granular bodies. Its well-circumscribed, low-grade behavior contrasts with diffuse astrocytomas and medulloblastoma, the other common posterior fossa tumor of childhood.
tileNotes: Rosenthal fibers are thick, eosinophilic, corkscrew-shaped intracytoplasmic inclusions of glial filaments. They are a characteristic histologic feature of pilocytic astrocytoma.
Glial fibrillary acidic protein is an intermediate filament of astrocytes, so this astrocytic tumor stains positive.
The tumor classically presents as a cerebellar cyst with a mural nodule in a child, causing ataxia or obstructive hydrocephalus.
The tumor cells are bipolar astrocytes with long, thin, hair-like processes, which give the tumor its name ('pilocytic' means hair cell).

entries.changeSummary: Reworded 'Well-differentiated (piloid) astrocytes' to 'Hair-like bipolar astrocytes' so the tile no longer echoes the title term.
entries.checkNote: Accurate rewording of the piloid cell tile with the same meaning; mild gain by removing the title echo.

check.note: Accurate rewording of the piloid cell tile with the same meaning; mild gain by removing the title echo.

entries.subject: Neurology

original.title: Immunodeficiency-associated primary CNS lymphoma clues
original.explanation: Primary CNS lymphoma is usually a CD20-positive B-cell lymphoma (commonly DLBCL); its immunodeficiency-associated form is strongly linked to EBV.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Neurology.pdf; Adult Primary Brain Tumors; PDF pp. 153

proposal.why: A periventricular enhancing mass is the classic PCNSL imaging clue; it anchors the set to the CNS and removes the echo of the title.

entries.auditNote: The tiles fit any immunodeficiency-associated DLBCL (e.g., PTLD), with nothing CNS-specific, and 'Immunocompromised host' echoes the title.

revised.title: Immunodeficiency-associated primary CNS lymphoma clues
revised.explanation: Primary CNS lymphoma in an immunodeficient host is typically an EBV-driven, CD20-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma that presents as an enhancing mass in the deep periventricular brain.
revised.detail: Primary CNS lymphoma is an extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphoma confined to the brain, eyes, leptomeninges or spinal cord. On imaging it favors deep periventricular white matter and the corpus callosum, and in AIDS lesions are often multiple and ring-enhancing, so the main differential is toxoplasmosis. Nearly all cases are diffuse large B-cell lymphomas expressing CD20. EBV is present in almost all immunodeficiency-associated cases (for example AIDS with a low CD4 count), whereas immunocompetent cases are usually EBV-negative.
tileNotes: Primary CNS lymphoma classically forms enhancing lesions in the deep periventricular white matter and corpus callosum. In immunodeficient patients the enhancement is often ring-like, mimicking toxoplasmosis.
The large majority of primary CNS lymphomas are diffuse large B-cell lymphomas.
The tumor cells are mature B cells that express the pan-B-cell marker CD20.
In immunodeficiency, EBV-infected B cells escape T-cell control and drive lymphoma; EBV DNA in CSF supports the diagnosis in AIDS.

entries.changeSummary: Replaced 'Immunocompromised host', which echoed the title, with 'Periventricular enhancing mass', which anchors the set to the CNS.
entries.checkNote: Periventricular enhancing mass is a correct imaging clue and removes the title echo.

check.note: Periventricular enhancing mass is a correct imaging clue and removes the title echo.

entries.subject: Neurology

original.title: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome findings
original.explanation: Lateral medullary injury (PICA/vertebral) affects the nucleus ambiguus, spinal trigeminal nucleus/tract, spinothalamic tract, and descending sympathetic fibers.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Neurology.pdf; Ischemic Cerebrovascular Accidents; PDF pp. 162

proposal.why: Drops the parenthetical nucleus label that does the localization for the player; the clinical meaning is the same.

entries.auditNote: Ipsilateral/contralateral pain-temperature wording and the '(nucleus ambiguus)' label point straight to Wallenberg.

revised.title: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome findings
revised.explanation: A lateral medullary infarct (PICA or vertebral artery) damages the nucleus ambiguus, spinal trigeminal nucleus and tract, lateral spinothalamic tract and descending sympathetic fibers.
revised.detail: Wallenberg syndrome produces a crossed sensory pattern: pain and temperature loss on the ipsilateral face (spinal trigeminal tract) and the contralateral body (spinothalamic tract, which has already crossed). Descending hypothalamospinal sympathetic fibers cause an ipsilateral Horner syndrome, and vestibular and cerebellar involvement add vertigo, nystagmus and ipsilateral ataxia. Involvement of the nucleus ambiguus (hoarseness, dysphagia, reduced gag) localizes the lesion to the medulla rather than the lateral pons, where facial nucleus involvement and hearing loss occur instead.
tileNotes: Damage to the nucleus ambiguus weakens the ipsilateral palatal, pharyngeal and laryngeal muscles (CN IX and X), causing hoarseness and dysphagia. This is the localizing sign for the medulla.
The spinal trigeminal nucleus and tract carry pain and temperature from the ipsilateral face, so their damage causes ipsilateral facial loss.
The lateral spinothalamic tract has already crossed in the spinal cord, so a lateral medullary lesion causes pain and temperature loss in the contralateral trunk and limbs.
Interruption of descending sympathetic fibers in the lateral medulla produces ipsilateral ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis.

entries.changeSummary: Reworded 'Dysphagia/dysphonia (nucleus ambiguus)' to 'Hoarseness and dysphagia', removing the localizing nucleus label.
entries.checkNote: Same clinical meaning without the localizing nucleus label; accurate.

check.note: Same clinical meaning without the localizing nucleus label; accurate.

entries.subject: Neurology

original.title: Epidural hematoma associations
original.explanation: A traumatic epidural hematoma classically involves middle meningeal arterial bleeding outside the dura with a biconvex CT collection that does not cross suture lines; some patients have a transient lucid interval.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Neurology.pdf; Aneurysms and Intracranial Hemorrhage; PDF pp. 171

proposal.why: A pterion (temporal bone) fracture and confinement by sutures are certain epidural features that need one more inferential step than naming the artery and shape, and they pair as a discrimination with the subdural set.
proposal.changes: Middle meningeal artery injury -> Pterion fracture; Biconvex (lentiform) CT collection -> Does not cross suture lines

entries.auditNote: Middle meningeal artery plus biconvex plus lucid interval is the iconic epidural triad.

revised.title: Epidural hematoma associations
revised.explanation: Epidural hematoma is classically arterial bleeding from a middle meningeal artery torn by a skull fracture at the pterion; the blood strips dura from the skull and is confined by the sutures, and some patients have a lucid interval.
revised.detail: The pterion is the thin junction of the frontal, parietal, temporal and sphenoid bones, and the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery runs beneath it. A fracture here tears the artery, and the blood collects between the skull and the periosteal dura. Because the dura is firmly attached at the sutures, the collection cannot spread past them and forms a biconvex shape on CT. A subdural hematoma, by contrast, results from torn bridging veins, lies beneath the dura, crosses suture lines and is crescent-shaped.
tileNotes: A temporal-region fracture at the pterion overlies and can tear the middle meningeal artery, the classic source of epidural bleeding.
The hematoma lies in the potential space between the inner table of the skull and the dura, which it strips away from the bone.
The dura is tightly adherent to the skull at the sutures, so an epidural collection is bounded by them, giving its biconvex (lentiform) shape on CT.
Some patients briefly lose consciousness, recover, then deteriorate as the arterial hematoma expands. It is a classic but inconsistent feature.

entries.changeSummary: Replaced 'Middle meningeal artery injury' with 'Pterion fracture' and 'Biconvex (lentiform) CT collection' with 'Does not cross suture lines'.
entries.checkNote: Pterion fracture and suture-bounded collection are classic, accurate epidural associations requiring more reasoning.

check.note: Pterion fracture and suture-bounded collection are classic, accurate epidural associations requiring more reasoning.

entries.subject: Neurology

original.title: Subdural hematoma associations
original.explanation: Bridging-vein injury produces a crescentic subdural collection that can cross suture lines; cerebral atrophy (elderly, alcohol use) increases susceptibility.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Neurology.pdf; Aneurysms and Intracranial Hemorrhage; PDF pp. 171

proposal.why: Crossing suture lines is a certain subdural feature and creates a direct discrimination with the epidural 'does not cross suture lines' tile.
proposal.changes: Crescent-shaped (concave) CT collection -> Crosses suture lines

entries.auditNote: Bridging veins plus crescent shape is the iconic subdural pair.

revised.title: Subdural hematoma associations
revised.explanation: Subdural hematoma results from tearing of bridging veins, so blood collects beneath the dura, can spread across suture lines, and occurs more easily when cerebral atrophy stretches those veins.
revised.detail: Bridging veins cross the subdural space from the cortex to the dural venous sinuses, and acceleration-deceleration forces can tear them. Because the collection lies beneath the dura, it is not limited by sutures and spreads over the hemisphere as a crescent on CT, though it does not cross the midline falx. Brain atrophy in older adults and people with chronic alcohol use stretches the veins and widens the subdural space, increasing risk; infants (abusive head trauma) and anticoagulated patients are also at risk. Epidural hematoma is the contrast: arterial, above the dura, and bounded by sutures.
tileNotes: Bridging veins run from the cerebral cortex to the dural sinuses and tear with acceleration-deceleration injury, the classic source of subdural bleeding.
The blood collects in the subdural space between the inner dural layer and the arachnoid.
Because the collection lies beneath the dura, the sutures do not limit it, and it spreads along the convexity as a crescent-shaped collection.
Cerebral atrophy stretches the bridging veins across a wider subdural space, so older adults can develop a subdural hematoma after minor trauma, often chronic.

entries.changeSummary: Replaced 'Crescent-shaped (concave) CT collection' with 'Crosses suture lines'.
entries.checkNote: Crossing suture lines is a correct subdural feature and pairs well with the epidural contrast.

check.note: Crossing suture lines is a correct subdural feature and pairs well with the epidural contrast.

entries.subject: Neurology

original.title: Subarachnoid hemorrhage clues
tiles: Blood in basal cisterns on CT
original.explanation: Blood in the subarachnoid space (often ruptured aneurysm) causes abrupt severe headache and meningeal irritation and may be seen in the basal cisterns on CT or detected as CSF xanthochromia.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Neurology.pdf; Aneurysms and Intracranial Hemorrhage; PDF pp. 171, 173

tiles: Blood in basal cisterns on CT
proposal.title: Subarachnoid hemorrhage associations
proposal.why: Delayed vasospasm (classically days 3 to 14) is a certain SAH association that needs recall beyond the presenting headache; 'associations' in the title covers a complication.
proposal.changes: Thunderclap headache -> Delayed cerebral vasospasm; title clues -> associations

entries.auditNote: 'Thunderclap headache' plus xanthochromia is instantly SAH.

revised.title: Subarachnoid hemorrhage associations
tiles: Blood in basal cisterns on CT
revised.explanation: Blood in the subarachnoid space, most often from a ruptured saccular aneurysm, irritates the meninges, appears in the basal cisterns on CT, is broken down to give CSF xanthochromia, and can trigger vasospasm days later.
revised.detail: Aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage classically presents with a sudden severe headache. Noncontrast CT shows hyperdense blood in the basal cisterns and sulci and is most sensitive early; if CT is negative, lumbar puncture after several hours can show xanthochromia from hemoglobin breakdown. Blood breakdown products around the cerebral arteries can cause vasospasm, typically between days 3 and 14, leading to delayed ischemic deficits; nimodipine is given to improve outcome. Rebleeding, hydrocephalus and hyponatremia are other complications.
tileNotes: Arterial narrowing provoked by blood breakdown products in the subarachnoid space typically occurs 3 to 14 days after the bleed and can cause delayed cerebral ischemia.
Subarachnoid blood irritates the meninges, producing neck stiffness, often developing hours after the bleed.
Acute subarachnoid blood is hyperdense on noncontrast CT and collects in the basal cisterns around the circle of Willis.
Red cells lysed in CSF release hemoglobin, which is converted to bilirubin over several hours, giving the CSF a yellow color. This helps distinguish true hemorrhage from a traumatic tap.

entries.changeSummary: Replaced 'Thunderclap headache' with 'Delayed cerebral vasospasm' and changed the title from 'clues' to 'associations' to cover a complication.
entries.checkNote: Vasospasm is a classic SAH association; retitling to associations keeps the set accurate and removes the thunderclap giveaway.

check.note: Vasospasm is a classic SAH association; retitling to associations keeps the set accurate and removes the thunderclap giveaway.

original.title: Cerebellar dysfunction examination signs
original.explanation: Cerebellar dysfunction impairs movement accuracy (dysmetria), rapid alternating movement (dysdiadochokinesia), target-directed movement (intention tremor), and axial balance (truncal ataxia).

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Neurology.pdf; Ischemic Cerebrovascular Accidents; Cerebellum and Ventricles; PDF pp. 162, 181

proposal.why: Scanning (ataxic) speech is a certain cerebellar sign that also pulls toward MS (Charcot triad), so it adds discrimination and removes one 'dys-' tile.

entries.auditNote: Straight from the DANISH mnemonic; all four are textbook cerebellar signs.
entries.reason: Cosmetic: scanning speech is the 'S' of the same DANISH mnemonic, so the swap leaves all four tiles straight from that list with no gain in reasoning.

entries.subject: Neurology

original.title: Parinaud (dorsal midbrain) syndrome clues
original.explanation: A pineal-region or dorsal midbrain lesion disrupts pretectal eye-movement circuitry (posterior commissure, riMLF) and can obstruct the cerebral aqueduct, causing hydrocephalus.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Neurology.pdf; Diencephalon; PDF pp. 192

proposal.why: The slash inside tile 4 reads like two tiles and is clumsy; same meaning in standard terms.

entries.auditNote: Classic Parinaud signs; light-near dissociation and vertical gaze palsy also point to PSP/neurosyphilis, giving some discrimination.

revised.title: Parinaud (dorsal midbrain) syndrome clues
revised.explanation: A dorsal midbrain lesion, classically a pineal region tumor, disrupts pretectal and posterior commissure eye-movement pathways and can compress the cerebral aqueduct, causing obstructive hydrocephalus.
revised.detail: Parinaud syndrome results from damage to the dorsal midbrain at the level of the superior colliculus and posterior commissure, most often from a pineal germinoma in a young male, but also from hydrocephalus, midbrain stroke or MS. The core eye findings are impaired upgaze, pupils that react poorly to light but constrict with near effort, convergence-retraction nystagmus on attempted upgaze and eyelid retraction (Collier sign). Compression of the aqueduct of Sylvius blocks CSF outflow from the third ventricle, causing noncommunicating hydrocephalus. Light-near dissociation also occurs with neurosyphilis (Argyll Robertson pupils) and vertical gaze palsy with progressive supranuclear palsy, which are look-alikes.
tileNotes: Damage to the vertical gaze centers and posterior commissure in the dorsal midbrain impairs upward gaze first.
The pretectal light reflex pathway is interrupted while the more ventral near-response pathway is spared, so the pupils constrict to accommodation but not to light.
On attempted upgaze, the eyes converge and retract into the orbits in jerky movements, a characteristic sign of dorsal midbrain dysfunction.
A pineal region mass compresses the cerebral aqueduct, blocking CSF flow and causing noncommunicating hydrocephalus, which can itself worsen the dorsal midbrain signs.

original.title: Major dopaminergic pathways
original.explanation: These four classic dopamine circuits underlie reward/positive psychotic symptoms, cortical/negative symptoms, movement, and prolactin inhibition respectively.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Neurology.pdf; Neurotransmitter Activity in Psychiatric Disease; PDF pp. 200

proposal.why: Removes the repeated 'pathway' stem; the bare names are the standard terms.

entries.auditNote: The four named dopamine pathways form a memorized set and all end in 'pathway'.

revised.title: Major dopaminergic pathways
revised.explanation: These are the four classic dopamine pathways, which mediate reward and positive psychotic symptoms, cognition and negative symptoms, motor control, and inhibition of prolactin release respectively.
revised.detail: Dopamine pathways explain both the therapeutic and adverse effects of antipsychotics. D2 blockade in the mesolimbic pathway reduces positive symptoms, while reduced mesocortical activity is linked to negative and cognitive symptoms. Blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway causes extrapyramidal symptoms, and in the tuberoinfundibular pathway it removes dopamine's inhibition of prolactin, causing hyperprolactinemia with galactorrhea and amenorrhea.
tileNotes: The mesolimbic pathway projects from the ventral tegmental area to the nucleus accumbens and limbic structures. Overactivity is associated with positive psychotic symptoms, and it is the main target of antipsychotics.
The mesocortical pathway projects from the ventral tegmental area to the prefrontal cortex. Reduced activity is associated with negative and cognitive symptoms of schizophrenia.

The nigrostriatal pathway projects from the substantia nigra pars compacta to the striatum and controls movement. Its degeneration causes Parkinson disease and its blockade causes extrapyramidal symptoms.
The tuberoinfundibular pathway projects from the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus to the median eminence, where dopamine inhibits prolactin secretion. Blockade causes hyperprolactinemia.

original.title: Alzheimer disease neuropathology clues
original.explanation: Alzheimer pathology features extracellular amyloid-beta plaques and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles made of hyperphosphorylated tau; vascular amyloid deposition (CAA) commonly coexists.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Neurology.pdf; Dementia; PDF pp. 204

proposal.why: Tau is the constituent of tangles (redundant); Hirano bodies are a standard Alzheimer histologic finding (hippocampus) and add a distinct teaching point.

entries.auditNote: Plaques and tangles are instant; hyperphosphorylated tau duplicates the tangle tile.

revised.title: Alzheimer disease neuropathology clues
revised.explanation: Alzheimer disease brains show extracellular amyloid-beta plaques, intracellular tau tangles, eosinophilic Hirano bodies in the hippocampus, and frequent amyloid deposition in vessel walls.
revised.detail: Alzheimer disease causes diffuse cortical atrophy, most marked in the hippocampus and temporal and parietal cortex, with enlarged ventricles and sulci. Microscopically, neuritic plaques with an amyloid-beta core and neurofibrillary tangles of hyperphosphorylated tau are the defining lesions, and tangle burden correlates best with dementia severity. Hirano bodies and granulovacuolar degeneration occur in hippocampal neurons, and amyloid-beta in cortical and leptomeningeal vessel walls (cerebral amyloid angiopathy) commonly coexists and predisposes to lobar hemorrhage. Look-alike inclusions include Lewy bodies (alpha-synuclein) and Pick bodies (tau in frontotemporal dementia).
tileNotes: Extracellular deposits of amyloid-beta, cleaved from amyloid precursor protein, form senile (neuritic) plaques in the cortex.
Intracellular aggregates of hyperphosphorylated tau form neurofibrillary tangles inside neurons. Their number correlates with the degree of dementia.
Hirano bodies are eosinophilic, rod-shaped intracellular inclusions rich in actin, found in hippocampal neurons and associated with Alzheimer disease.
Amyloid-beta deposits in the walls of cortical and meningeal vessels in most Alzheimer brains, weakening them and predisposing to lobar intracerebral hemorrhage.

original.title: Potentially treatable contributors to cognitive impairment
original.explanation: These are potentially treatable conditions that can contribute to or mimic a dementia presentation and should be screened for in cognitive decline.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Neurology.pdf; Dementia; PDF pp. 210

proposal.why: '(pseudodementia)' states the connection outright and 'Thyroid disease (hypothyroidism)' is redundant; meaning unchanged.

entries.auditNote: Standard reversible-dementia screen; normal pressure hydrocephalus is the obvious missing member, and the parentheticals give the link away.

revised.title: Potentially treatable contributors to cognitive impairment
revised.explanation: Each is a treatable condition that can cause or mimic cognitive decline and is screened for when evaluating dementia.
revised.detail: The workup of cognitive impairment looks for conditions whose treatment can improve cognition: depression, hypothyroidism, vitamin B12 deficiency and neurosyphilis are classic examples, along with normal pressure hydrocephalus and medication effects. Depression can mimic dementia (pseudodementia) and typically improves with treatment. Established neurologic damage from B12 deficiency or neurosyphilis may not fully reverse, so these are better called treatable than reversible. Neurodegenerative dementias such as Alzheimer disease are the contrast group.
tileNotes: Depression in older adults can present with poor concentration and memory complaints that mimic dementia (pseudodementia) and improve when the depression is treated.
Thyroid hormone deficiency slows cognition and causes memory problems that can improve with levothyroxine replacement.
Tertiary syphilis can cause a progressive dementia (general paresis). Penicillin can halt progression, although established deficits may persist.
Cobalamin deficiency can cause cognitive impairment along with subacute combined degeneration and megaloblastic anemia, and it is treatable with B12 replacement.

original.title: Generalized-onset seizure types
original.explanation: These are classic generalized-onset seizure forms distinguished by awareness change and motor pattern.

proposal.changes: Dropped 'seizure' from all tiles and 'Generalized' from tile 2.

revised.title: Generalized-onset seizure types
revised.explanation: These are classic generalized-onset seizure types, which begin in bilateral cortical networks and differ by impairment of awareness and motor pattern.
revised.detail: Generalized-onset seizures engage both hemispheres from the start, in contrast to focal-onset seizures, which begin in one hemisphere and may spread. Absence seizures cause brief staring with 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges, tonic-clonic seizures cause stiffening followed by rhythmic jerking, myoclonic seizures cause brief shock-like jerks, and atonic seizures cause sudden loss of tone and drop attacks. Under the 2017 ILAE classification, tonic-clonic, myoclonic and atonic seizures can also have focal or unknown onset, so the title specifies generalized onset.
tileNotes: Absence seizures are brief episodes of staring and impaired awareness without postictal confusion, with 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges on EEG. They are always generalized in onset.
Tonic-clonic seizures begin with generalized stiffening followed by rhythmic jerking of all limbs, usually with postictal confusion.
Myoclonic seizures are brief, shock-like muscle jerks, as in juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, typically without loss of awareness.
Atonic seizures cause sudden loss of postural tone, producing head drops or falls (drop attacks).

original.title: Gq-coupled receptors
original.explanation: Each couples preferentially to Gq/11, activating phospholipase C-beta to generate IP3 and DAG and raise intracellular calcium.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Pharmacology.pdf; Autonomic System > Autonomic Secondary Messengers and Other Involuntary Signaling Systems, pp. 25, 27

proposal.why: Removes the repeated 'receptor' stem; bare receptor names are standard.

entries.auditNote: 'HAVe 1 M&M' mnemonic; all four end in 'receptor'.

revised.title: Gq-coupled receptors
revised.explanation: Each receptor couples preferentially to Gq, which activates phospholipase C to generate IP3 and DAG, raising intracellular calcium and activating protein kinase C.
revised.detail: Gq-coupled receptors signal through phospholipase C-beta, which cleaves PIP2 into IP3 (releasing calcium from the endoplasmic reticulum) and DAG (activating protein kinase C). Other Gq receptors include V1, AT1 and 5-HT2. The contrast groups are Gs receptors (beta-1, beta-2, D1, H2, V2), which raise cAMP, and Gi receptors (M2, alpha-2, D2), which lower it.
tileNotes: The M1 muscarinic receptor is found in the CNS and enteric nervous system and signals through Gq.
The M3 muscarinic receptor mediates smooth muscle contraction (bladder, bronchi, gut), exocrine secretion and nitric oxide release from endothelium, via Gq.
The alpha-1 adrenergic receptor causes vascular smooth muscle contraction, mydriasis and bladder sphincter contraction through Gq signaling.
The H1 histamine receptor mediates bronchoconstriction, increased vascular permeability, pruritus and nasal mucus production through Gq.

original.title: Gs-coupled receptors
original.explanation: Each couples preferentially to Gs, stimulating adenylyl cyclase and raising cAMP.

revised.title: Gs-coupled receptors
revised.explanation: Each receptor couples preferentially to Gs, which stimulates adenylyl cyclase, raises cAMP and activates protein kinase A.
revised.detail: Gs-coupled receptors increase cAMP through adenylyl cyclase, and the resulting protein kinase A activity produces the tissue effect. Other Gs receptors include H2 and D5. Gi receptors (M2, alpha-2, D2) inhibit adenylyl cyclase, and Gq receptors (M1, M3, alpha-1, H1, V1) act through phospholipase C instead.
tileNotes: The beta-1 adrenergic receptor increases heart rate and contractility and stimulates renin release through Gs and cAMP.
The beta-2 adrenergic receptor relaxes bronchial, vascular and uterine smooth muscle and promotes glycogenolysis through Gs.
The D1 dopamine receptor relaxes renal vascular smooth muscle and modulates striatal motor circuits through Gs.
The V2 vasopressin receptor in the renal collecting duct raises cAMP, driving aquaporin-2 insertion and water reabsorption.

original.title: Classic narcolepsy symptom tetrad
original.explanation: Narcolepsy can combine excessive daytime sleepiness with REM-intrusion phenomena: cataplexy, sleep paralysis, and hypnagogic/hypnopompic hallucinations.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Psychiatry.pdf; Sleep and Psychosomatic Conditions / Sleep Disorders; PDF p. 50

proposal.why: Cuts the repeated 'sleep' stem to two tiles using the standard term with identical meaning.

entries.auditNote: Classic narcolepsy tetrad; three tiles contain 'sleep'.

revised.title: Classic narcolepsy symptom tetrad
revised.explanation: Narcolepsy combines excessive daytime sleepiness with intrusion of REM sleep phenomena into wakefulness: cataplexy, sleep paralysis and hallucinations at sleep onset or awakening.
revised.detail: Narcolepsy type 1 results from loss of hypothalamic orexin (hypocretin) neurons, which normally stabilize wakefulness and suppress REM sleep. Patients enter REM sleep abnormally quickly (sleep-onset REM periods on polysomnography and the multiple sleep latency test), and REM features such as muscle atonia and dreaming intrude into waking. Cataplexy defines type 1 and is absent in type 2, and only a minority of patients have all four features. Treatment includes modafinil or stimulants for sleepiness and sodium oxybate for cataplexy.
tileNotes: Recurrent irresistible sleepiness and lapses into sleep during the day are present in all patients and are usually the first symptom.
Cataplexy is sudden, brief loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotion such as laughter, with preserved consciousness. It is REM atonia intruding into wakefulness and defines narcolepsy type 1.
Sleep paralysis is a brief inability to move while falling asleep or waking up, caused by persistent REM atonia.
Vivid dream-like hallucinations occur at sleep onset (hypnagogic) or on awakening (hypnopompic), reflecting REM dream activity intruding into wakefulness.

original.title: Clinical clues to anorexia-related undernutrition
original.explanation: Prolonged undernutrition in anorexia can produce fine lanugo hair, reproductive suppression (amenorrhea), reduced bone density, and nutrient deficits; these are complications, not mandatory criteria.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Psychiatry.pdf; Anxiety, Trauma, and Stress Disorders / Eating Disorders; PDF p. 29

proposal.why: Sinus bradycardia is a standard, discrete clinical finding of anorexia-related undernutrition; the vague 'Nutritional deficiencies' tile is not a specific clue.

entries.auditNote: Lanugo plus amenorrhea gives it away; 'Nutritional deficiencies' is a broad category, not a discrete clinical clue.

revised.title: Clinical clues to anorexia-related undernutrition
revised.explanation: Prolonged starvation in anorexia nervosa produces fine lanugo hair, suppression of the reproductive axis, loss of bone density and a slow resting heart rate; these are complications, not diagnostic criteria.
revised.detail: Anorexia nervosa causes adaptive and harmful changes across organ systems as the body conserves energy. Low leptin and suppressed GnRH cause hypothalamic amenorrhea and low estrogen, which, together with low body weight and high cortisol, leads to bone loss. Increased vagal tone and reduced metabolic demand cause sinus bradycardia and hypotension, and lanugo develops as an adaptation to heat loss. Refeeding syndrome (hypophosphatemia) is a key risk during treatment.
tileNotes: Lanugo is fine, soft, downy hair that grows on the face, back and limbs in severe undernutrition.
Suppressed hypothalamic GnRH secretion causes low LH, FSH and estrogen, leading to amenorrhea. It is common but no longer a required DSM-5 criterion.
Estrogen deficiency, low body weight and elevated cortisol reduce bone mineral density, causing osteopenia or osteoporosis and fracture risk.
Increased vagal tone and reduced metabolic rate cause sinus bradycardia, a common finding that can be marked in severe undernutrition.

entries.changeSummary: Replaced the broad 'Nutritional deficiencies' tile with 'Bradycardia', a discrete clinical finding.
entries.checkNote: Bradycardia is a discrete, well-established starvation finding replacing a vague category tile.

original.title: SSRIs inhibiting serotonin reuptake
original.explanation: These selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors raise synaptic serotonin by inhibiting the serotonin transporter.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Psychiatry.pdf; Psychiatric Pharmacology / SSRIs; PDF p. 74

proposal.why: Escitalopram duplicates citalopram (S-enantiomer); paroxetine is certainly an SSRI and adds a distinct teaching point (most anticholinergic, discontinuation syndrome).

entries.auditNote: Best-known SSRIs; citalopram and escitalopram are an enantiomer pair, so one tile gives away the other.

revised.title: SSRIs inhibiting serotonin reuptake
revised.explanation: These selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors block the presynaptic serotonin transporter, raising synaptic serotonin.
revised.detail: SSRIs are first-line treatment for depression and anxiety disorders and have a delayed therapeutic onset of several weeks. Members differ in important ways: fluoxetine has the longest half-life (lowest discontinuation risk), paroxetine is the most anticholinergic with the worst discontinuation syndrome, citalopram prolongs the QT interval in a dose-dependent way, and sertraline is widely used with few interactions. All can cause sexual dysfunction and, combined with other serotonergic drugs, serotonin syndrome. SNRIs (venlafaxine, duloxetine) and TCAs also block serotonin reuptake but are not selective.
tileNotes: Citalopram is an SSRI notable for dose-dependent QT prolongation.
Paroxetine is an SSRI with the most anticholinergic effects, a short half-life and a prominent discontinuation syndrome.
Sertraline is an SSRI commonly used for depression, anxiety disorders and PTSD.
Fluoxetine is an SSRI with a long-acting active metabolite (norfluoxetine), which minimizes discontinuation symptoms.

entries.changeSummary: Replaced 'Escitalopram', the S-enantiomer of citalopram, with 'Paroxetine'.
entries.checkNote: Paroxetine removes the enantiomer near-duplicate; notes are accurate.

original.title: Tricyclic antidepressants
original.explanation: These TCAs act via monoamine reuptake inhibition and have clinically important receptor-blocking (anticholinergic, antihistaminic, alpha-adrenergic) effects; relative serotonin vs norepinephrine effects differ.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Psychiatry.pdf; Psychiatric Pharmacology / Tricyclic Antidepressants; PDF p. 76

proposal.why: Nortriptyline repeats the '-triptyline' stem of amitriptyline (and is its metabolite); doxepin is certainly a TCA without the revealing suffix.

revised.title: Tricyclic antidepressants
revised.explanation: These tricyclic antidepressants inhibit serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake and also block muscarinic, histamine H1 and alpha-1 receptors.
revised.detail: TCAs share a three-ring structure and inhibit reuptake of norepinephrine and serotonin, with clomipramine the most serotonergic. Receptor blockade causes anticholinergic effects, sedation and orthostatic hypotension. In overdose, sodium channel blockade causes QRS widening and arrhythmias, along with seizures and coma. Tetracyclic drugs (maprotiline) and newer agents (SSRIs, SNRIs, mirtazapine) are the look-alike categories.
tileNotes: Amitriptyline is a tertiary amine TCA used for depression, neuropathic pain and migraine prophylaxis. It is strongly anticholinergic and sedating.
Doxepin is a tertiary amine TCA with potent H1 blockade, used for depression and, at low doses, insomnia and pruritus.
Imipramine is the prototypical TCA, also used for nocturnal enuresis.
Clomipramine is the most serotonergic TCA and is used for obsessive-compulsive disorder.

original.title: Lithium-associated adverse effects
original.explanation: Lithium impairs renal concentrating ability (nephrogenic DI), can cause hypothyroidism and fine tremor as patient adverse effects; prenatal exposure carries a classic association with Ebstein anomaly.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Psychiatry.pdf; Psychiatric Pharmacology / Lithium; PDF p. 85

proposal.why: Ebstein anomaly is the instant lithium cue and belongs to a different exposure context (prenatal). Lithium-associated hyperparathyroidism with hypercalcemia is a well-established patient adverse effect.

entries.auditNote: Ebstein anomaly plus nephrogenic DI is a textbook lithium giveaway, and Ebstein is a fetal exposure effect mixed in with patient adverse effects.

revised.title: Lithium-associated adverse effects
revised.explanation: Long-term lithium impairs renal water reabsorption, thyroid hormone release and parathyroid calcium sensing, and commonly causes a fine tremor.
revised.detail: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index and requires monitoring of serum levels, renal function, thyroid function and calcium. It enters collecting duct cells through ENaC and blocks the ADH response, causing polyuria and nephrogenic DI. It inhibits thyroid hormone release, causing hypothyroidism and goiter, and raises the parathyroid set point for calcium, causing hyperparathyroidism with hypercalcemia. Fine tremor is common at therapeutic levels, while coarse tremor, ataxia and confusion suggest toxicity. Ebstein anomaly is a separate prenatal exposure association.
tileNotes: Lithium accumulates in collecting duct principal cells and impairs the response to ADH, causing polyuria and polydipsia. Amiloride can reduce it.
Lithium inhibits thyroid hormone synthesis and release, causing hypothyroidism and goiter.
A fine postural tremor is a common adverse effect at therapeutic levels; a coarse tremor suggests toxicity.
Lithium shifts the parathyroid calcium-sensing set point upward, causing hyperparathyroidism and hypercalcemia.
