original.title: Classic neuroleptic malignant syndrome findings
original.explanation: NMS classically combines hyperthermia, marked (lead-pipe) rigidity, altered mental status, and autonomic instability after dopamine blockade.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Psychiatry.pdf; Psychiatric Pharmacology / Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome; PDF pp. 88-89

proposal.why: The four tiles are the memorized NMS tetrad (FARM). A markedly elevated CK is a classic, defining NMS lab finding, and swapping it in for fever breaks the mnemonic without losing accuracy.

entries.auditNote: These four tiles are the memorized NMS tetrad (FARM), and lead-pipe rigidity alone gives it away.

revised.title: Classic neuroleptic malignant syndrome findings
revised.explanation: After dopamine D2 blockade, neuroleptic malignant syndrome produces severe lead-pipe rigidity with muscle breakdown (high CK), altered mental status and autonomic instability.
revised.detail: NMS is a rare, potentially fatal reaction to dopamine antagonists, typically developing over days, and can also follow abrupt withdrawal of dopaminergic drugs in Parkinson disease. Its features are hyperthermia, generalized rigidity, altered mental status and autonomic instability, with markedly elevated CK and possible myoglobinuric renal failure. Treatment is stopping the drug, supportive care, and dantrolene or bromocriptine. Serotonin syndrome shares fever, confusion and autonomic instability but has rapid onset with clonus and hyperreflexia rather than lead-pipe rigidity.
tileNotes: Sustained muscle rigidity causes rhabdomyolysis, so creatine kinase is markedly elevated, often to many thousands of units per liter, with risk of myoglobinuric renal failure.
Uniform, generalized resistance to passive movement throughout the range of motion results from central dopamine blockade. It distinguishes NMS from serotonin syndrome.
Confusion, agitation or reduced consciousness progressing to stupor is a core feature.
Labile blood pressure, tachycardia, tachypnea and diaphoresis reflect autonomic dysregulation.

original.title: Mesonephric duct derivatives
original.explanation: The male internal reproductive ducts develop from the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct under testosterone stimulation.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Reproduction.pdf; Fetal Development > Sexual Differentiation, PDF p. 9

proposal.why: Swapping in the female mesonephric remnant breaks the SEED mnemonic and makes players think about the duct's fate in both sexes. A Gartner duct is certainly a mesonephric duct remnant.

entries.auditNote: These four tiles spell the SEED mnemonic for Wolffian derivatives exactly.

revised.title: Mesonephric duct derivatives
revised.explanation: Each structure develops from the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct: in males under testosterone stimulation, and in females as a vestigial remnant when the duct regresses.
revised.detail: In males, testosterone from Leydig cells maintains the mesonephric duct, which forms the epididymis, ductus deferens, seminal vesicles and ejaculatory ducts. In females, the absence of testosterone allows the duct to regress, leaving remnants such as Gartner duct in the lateral vaginal wall, which can form Gartner duct cysts. The paramesonephric (Mullerian) duct is the contrast: it forms the fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix and upper vagina in females and leaves the appendix testis in males.
tileNotes: The epididymis forms from the cranial part of the mesonephric duct and stores and matures sperm.
Gartner duct is the vestigial mesonephric duct remnant in females, lying along the lateral wall of the vagina or uterus, where it can form a Gartner duct cyst.
The seminal vesicle buds from the distal mesonephric duct and produces most of the seminal fluid, including fructose.
The ejaculatory duct forms from the terminal mesonephric duct beyond the seminal vesicle and opens into the prostatic urethra.

original.title: Neural crest derivatives
original.explanation: Neural crest cells give rise to melanocytes, adrenal medullary chromaffin cells, peripheral (sensory/autonomic) neurons, and the forebrain leptomeninges (pia-arachnoid).

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Reproduction.pdf; Fetal Development > Germ Layers, PDF p. 5

proposal.why: Leptomeninges are only partly neural crest-derived (forebrain only). Odontoblasts are an unambiguous neural crest derivative.

entries.auditNote: Only forebrain leptomeninges come from neural crest, so that tile needs an unstated exception.

revised.title: Neural crest derivatives
revised.explanation: Neural crest cells migrate from the dorsal neural tube and give rise to melanocytes, adrenal medullary chromaffin cells, sensory and autonomic neurons, and the odontoblasts of the teeth.
revised.detail: Neural crest cells delaminate from the edges of the neural folds and migrate widely. Their derivatives include peripheral sensory and autonomic ganglia, Schwann cells, melanocytes, chromaffin cells, parafollicular C cells of the thyroid, odontoblasts and much of the craniofacial skeleton. Defective migration explains Hirschsprung disease. The contrast is neuroectoderm (neural tube), which forms the CNS, including central neurons, oligodendrocytes and astrocytes.
tileNotes: Melanocytes migrate from the neural crest to the skin, hair follicles and uveal tract.
Chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla are neural crest-derived modified postganglionic sympathetic neurons that secrete epinephrine and norepinephrine.
Neurons of the dorsal root ganglia, autonomic ganglia and enteric plexuses, and many cranial sensory ganglion neurons, arise from neural crest, unlike CNS neurons.
Odontoblasts, which produce tooth dentin, arise from cranial neural crest mesenchyme.

revised.title: Risk factors for placental abruption
revised.explanation: Each increases the risk of premature separation of the placenta from the uterine wall, through vasoconstriction and vascular injury, hypertensive placental vasculopathy, or shearing force.
revised.detail: Placental abruption presents with painful vaginal bleeding, a tender, firm uterus and possible fetal distress or DIC. Risk factors include hypertension and preeclampsia, cocaine, smoking, abdominal trauma (such as motor vehicle collision or assault), prior abruption and rapid uterine decompression. Placenta previa is the contrast: typically painless bleeding from a placenta covering the cervical os, with risk factors of prior cesarean delivery and multiparity.

Smoking causes decidual vasculopathy and placental ischemia, roughly doubling the risk of abruption.
Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy damage decidual spiral arteries, predisposing to abruption.
Blunt abdominal trauma, such as a motor vehicle collision, can shear the inelastic placenta from the elastic uterine wall.

revised.title: States of prolonged unopposed estrogen exposure
revised.explanation: Each exposes the endometrium to estrogen over a long period without adequate progesterone opposition, promoting endometrial hyperplasia and type I endometrial carcinoma.
revised.detail: Progesterone, produced after ovulation, opposes estrogen-driven endometrial proliferation. Anovulation (PCOS), excess peripheral estrogen production (obesity), a longer reproductive span (late menopause) and estrogen-secreting tumors (granulosa cell tumor) all allow prolonged estrogen stimulation. This explains their shared association with endometrial hyperplasia and endometrioid (type I) endometrial carcinoma. Type II (serous) endometrial carcinoma is not estrogen-driven and arises in atrophic endometrium.

Adipose tissue aromatase converts androgens to estrone, and obesity is often accompanied by anovulation, increasing unopposed estrogen.
A later menopause extends the years of endogenous estrogen exposure, including anovulatory perimenopausal cycles without progesterone.
Granulosa cell tumors of the ovary secrete estrogen, which can cause endometrial hyperplasia, abnormal bleeding or precocious puberty.

revised.explanation: Under the US Medical Eligibility Criteria, each is Category 4 (unacceptable health risk) for estrogen-containing contraception because estrogen adds arterial or venous thrombotic risk.
revised.detail: Estrogen increases hepatic production of clotting factors and raises the risk of venous thromboembolism, stroke and myocardial infarction. Conditions with existing high thrombotic or arterial risk, such as acute DVT or PE, migraine with aura, history of stroke and ischemic heart disease, are therefore Category 4 for combined pills, patch and ring. A history of DVT with low recurrence risk is Category 3. Progestin-only methods and copper IUDs are generally acceptable alternatives.

tiles: Reduced or absent Doppler blood flow
original.explanation: Spermatic cord twisting (often a bell-clapper deformity) produces sudden severe pain, a high-riding/transverse testis, an absent cremasteric reflex, and reduced or absent intratesticular flow on color Doppler (sensitivity ~90-100%).

revised.title: Classic clues to testicular torsion
revised.explanation: Twisting of the spermatic cord, often with a bell-clapper deformity, causes sudden severe scrotal pain, a high-riding testis, loss of the cremasteric reflex and reduced or absent blood flow on color Doppler.
revised.detail: Testicular torsion is a surgical emergency, most common in adolescents, in which rotation of the spermatic cord obstructs venous outflow and then arterial inflow. Testicular salvage is highest with detorsion within about 6 hours. The bell-clapper deformity, inadequate fixation of the testis to the tunica vaginalis, allows the testis to rotate and lie horizontally. Epididymitis is the main look-alike: onset is more gradual, the cremasteric reflex is usually preserved, pain may ease with elevation (Prehn sign), and Doppler flow is increased. Clinical suspicion should not be delayed for imaging, and partial torsion can show some flow.
tileNotes: Abrupt onset of severe unilateral scrotal pain, often with nausea and vomiting, reflects acute ischemia from cord twisting.
Shortening of the twisted cord pulls the testis up, and it often lies horizontally because of a bell-clapper deformity.
Stroking the inner thigh normally elevates the testis. The reflex is usually absent on the affected side in torsion.
Color Doppler ultrasound shows decreased or absent intratesticular blood flow. Normal flow does not exclude partial or intermittent torsion.

revised.title: Drugs associated with pulmonary fibrosis
revised.explanation: Each drug can cause drug-induced lung injury that progresses to pulmonary fibrosis.
revised.detail: Drug-induced pulmonary fibrosis presents with progressive dyspnea, dry cough, restrictive spirometry and reduced DLCO. Bleomycin and busulfan are antineoplastic agents, amiodarone is an antiarrhythmic and nitrofurantoin is an antibiotic. Methotrexate and carmustine are also associated with lung toxicity, though methotrexate mainly causes hypersensitivity pneumonitis. Pulmonary function testing is used to monitor at-risk patients.

Amiodarone, an iodine-rich antiarrhythmic, accumulates in lung tissue and can cause interstitial pneumonitis progressing to fibrosis. Patients need baseline and follow-up pulmonary function tests.
Long-term nitrofurantoin use, typically for urinary tract infection prophylaxis, can cause chronic interstitial pneumonitis and fibrosis.
Busulfan, an alkylating agent used in conditioning before stem cell transplant, can cause pulmonary fibrosis ('busulfan lung').

original.title: Factors shifting the oxygen dissociation curve right
original.explanation: Each reduces hemoglobin oxygen affinity and promotes oxygen unloading at a given oxygen tension.

entries.source: Bootcamp.com Pulmonology.pdf; Respiratory Physiology Part Two - Blood > Hemoglobin; PDF p. 28

proposal.why: Removes the repeated 'Increased' stem using standard equivalent terms.

revised.title: Factors shifting the oxygen dissociation curve right
revised.explanation: Each lowers hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, raising the P50 and promoting oxygen unloading to tissues at a given oxygen tension.
revised.detail: A right shift helps deliver oxygen to metabolically active tissue, which is acidic, warm and rich in CO2. Hydrogen ions and CO2 stabilize the deoxygenated (T) form of hemoglobin (the Bohr effect), heat reduces oxygen binding, and 2,3-BPG binds deoxyhemoglobin and reduces its affinity; 2,3-BPG rises with chronic hypoxia, high altitude and anemia. The left-shift factors are the mirror image (alkalemia, hypothermia, hypocapnia, low 2,3-BPG), plus fetal hemoglobin and carbon monoxide.
tileNotes: A lower pH stabilizes the deoxygenated form of hemoglobin, reducing oxygen affinity (the Bohr effect).
A higher temperature, as in exercising muscle or fever, weakens the hemoglobin-oxygen bond and favors unloading.
Increased CO2 lowers pH and forms carbamino compounds with hemoglobin, both reducing oxygen affinity.
2,3-bisphosphoglycerate binds deoxyhemoglobin and stabilizes the T state. Levels rise in chronic hypoxia, high altitude and anemia.

original.title: Factors shifting the oxygen dissociation curve left

proposal.why: Removes the 'Decreased' stem with standard terms, and replacing the mirror-image 2,3-BPG tile with fetal hemoglobin (a classic, certain left shift) makes it less mechanical.

entries.auditNote: Three tiles start with 'Decreased'; the set is a straight mirror image of the right-shift list.

revised.title: Factors shifting the oxygen dissociation curve left
revised.explanation: Each increases hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, lowering the P50 and reducing oxygen unloading to tissues at a given oxygen tension.
revised.detail: A left-shifted curve means hemoglobin holds oxygen more tightly. Alkalemia, low CO2 and cold all favor the oxygenated (R) state, the reverse of the Bohr effect. Fetal hemoglobin (alpha2 gamma2) binds 2,3-BPG poorly, giving it a higher oxygen affinity than maternal adult hemoglobin, which lets the fetus extract oxygen across the placenta. Carbon monoxide, methemoglobin and low 2,3-BPG also shift the curve left.
tileNotes: A higher pH reduces stabilization of deoxyhemoglobin, increasing oxygen affinity.
Lower temperature strengthens oxygen binding to hemoglobin and reduces unloading.
Low CO2 raises pH and reduces carbamino formation, increasing oxygen affinity.
Fetal hemoglobin has gamma chains that bind 2,3-BPG weakly, so its oxygen affinity is higher and its curve lies to the left of adult hemoglobin.

revised.title: Obstructive lung diseases
revised.explanation: Each disease limits expiratory airflow, producing a reduced FEV1/FVC ratio, through loss of elastic recoil, mucus obstruction or bronchoconstriction.
revised.detail: Obstructive diseases reduce FEV1 more than FVC, so the FEV1/FVC ratio falls, and air trapping raises total lung capacity and residual volume. Asthma is characteristically reversible with bronchodilators, while emphysema and chronic bronchitis (COPD) are largely irreversible. Cystic fibrosis causes obstruction through thick mucus and bronchiectasis. Restrictive diseases (pulmonary fibrosis, neuromuscular weakness) are the contrast: total lung capacity is reduced with a normal or increased FEV1/FVC.
tileNotes: Destruction of alveolar walls reduces elastic recoil, so small airways collapse on expiration. Diffusing capacity is reduced.
Chronic productive cough for at least 3 months in each of 2 consecutive years, with mucus gland hypertrophy narrowing the airways.
Reversible bronchoconstriction, airway inflammation and mucus plugging cause episodic obstruction that improves with bronchodilators.
CFTR dysfunction produces thick mucus, recurrent infection and bronchiectasis, causing progressive obstructive lung disease.

revised.detail: Squamous cell carcinoma usually arises in a central bronchus in smokers and is the lung cancer most likely to cavitate as its center necroses. Histology shows keratinization (keratin pearls) and intercellular bridges, which are desmosomes between tumor cells. PTHrP secretion causes humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy. Adenocarcinoma, the main contrast, is typically peripheral, is the most common type in nonsmokers, and shows glands or mucin.

The tumor typically arises in a central (hilar) bronchus and is strongly associated with smoking.
Tumor secretion of parathyroid hormone-related peptide causes humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy.

revised.title: QT-prolonging drugs
revised.explanation: Each prolongs the QT interval, mainly by blocking cardiac potassium channels, raising the risk of torsades de pointes.
revised.detail: Drug-induced QT prolongation usually comes from blockade of the delayed rectifier potassium current (hERG/IKr), which slows ventricular repolarization. Classic offenders include class IA and III antiarrhythmics, macrolide and fluoroquinolone antibiotics, antipsychotics, antidepressants, azole antifungals, and antiemetics such as ondansetron. Risk rises with hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and use of several QT-prolonging drugs together.

Macrolide antibiotics such as erythromycin and azithromycin block the delayed rectifier potassium current and prolong the QT interval.
Fluoroquinolones such as levofloxacin and moxifloxacin prolong the QT interval, especially with other risk factors.
A 5-HT3 antagonist antiemetic that causes dose-related QT prolongation, a standard warning especially with IV dosing.

revised.title: Cyanotic congenital heart disease

revised.detail: Cyanotic lesions send deoxygenated blood to the body. They include the classic 5 Ts (tetralogy, transposition, truncus, tricuspid atresia, total anomalous pulmonary venous return) and others such as pulmonary atresia and hypoplastic left heart syndrome, all targets of newborn pulse oximetry screening for critical congenital heart disease. entries.subject: Dermatology, Heme/Onc

original.title: Skin cancers
original.explanation: All are skin malignancies linked to UV exposure, ranging from the most common and indolent (BCC) to the most aggressive (melanoma, Merkel cell). Merkel cell carcinoma is also driven by a polyomavirus.
tileExplanations: Most common; pearly papule with rolled borders and telangiectasias; rarely metastasizes.
Ulcerated or scaly lesion that can arise from actinic keratosis; can metastasize.
Pigmented lesion (ABCDE); prognosis by Breslow depth; high metastatic potential.
Rare, aggressive neuroendocrine tumor linked to UV damage and Merkel cell polyomavirus.

revised.title: UV-associated skin cancers
revised.explanation: Each is a skin malignancy for which ultraviolet exposure is a major risk factor, ranging from the most common and indolent (BCC) to aggressive tumors (melanoma, Merkel cell).
revised.detail: Ultraviolet light damages keratinocyte and melanocyte DNA, forming pyrimidine dimers, and is the main risk factor for BCC, SCC, and melanoma. Merkel cell carcinoma is linked to both UV damage and Merkel cell polyomavirus and is more common in immunosuppressed patients. Kaposi sarcoma (HHV-8), mycosis fungoides (cutaneous T-cell lymphoma), and dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans are skin cancers that are not UV-driven.
tileNotes: Most common; pearly papule with rolled borders and telangiectasias; rarely metastasizes.
Ulcerated or scaly lesion that can arise from actinic keratosis; can metastasize.
Pigmented lesion (ABCDE); prognosis by Breslow depth; high metastatic potential.
Rare, aggressive neuroendocrine tumor linked to UV damage and Merkel cell polyomavirus.

entries.subject: Dermatology, Immunology

original.title: Severe cutaneous drug reactions
original.explanation: These are the severe cutaneous adverse drug reactions (SCARs), each with a distinct picture. SJS and TEN cause epidermal detachment and mucositis, DRESS causes a rash with eosinophilia and internal organ involvement, and AGEP causes sterile pustules with fever and neutrophilia.
tileExplanations: Epidermal detachment of <10% of body surface area with mucosal involvement, usually drug-triggered.
The severe end of the SJS spectrum, with detachment of >30% of BSA.
Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms: rash, fever, eosinophilia and organ (often liver) involvement 2 to 6 weeks after the drug.
Many small sterile non-follicular pustules on red skin with fever and neutrophilia, appearing within days of the drug.
